_ - - - - - THE Lik3/Ettr OF A CAGED LARK. Ye lovely skies of azure hue, Ye fields where, joyous, once I flew, Ye little streamlets dear; Have I then sung my last adieu? Shall I no more see aught of you Am I a pris'ner here? qbaii I again ascend. At break of day, triy voice to blena With others tuneful song. The sun will oft again arise, But never more will meet my eyes, That here for Naturefong. By copses green and sparkling brook, My course each sunny day I took, But now my flights are o'er; . Oh, corn-fields line and woodland gay! Oh, hedges rich with ro:e or may! I ne'er shall see you more. What do I care for cage of gold,', For softest nest for seed untold? They mean captivity! Who will my sorrow, pitying see? Let him give priceless joy to me— Glee me my liberty! —Little Folks' Magazine.

word of one °Meer Would be taken, and the governor or director would profess his implicit belief in it, in preference to the oaths of fifty prisoners. But it is not exactly safe for a warder to get the name of being a tyrant on the works; or he may some day be dropped on, and by a well-laid scheme be either injured or killed, the occurrence being— apparently—a pure accident. One such case of revenge lies been well authenticated. An apothecary in the prison infir- mary, at Dartmoor, was a terrible tyrant, and made himself obnoxious to everyone, both officers and convicts. It seems he was in the habit of taking every morning a "screw," in the shape of a little dose of bitters, to correct tlte effects of the last evening's festivities. At a public-house in Prince's Town, the officers of the prison meet of an evening, and over their pipes and grog, or beer, relate the little incidents of 1 the day, and crack their jokes about having served this fel- low out, got that chap a dose he didn't relish, and " run " somebody in. Some officers hardly ever had a comfortablei dinner-hour, as they had reports of some poor beggar of al convict or another every day, and when together in the evenings boasted of their doings. So also did Master Apothe'cary : and too often his indulgence in glasses of something short, on these occasions, necessitated a " screw " in the mo•ning to counteract the effects of his little sprees, and enable him to pull himself together before going his rounds with the doctor. He, himself, took care to mix his special bottle of "pick me up,"!-and kept it in his compound- ing room, on a certain shelf nearest the door, the first of a row of sin•ilar bottles. One morning, he came into the prison as usual, poured out his customary pick me up," and swallowed it. A moment afterwards he knew that he had not got his proper medicine, and he called out, "lie's done for me; he's done for me; send for Doctor Howell." The doctor was sent for; the hospital warders and orderlies did what they could for him, or made a show of doing so. But he rapidly got worse ; went into fits of contortions; and as the doctor entered the room the man died, his body drawn up in such a way as needed no examination of the bottle to find tbat he had swallowed such a dose of strychnine as would have poisoned twenty men. The first bottle on the shelf contained the poison ; the very next bottle contained his own mixture. Whether he or some warder had acciden- tally misplaced and changed the bottles, or whether some convict had intentionally done it, was never known. There were plenty about the place who were quite capable of doing so, and there were many opportunities for effecting such a change. The room in which the drugs were kept was at the end of a large ward, and in full view of every bed and its occupant. Every prisoner in those beds must have seen'him each morning taking his "pick me up," and nothing would be easier than for some man to have slipped out of bed, night or day, and change the bottles. The cruelties practised at Dartmoor by warders and doc- tors. as witnessed by Mr. Davitt, are enough to make one's blood boil with indignation. Davitt declares that he often saw warders strike prisoners in Partmoor. In one case a man named Rustta, an Italian, who had been sentenced to five years' penal servitude, whilst confined in Woking con- vict prison, made an attempt on the life of the governor by 1 striking him with a sharpened nail one morning on coming out of chapel ; he was tried again and got 20 years' penal servitude. When Davitt was at Milbank, serving his nine months' probation, he noticed that Rustta was almost con- stantly under punishment. A convict who assaults an officer, to whatever prison he may afterwards be sent, will find tliat his character as a dangerous man goes with him; and warders appear to take a fiendish delight in torturing such men in every possible way. On Davitt being removed to Dartmoor, he found Rustta already there. He was shortly afterwards found with a large nail in his possession, and it being probably suspected that he intended to commit another assault with it, he was sentenced to 28 days' bread and wate-. This meant three days' bread and water, then one day's penal class diet; then three days' bread and water again, and so on, till the month's punishment was over. What became of him for the next 18 months, Davitt did not know, but when next he saw the man he had lost his right arm. The man had been in the punishment cells most of the time, with an occasional day or two's interval in the hospital, of course on low diet. It is well-known that Dart- moor is a very damp prison, and the cells under the infir- mary, in which refractory patients are punished, are quite wet. As a rule, prisoners in the puishment cells walk about to put on the time ; but Rustta was too weak to walk about much, and he passed his time moodily leaning against the walls. In some way or other, how, Davitt was not informed, mortification set in in the man's arm, and it had to be ampu- tated. Surely that would suffice to stop the tyranny of those warders who were apparently determined to punish him in as many ways as possible. But it was not so. Af er the loss of his arm, he was attached to the tailors' party., tlt will naturally be wondered what a man with one arm could do in a tailor's shop. He probably made prison bras—of two strips of cloth stitched together, the material being pinned to the knee of his trousers while he slowly and laboriously stitched it with his one hand. His constant punishments of bread and water had so weakened him, that one day; on *parade, he could not keep up with the rest Of his party, and the brutal warder struck him on the shoulder of the arm that had been amputated. poor Rustta fell down on the parade ground, and the warder was reprimanded by his superior. But the system of punishment for trivial offences, and no offences at all, went on all the same, and about four months afterwards Rustta died, a victim to that tyranny which, in every convict prison, is the fate of a con- vict who commits an assault upon an officer. If he gets through the ordeal to which he will inevitably be subjedted to whatever prison he may be sent, it will be because he has a constitution of iron, strength and skill sufficient to enable 1 him to perform any task which may be put upon him, and the patience of Job, to submit to all kinds of insults and injustice. If, with these, the convict is imbued with a reso- lute determination not to allow the warders to get lihn into trouble, he may, in time, lose the character of a "screw Ismasher," the appellation bestowed on the convict who is foolish enough to strike, or attempt to strike, a prison officer. Davitt saw other instances ef gross cruelty at Dartmoor, such as, with his strong hatred of oppression, must have made his blood boil. The gross negligence shown by the doctors, led to the deaths of men, who, if they had been treated properly, might have lived to be released, and died surrounded by their friends. One man named Madden was often seen to fall out on the parade ground in the morning, to see the doctor. He was never admitted to the infirmary, the doctor probably telling him there was nothing the mat- ter with him, a customary thing, unless the man'adisease or ailment could be seen. One morning the man dropped dead on parade ;. a striking comment on the doctor's ability! Another convict, named Mason, employed in a cart party, often complained of something wrong in his inside which he could not define, and asked the doctor what it was. Of course he was told it was nothing beyond his own imagination; but he died suddenly from ossification of the lungs. _

Mr. Davitt was half-starved at Dartmoti`r, too rooa not being at all sufficient for a man of his physique. But be has never admitted trying to eat any of the substitutes which other convicts used to make up their supply of food. It mav seem preposterous, but it is nevertheless true, that convicts have been seen eating dead mice, candles, rats, grass, dogs, earth, worma, and other equally disgusting things. It will readily be understood what a terrible punish- ment bread and water diet is to convicts suffering the pangs of hunger to such an extent as to cause them to eat such disgusting things. -

Ar; F 2 ELY LATE:Z.—Mr. J. Irving, of Leagram Lodge, Chipping, writes to us :—" I have a young pullet of the Cuckoo Creel breed. She laid her first egg on the Bth inst. The hen that hatched her was set on the 10th March last, and she was hatched on the 2nd April. Consequently, she was just 18 weeks and one day old when he laid her first egg. I have never known a hen to ley at so early an age." The comparative values of store lambs within living memory, pays the Newcastle Journal, are somewhat as- tounding. According to the report of a recent lamb sale at Kelso, lambs were selling at £2 6s. 6d. per head, whereas Mr. John Scott, of the late firm of John and Andrew Scott, cattle selsamen, and his late father, Mr. Robert Scott, have S lid fairly good lambs at Newcastle-on-Tyne, within the lest sixty years, at the odd six shillings and sixpence, a difference of 40s. per head. CLEANLINESS AT MILKING TIME —The sides and udder of every cow should, before milking, be thoroughly brushed and cleansed of everything that can fall into the milk pail. The farmer should place over the can which is to convey his milk two cloth strainers, of unequal thickness, the thicker one being below the other. The lower one is best made of thick woollen flannel. A woollen strainer will often take out a good deal of ,foreign matter that a linen or a cotton one would let through. As often as matter accu- mulates upon them they should be turned over and rinsed till they are clean. This would be but a small item for each dairyman to do, and it would make a material differ- eace in the quality of the butter or che.ese that is to be made from it. This little attention to cleanliness would, like every other tidy act connected with the dairy, pay well in the long run, because it would make the goods so much more satisfactory and desirable. The Paris police have just made a very successful raid upon the milkmen, who have long been suspected of mixing • water with milk when it arrives at the Betignolles Station from farms in the country. The milk cans are all unloaded in a large warehouse at the side of the station, and five•aed- twetVy policemen were posted outside, loopholes having been made in the wall to enable thorn to watch the move- ments of the milkmen. Just when they had brought in the water and /ere beginning to make their customary mixture the police rushed in aad caught them. They were at first inclined to resist, bat the presence of the Commissary with his tricolor scarf seems to have overawed them, and they allowed him to mike a very important capture. They were also feund to have a large quantity of bi-carbonate of lime, together with a contrivance for removing the sealed covers which some of the milk cans have, and for putting them on agein after the contents have been adulterated. _

"OUR OLD NOBILITY.' - [Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistook-street, London, MC., and reprinted by permission.]- THE BOYLES.

"Treason, sacrilege, and proscription," says Gibbon, "are often the best titles of ancient nobility." The Boyles are not very ancient, but to them the third item in this state- ment is most appropriate. In the present paper lam speaking exclusively of the Irish Boyles; the Boyles Earls of Glasgow are quite a distinct house. Until the time of Elizabeth the ancestors of the Earl of Cork and Orrery and of the Earl of Shannon were an obscure Herefordshire family. In that reign the founder of the hoc se, a younger son of a younger son, was a law student in Ilindon, so impecunious that he was unable to continue his studies, and therefore resolved to become an adventurer in Ireland. One of his descendants, the present Earl of Cork and Orrery has in
Cork 19,689 acres. Kerry 11,552 „ Limerick Wexford Somerset
T0ta1...37,632 „ with a rent-roll of £9,16.

Another descendant, the Earl of Shannon, has 12,743 acres in Cork, with a rent-roll of £9,322. The first Earl of Cork, who arrived in Ireland in 1588—less than three hundred years ago—tells us in his autobiography, "All my wealth was £27 3s. in money, a diamond ring, a bracelet of gold, a taffety doublet, a pair of black-velvet breeches laced and cut upon taffety, two cloaks, competent linen and necessaries, with my rapier and dagger." A modest inventory this; he was very much like the typical country boy, who reaches London with the traditional half-crown in his pocket. How- ever, like the " undertakers''—most appropriate name—who went over to Ireland in Elizabeth's reign, in order to enrich themselves, he did not very long remain in this impecunious condition, and before his death he could compute his income at £5O a day, exclusive of houses and parks. Boyle had not been long in Ireland when he laid the, foundation of his fortunes by a marriage with a Limerick heiress, who brought him an estate of £5OO per annum. His rise was so rapid that his purchases of lands excited the un- founded suspicion that he was in the pay of Spain, and he came over to England to justify himself. After a short imprisonment he was released. by El iziabeth. and appointed Clerk of the Council in Munster. The rebellion of Fitz- gerald, Earl of Desniond, though a misfor une to Boyle at the oatset, proved in the end to be greatly to his advantage, as he obtained a large part of the confiscated Desmond pro- p3rly Sir Walter Raleigh, too, who had acquired consider- able lands in Munster, in 1602, sold them to Boyle for the small sum of £1,500. This property, the greater part of which is now in the possession of the Duke of Devonshire, is woit'i considerably more than £30,000 per annum. Later on he appears to have obtained grants of land as assignee of Carew and others. He also obtained by purchase the estate of Marston, in Somerset, which is still the seat of the family. Boyle, who had been created Earl of Cork, in his old age assisted Charles I. in preparing for his expedition against' the Scots at a cost of £20,000, a very large sum in those days. lam not surprised at his rapid acquisition of con- fiscated lands, but looking at his purchases, the lavish scale of his expenditure, and his pecuniary assistance to Charles 1., and to the poverty of Ireland, I cannot understand whence he obtained so much money. From an English point of view, it was no wonder that he became known as "the great Earl of Cork;" but the Irish must have regarded him very much as a Zulu dispossessed of his lands regards a Dutch Boer. An inquiry having been made into the con- dition of Munster in 1611, it was reported that al Lord Cork's lands were inhabited by English. We are also told that "he encouraged the settlement of Protestants, the suppression of Popery, and the transportation of many septa and barbarous clans from the fruitful province of Leinster into the wilds of Kerry "—very agreeably, no doubt, to the new colonists of the fruitful province, but very much to the disadvantage of those who were driven away to the wilds.

Brian/um Mats - Da the best we can, we c ennot by any device yet contrived remove from milk all that is de- sirable to get out of it to make it the most wholesome and palatable food it is susceptible of being, or to fit it for making the hest possible products of butter or cheese, eve. cially the latter. The objectionable matters in milk are not confined ta what falls into it after it is out of the udder. It contains considerable matter foreign to its necessary consti- tuents when it comes from the mammary glands. The cen- trifuge, which makes an instantaneous separation of cream from the rest of the milk, demonstrates this very frilly. By rapidly rotating milk in a suitably constructed vessel, the heavier parts are, by the centrifugal force developed, thrown to the outer part of the vessel, and the cream or lighter part into the centre. After rotating rapidly for a certain length of time, there collects on the side of the vessel most distant from the centre a coating of solid matter, which varies in quantity in different samples of milk. It averages, per- haps, 1 lb. to 1,000 lbs. of milk. It is a small percentage, but it is enough to mould the character of the milk. When examined with a microscope, it is found to be composed of fragments of half-dissolved membranes, which have probably came from the rapidly-wasting structure of the milk glands, bits of solid casein, and particles of another albaminoed known as leucin, along with specks of dirt, duet, hair, etc., which have fallen into it in handling. From the great rapidity with which this matter goes to decay, it is prob- ably loaded with organic germs. At any rate, it goes into destruntive decomposition at once, and in a few hours turns dark, like mortifying flesh, and becomes extremely offen- sive. The milk thus freed from this decaying matter assumes a new and delicious flavour it did Rot possess be- fore. Both the cream and skim milk obtained from the centrifuge have a characteristic delicacy of taste which , does not belong to them when obtained in the usual way. Milk filtered through pulverised charcoal takes on the same I peculiar relish, and the matter separated by the coal decom- poses with the same haste and offensiveness as that obtained from the side of the centrifuge. Some rapid, cheap, and efficient means of ridding milk of this extraneous matter, so prone to swift decay, is a desideratum. Whenever this separation is effected, milk will assume a new value as food and a sanitary agent. That it will be done there can hardly be a doubt; bat at present we have no means of straining out such minute particles. The strainers in use are not fine enough to arrest them, and they glide through without hindrance. In the meantime, no effort should be spared on the part of dairymen or factory men to strain out every- thing that can possibly be separated, with a view to greater cleanliness, and to advancing the quality and value of dairy products. To tolerate a plain defect in cleanliness, and allow it to grow into use, is not only unjust to consumers, but is impolitic for producers and dangerous to the whole dairy interest, from its tendency to stimulate the produc- tion of artificial products, against which such charges may not lie.—Lire Stock Journal.

The Earl of Cork appears to have taken particular care of his relatives. His brother obtained two Irish Bishoprics— Cork and Coyne, and Ross. Another relative became Archbishop of Tuam, and yet another Bishop of Water- ford. Somewhat later one of the descendants of the priestly Boyles became Archbishop of Armagh, and obtained a considerable grant of lands in Wicklow. Subsequently he became Lord Chanca or of Ireland, and his son, who inherited his estates, was created Viscount Blesinton, a title now extinct. The sons of the first Earl of Cork inherited the abilities or the good luck of their father. Three of them were created Irish peers in his lifetime, and the fifth, Robert Boyle, dis- tinguished for his reputation as a philosopher, more than once refused a peerage. The second son, Viscount Boyle, was killed in the Irish Rebellion of 1642. The eldest son (afterwards second Earl) further advanced his fortunes by a marriage with the daughter and heiress of Clifford. Earl of Cumberland, who possessed large property in the North of England. He took the Royalist side in the Civil War, but contrived to escape the sequestration of his estates, and after the Restoration was appointed Lord High Treasurer of Ireland, and was created Earl of Burlington. His great- grandson, the fourth Earl, claimed and obtained the ancient barony of Clifford, and at his death his daughter and only child, who married a Duke of Devonshire, carried the Clifford property and part of the Irish estates to the Cavendishes. He was distinguished for his architectural taste, and was the builder of Old Burlington House in Pic- cadilly; Cork-street is still to be found at the end of the Burlington Arcade. Burlington House, as well as Chiswick House which had been acquired by purchase, passed to the Cavendish

At the death of this Earl the Cork title and estates passed to the Earl of Orrery, whose descendants still possess both tides. We must now go back to the third son of the first Earl who in his father's lifetime had been created Lord Broghill, and who was a conspicuous figure in the time of the Commonwealth. Frequent allusions are made to him in Cromwell's letters, he having been one of the Protector's principal lieutenants in the subjugation of Ireland. He was a prominent member of Cromwell's first Parliament, and sat upon the Committee on Kingship, to which scheme he was strongly favourable; if we may trust a family chaplain, with the base design of making Cromwell unpopular. From the Cromwell Parliament he obtained two grants of con- fiscated lands, one to the value of £l,OOO per annum, and the other of 2,000 acres of cultivated soil. After the Pro- tector's death, Lord Broghill sent his younger brother to invite Charles 11. over to Ireland, for which service the said brother was created Viscount Shannon at the Restoration, a title which expired with his grandson. Broghill himself was created Earl of Orrery, and appointed to a number of lucrative offices in Ireland. Like the aristocratic Protestants of the time of the Tudors, the aristocratic Puritans of the time of the Stuarts were quite ready to make their convic- tions subordinate to their interests. Broghill had much more substantial rewards than an earldom. Besides his numerous offices, he had five grants under the Irish Act of Settlement, which, by the way, was drawn upby his own hand. He also farmed the excise of beer and spirits in Ire- land, and on the suppression of his office as President of Munster he obtained a pension of £BOO per annum. Later on I find him obtaining a grant of £5,000, and of £5OO per annum from Crown lands.

Another thing of which Mr. Davitt complains was the great and culpable indifference shown with regard to the lives of the convicts so far as ensuring immunity for acci- dents whilst at work. The Convict Prison Department have constantly been compelled to enlarge old convict prisons or build new ones since transportation was abolished. New wings have been added at Pentonville, Irrixton, Chatham, Dartmoor, Portsmouth, Portland, and Woking, and a new prison at Wormwood Scrubs. Daring the build- ing of a new wing at Dartmoor the superintendence of the scaffolding and other matters of a similarly important nature were entrusted to an ex "bog-trotter,' a man who bad previously to entering the convict 2Prvice been a turf cutter on his native bogs. What could such a man be ex- pected to know about scaffolding? And yet the lives of the bricklayers and hod-carriers were placed in his hands, with the almost inevitable result that one morning the scaffolding gave way, and three convicts were killed—sent to their account without any chance of redeeming their lost characters, or showing that their sorrow and remorse were sincere. If such a man as the " bog-trotter " warder I were employed to superintend the erection of scaffolding ' whereon free men were to work, and the loss of three lives resulted from his sheer ignorance of his duties, would the public be satisfied unless a verdict of manslaughter were brought against somebody—either the incompetent scaffold superintendent or those who appointed him? Inside the walls of a convict prison, however, public opinion cannot penetrate. When a man dies, either from disease, accident, or from excessive punishment on starvation diet, a jury is composed of persons who are almost all connected in some way with the prison, and they naturally side with' the prison anthorities, and come to the very convenient decision either that the man died from "natural causes," or, in case of accident, that no one was in the least to blame.

How TO DRESS RATIONALLY. —R ;Omni dress must be hygienic, and hygienic dress must be rational and attrac- tive. To Insure complete success the reforms of both must be brought about as quietly and undemonstratively as pos. Bible. Certain old superstitions will, have to be exploded, such as—that warmth is only secured by repeated layers of clothe., without any regard to their heat-retaining powers, or that very loose or very tight coverings increase the temperature ; that the eTposure of one part of the body is compensated for by the addition of extra clothing on an- other, particularly when the parts exposed are often the most vital, where consumption first begins; that because it Is urgently recommended to renounce tight-lacing, and un- equal pressure anywhere, human pillows tied in the middle must inevitably be the result; tbat when it is suggested to chaDge or divide the under-skirt in such a way as to secure freer action in walking, women should be instantly accused of launching into masculine attire.—Cassell's Family Maya- fine.

THE VIOLIN FOR GIRLS.—The rage for teaching girls the violin, which at present exists in England, is little more than a fashion, and, unless it is directed with more know. ledge and care on the part of parents than most of them now show, it will die like one. And we are not quite clear that, if this cars is withheld, a more suitable and salutary end could overtake it. A new terror would be added to society were every budding miss, no better instructed in the art than under the present regime she is likely to be, permitted or required to compel the silence of the drawing. room while she scraped out one of Bellini's airs with varia- tions. But if the movement be intelligently guided—if parents will insist that their daughters be taught the art of violin.playing, and not merely to play tunes on the violin If their music is truly pursued as an art, and not as a mere accomplishment—if practice on the violin is as vigorously exacted as practice on the piano, or as the study of French, German, or history—if the teachers will be stern, conscien- tious and inflexible, and at the same time impart to their pupils that ardour and enthusiasm for the instrument with- out which the study of it is like the passage of an arid and endless desert—then, indeed, the movement is one which we hail with abundant pleasure, and for which we both desire and anticipate success. It will indefinitely extend the horizon of domestic music, which is far too limited in this country. It will open up to young ladies the treasures of the stringed music of the great writers—treasures of which they aro now, for the moat part, ignorant. It will enable them to enjoy the great pleasure of playing in symphony parties where the great orchestral works are performed, and we may whisper the hope that they will gradually improve I, these meetings. Above all, they will be enabled to take part ' in quartet-playing, which is perhaps one of the purest and most delightful pleasures life affords, one of the strongest incentives to study, and one of its sweetest rewards. The string quartet is not, by a hundredth part, as common in this country as it should be; and any movement which . promises to place it within the reach of young ladies, and of A larger number of our young people generally, cannot be too strongly commended-. But, as we have before said, it must be intelligently, earnestly, and vigorously directed.— Cassell's Family Magazine. • Thereon why so many are unable to take Cocoa Is that tha varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plee 4 rendering them soluble; while really making them thick,-heavy, and indigalt`ble. The fourth Earl of Orrery was a distinguished scholar, who bequAthed his library and philosophical instrumenits to Christ Church College, Oxford, where he was educated, and after whom Mr. George Graham, the inventer of "The Orrery," bestowed the name on that astronomical instru- ment. His son, the fifth Earl, as I have already indicated, became also fifth Earl of Cork. A younger grandson of Lord Broghill, first Earl of Orrery, after filling the offices of 'Speaker of the Irish House of Commons, Chancellor of the Exch.quer, and Lord Justice, was elevated to the Irish Peer-, age under the title of Earl of Shannon. His descendent sits in the House of Lords under the English title of Baron Carleton, and possesses 12,743 acres in Cork, with a rent-roll of £9322.

As before remarked, Davitt was in many ways treated with exceptional harshness at Dartmo)r. He was more strictly watched than any other prisoner; and while con- forming to the prison rules to the very letter, he was deprived of the privileges to which by such conformity he was entitled. For instance, while other convicts were allowed visits by their friends, twice, thrice, or four times a year, according to the class the convict is in, Davitt was no t allowed to have a single visit during the whole of his im- prisonment. Davitt principally corresponded with his mother, who was in America, but he also received three lett.rs from friends who were not relatives, in reply to letters written by him. But be was not allowed to see any cf these friends.

Apart from the unquestionable wrongs which the Irish have had to endure at the hands.of successive generations of confiscators, the world has not had much reason to regret the rise of the Boyles to affluence-and power. Literature, art, and science have found in them earnest patrons and even ardent votaries. One of them obtained an elaborate eulogy from Burnet; another was complimented as "the generous Burlington" by Gay; another was the friend of Swift; and yet another the friend of Pope, to.:whom the poet dedicated his essay on "Taste," and wrote a number of letters. Lord Beaconsfield has told us, in one of his earlier works, that "greatness no longer depends on rentals, the world is too rich; nor on pedigrees, the world is too knowing ;" and this truth the Boyles have generally appeared to recognise. In more recent times the Boyles have hardly retained the prominent position they formerly occupied ; but the present Earl of Cor4 is known as one of the most consistent and active members of the Liberal party._

Mr. Davitt speaks very stroni,ly on the fact that a convict, once he dons the striped grey dresN loses all right of redress for any wrongs he may suffer at the hands of the warders. No notice whatever is taken of any statement he may make to the governor; in fact, such a mode of tryinc, to obtain re- dress, almost certainly results in a convict being punished for bringing unfounded charges against an officer. Governors of convict prisons do not scruple to declare that when a man becomes a convict, he is necessarilyi placed in such a position that under no 'conceivable position l's his word to be believed, as compared with the word of an officer. Prism warders are soppesd never to strike convicts, except in self-defence, yet they do so with impunity, a mere denial being sufficient to exculpate them if complaint is made. While Divitt was at Dartmoor, he saw a principal warder (a suoerior officer) knock down a youth with the butt end (.f a rifle. The officer had told the boy (Pavia so styles him, but no convicts under seventeen are sent to Dartmoor) that he would report him for not attending to his work properly., I he boy, who was of an excitable temper, attempted to strike the principal warder with a hay rake, and was immediately felled with the butt end of a ride. Five rilm in the party cried " Shame "

who, however, did not resign the latter post and the effice of Chief Secretary was filled by the appointment of Lord Frederick Cavendish, hitherto Finance Secretary to the Treasury. A few hours after being sworn into office, the latter gentleman was murdered in Phoenix Park, Dublin. Lord Frederick Cavendish was succeeded at the Irish Office by Mr. George Otto Trevelyan, who had hitherto filled the office of Secretary to the Admiralty, while a successor for Mr. Trevelyan at the Admiralty was found in Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, who had previously acted as Finance Secretary to the War Office. The post which Lord Frederick Cavendish had vacated on his ap- pointment-as Irish Secretary, viz., that of Financial Secre- tary to the Treasury, was accepted by Mr. L. H. Courtney, the Under Secretary for the Colonies; while the Honourable Evelyn Ashley, Secretary to the Board of Trade, succeeded Mr. Courtney at the Colonial Office. At the War Office, ' Sir Arthur Divett Hayter, one of the Lords of the Treasury, took the post vacated by Mr. Campbell-Bannerman; while Mr. John Holms, also a Lord of the Treasury, was appointed secretary to the Board of Trade, in succession to Mr. Ashley. The two lordships of the Treasury thus vacated were filled respectively by the appointment of Mr. Herbert Gladstone and Mr. R. W. Doff, member for Banffshire. The other Cabinet Minister, Mr. John Bright, Chancellor of the Ducky Df Lancaster, retired in the midlle of July, being unable to agree in the active Egyptian policy of the Government. The vacancy has not yet been filled up. In the House of Commons the first vacancy was created by the retirement, through ill-health, of Sir Charles Russell, , one of the members for Westminster, whose place was occupied by Lord Algernon Percy (Conservative). Mr. C. S. Alsopp (Conservative) was returned for Taunton in place of Sir W. Palliser, deceased. Mr. Sullivan, B.L , who had contemplated retirement from public life for some months, having accepted an" office of profit under the Crown" at the opening of the session, rendered necessary a new election for Meath county, when Michael Devitt, though ineligible to sit, was returned unopposed. Mr. Bradlaugh having been expelled from the House, a new writ was issued for Northampton, the re-election for that borough taking place on the 2nd March, when Mr. Bradlaugh was again returnc:d. Mr. Walter Powell, member for Mal mesbury, having ascended in a balloon, was never heard of again. His seat was filled by the return of Mr. C. W. Miles (Conservative). Mr. Jones Parry, formerly member of the same borough, was elected for the Carnarvon district; while Mr. C. T. D. Acland was elected to till the vacancy for East Cornwall, caused by the elevation of the Hon. Agar-Robartes to the Upper House in succession to his father, Lord Robartes. Mr. M. Devitt having been formerly declared ineligible to sit in the House, a new election took place, when Mr. Edward Sheil, formerly representative for Athlone, was returned.unopposed. Major Vaughan Lee (Conservative), one of the representatives for West Somerset, having resigned his seat through ill-health, Mr. E. J. Stanley (Conservative) was returned unopposed. The murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish created a viicancy for the North-west Riding of Yorkshire, which was filled by Mr. Isaac Holden (Liberal). The other impending changes are that for the Haddington Burghs, for which Sir D. Wed- derburn has resigned the seat, and that for Halifax, which seat Mr. J. D. Hutchinson has announced his intention of resigning owing to impaired health.

EATING BEFORE SIXEPING.--11,1111 is the only animal that can be taught to sleep quietly on an empty stomach. Toe brute creation resent all efforts to coax them to such a • violation of the laws of nature. The lion roars in the forest until he has found his prey, and when he has devoured it he sleeps over it until he needs another meal. The horse will paw all night in the stable, and the pig will squeal in the pen, refusing all rest or sleep until they are fed.- The animals which chew the cud have their own provision for a - late reed just before dropping off to their nightly slumbers. Man can train himself to the habit of sleeping without a preceding meal, but oniv after long years of practice. A 5 he comes into the world nature is too strong for him, and he • mtr;t be fed before he will sleep. A child's stomach is small, 1 and when pesfrctly tilled, if no sickness disturbs it, sleep follows naturally and inevitably. A 9 digestion goes on the StOMAch begins to empty. A eingle fcld in it will make the little sleeper restless; two will waken it, and if it is hushed

azain to repose Ps nap is short, and three folds pat an end to the elualber. Paregoric or other narcotic may close its eyes again, but without food or some stunifying drug it will not .alie". no matter how healthy it may be. Not even an angel who learned the mt of minstrelsy in a caestial clloir can sing a baby to sleep on an empty stomach. We use the oft-quoted s!ee-eling as sweetly as an infant" because this slumber of a child follows imtardia'ely after its stomach is completely filled with wholesome food. Tha sleep that comes to adults _ _ _ _ _

long hours after partaking of food, and when the stomach •- Is nearly or quite empty, is not after the type cf infantile repose. There 13 all the difference in the world between the sleep of refreshment and the slcep cf exhaustion. To sleep well the blood that swells the veins in the bead during our busy hours must flow back, leaving a greatly diminished volume behind the brow that lately throbbed with such vehemence. To dige.st well this blood is needed at the stomach and nearer the fountains of life. It is a fact estab- lished beyond the possibility of cen•radiction that sleep aids digestion, and that the process of digestion is conducive to refreshing sleep. It needs no argument to convince us of this mutual relation. The drowsiness which always follows the well-ordered meal is itself a testimony of nature to this inter-dependence. div.head: STATE i)F IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE i)F IRELAND.
A sub-constable natnal Brown was shot at Parsonstown, on Saturday night, at the entrance to a public-house, which he had just quitted, along with another officer. His assassin escaped.

A Claremorris corresponient telegraphs that a man named O'Brien, living near that place, shot his wife on Sunday nipt, it is supposed from motives of jealousy. She was so injured that she has died from her wounds. _ _

"On Monday the sum of £lBO,OOO was distributed amongst the members of the Royal Irish Constabulary, in propor- tions determined by the Castle officials. This prompt re- demption of on of several promises recently made by the Government has produced an excellent effect upon the men, who have now completely abandoned the agitation in which they lately indulged. The grant is made for special services rendered by the police during the past three years and in the majority of cases is equivalent to three months' pay.

• Mr. Mitchell Henry has never hesitated either in or out of Parliament to express his opinion on the character of the obstruction which has been set up in the House by the Irreconcilables. In a letter to a public board in Galway, the hon, member declares his conviction that that obstruc- tion not only delayed the Land Act, bat also produced the Coercion Act, and prevented Parliament from dealing as it intended to do with many questions of importance to Irish- men. As it is, "all sympathy for tbe country has been destroyed, and the reputation of the. Irish people as a God- fearing, honest, and gallant race has been shaken." The Ladies' Land League of Ireland was formally dis- solved at a meeting of its members on Thursday in Dublin, its special fur.ction—that of providing a machinery for the relief of evicted tenants—having been superseded by the Dublin Mansion House Committee. Thanks were tendered to the ladies of Ireland who had so efficiently carried out the work of the League for the past 18 months, and they were asked to "cultivate and develope the-national spirit" which had been evoked by the League. A committee was appointed to close the accounts, &c., and draw up a report of their operations for publication. The Special Commission in Dublin is justifying itself by results, and these are all the more satisfactory because they are obtained in the regular and constitutional manner, and without the suspension of trial by jury. Mr. Justice Lawson, in the sentences he has passed, has shown no dis- position to err on the side of leniency. In the Com- mission Court, on Monday, three young men, named Kin- sella, Bryan, and Duggan, found guilty of committing a savage assault on John Sullivan, at Mallow, were sentenced to 20, 15, and 10 years' penal servitude respectively. A man named Rooks was sentenced to 15 years', and three others, named Connor, Savage, ind Costello to 10 years' penal servitude for " Moonlighting " offences. Lawrence Kenny, convicted of firing at Sergeant Mac tuley, of the sth Fusiliers. in Mulling,,ar, was sentenced to penal servitude for the remainder of his life.

CONVICTION UNDER THE CRIMES ACT.—A second con- viction under the Crimes Act took place on Saturday, a young man named Francis Hynes having been found guilty of murderifig John Doloughty, at Knockanac, near Ennis, on the afternoon of Sunday, July 9th, as the man was re- turning home from a place of worship. 111-feeling had been entertained towards Doloughty by.Hynes fur a considerable time prior to the murder, and menaces had been used towards him to such an extent that he had bad Hynes bound over to keep the peace. instead of this, however, Hynes, em- boldentd, as the judge remarked, by the impunity with which crime was committed in County Clare, met Doloughty on the highway and shot him. The man did not die im- mediately, and revealed the name of his assassin. It is, therefore, a matter for congratulation that a jury has been found to return a verdict of guilty.

THE NATIONAL LAND LEAGUE CONVENTION. The annual convention of the National Lana League of Gre It Britain was held in Manchester on Sattfrday. Dr. Commins, M.P., presided. It was agreed to alter the name of the League to "The National Land and Labour League of Great Britain," and a number of alterations were made in its constitution and rules. The "organisers " for Scot- land, the North of England, and the Midland counties sub— mitted reports which were considered very satisfactory, the Scotch delegate reporting that the Highlands of Scotland were now ready for the cry of "the land for the people." The Convention pledged itself to support any well-digested scheme for paying the Irish members of Parliament. A vote- of thanks was unanimously accorded to Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P. It was agreed that the next convention should be held at Leeds. At a largely attended public meeting held on Sunday afternoon in the Free-trade Hall, speeches were delivered by Dr. Commins, M.P., Mr. Biggar, M.P., Mr. T. I'. O'Connor, M.P., Mrs. Moore. and others, and a resolution was adopted expressing thanks to the Irish Parliamentary party for the faithful discharge of its duties during the past session, and confidence that the party is destined to achieve still mightier triumphs than had yet been achieved for the people of Ireland. The speeches throughout breathed uncom- promising hostility to the Government, but Mr. T. P. O'Connor felt bound to say that Irish affairs were now ad- ministered "in a very different spirit " from that which prevailed six months ago. The present Chief Secretary, he said, was "a man of good, kind, and even generous inten- tions," and his demeanour in Parliament towards the Irish members ;vas characterised by reason and conciliation. UNVEILING THE O'CONNELL MONUMENT IN DUBLIN.

The unveiling of the O'Connell Monument and the open- ing of the Industrial Exhibition, which took place in Dublin on Tuesday, were made the occasion of a grand demonstra- tion by the people of the Irish capital. The city was decorated with flags—amongst which the green, of course, largely predominated—and triumphal arches Spanned many of the streets, the people themselves wearing green rosettes, and medals bearing effigies ci " the great Liberator," and of the present leaders of the National party. There was a pro- cession to the exhibition building, in which Mr. Parnell, Mr. Dillon, and other members of Parliament, as well as Mr. Davitt, joined, and the. opening ceremony wax performed by the Lord Mayor of Dublin (Mr. Dawson, M.P.) Reply- ing to an address the Lord Mayor said that the success of the exhibition was a tribute to the energy and self-reliance of the trades and working classes. The promoters did not desire to exclude the productions and manufacture of other lands, but rather to encourage and develcpe their own. The O'Connell statue was unveiled amid great popular rejoicing. The Lord Mayor, in accepting the gift on behalf of the Dublin Corporation and of the Irish race, delivered a long address upon the life and work of O'Connell, and called upon the Irish people to perpetuate in better form than the erec- tion of a statue the noble objects at which the great Libera- tor aimed. Mr. Parnell agreed that the most enduring monu- ment to O'Connell would be to strive:to gain the ends to which he devoted his great life. He hoped that dreing the next few years the progress of Ireland towards freedom might equal that which she bad made since the great centenary demonstration. Mr. Gray, M.P., addcd an injunc- tion to persevere in the efforts which had so far led to success, it remaining for them, by a detotmined attitude, to reap the fruit from the ground which had been prepared for

tttem. Calls were made for Mr. Dillon, but he did not speak, ind the formal proceedings ended. PRESENTATION OF THE FRE EDOM OF THE CITY OF DUBLIN TO MESSRS. PARNELL dr DILLON. The freedom of the city of Dublin was on Wednesday presented to Mr. Parnell, M.P., and Mr. Dillon, M.P., by the Corporation. There was an influential gathering at the ceremony, upon which the news of Mr. Gray's imprisonment produced a " mingled " effect, cheers, groans, and hisses being freely indulged in. Mr. Parnell, in his address, pin.- trilinhiner ",',.'fl• -• •

uurrent politics. He said that the only place where freedom of speech existed for the Irish members was the House of Commons, and on that floor he intended to speak and work until the legisla- tive independence of Ireland was gained. Mr. Dillon alio spoke with diffidence under the shadow of a recent event, and briefly returned thanks for the honour conferred upon him.

TRAP E NOTES. FARMING AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Express says:—" With a continuance of fine weather, har- vest work has progressed rapidly. The annual crop returns published in this issue show that the consensus of opinion expressed by correspondents of the Mark Lane Express in favour of the harvest of 1882 being better than that of any during the past seven years has been realised. Of samples which have hitherto been placed on the market, the larger proportion have scat•cely been hard enough for grinding, but the harvest season so far has been highly favourable to the crop being secured in good condition. The yield is spoken of at market as being very variable, and the quality so far rather indifferent. On Friday a sample of Talavera wheat, something under fair average quality, was sold at Mark-lane at 535. per 5041133. This may be taken as a fair tasis of values in the market on that day, other samples making about relative values, according to condition and quality. Last year's wheat was almost unsaleable, except the finest which is generally showing cheaper. Trade for foreign wheat off stands in London dull and slow since the holidays. Some American new crop was offered on Friday, sellers asking 50s. Flour rather cheaper. Barley quiet. Prices for maize sus- tained." The Farmer says:—" Weather warm and sunny. Market thinly attended. Wheat and oats in large supply. Trade inacti% e. Prices in favour of buyers. English wheat 505.; old sorts unchanged; new samples 545. per quarter; quality various. Foreign wheat is. to 2s. cheaper from a fortnight ago. Maize Od. dearer. Oats and beans cheaper. Barley and peas rather dearer. New large for malting 38s. Business was discouraging. Foreign flour is. per sack • lower."

THE LUSOUR MARKET.—The labour market has been a good deal affected by the Bank Holiday during the past week; otherwise it remains in a fairly satisfactory con- dition. Navvies and drainers are in active demand in several districts, and now that harvest has commenced there are few complaints Of want of employment in rural dis- tricts. Meanwhile very active steps are being taken by several counties in the repression of mendicity, so that migration without full information beforehand should be cautiously entered on. In the Glasgow district there is reported to be some scarcity of good furnace-men, and at Leeds good hands in the boot trade are in demand. Round Sheffield many colliee.es are working at little or no profit; but in some districts the coal trade is again rather more active. MeanwMile a representative meeting of miners from all parts haskeen arranged for next month at Manchester, when it is prob tble a limitation of output will be advocated by some sections of the men. The textile trades have entered upon few important charges, but at Kidderminster the carpet branch is again quiet. At Huddersfield pro- spects are good. In Ireland an advance has been granted to the constabulary, but in England only certain sections of the letter-carriers have obtained an increase in their pay. In the United States the strike of freight-handlers has come to an end, the companies haybing supplied themselves with the necessary labour. Advices from Queensland indicate a demand for labour at Rockhampton; and for the Cape of Good Hope recruits for the ir,fantry are being advertised for. The programme of the Trades' Union Congress which meets at Manchester next week has been issued.—Labour News.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES: MAN- CHESTER, WEDNESDAY.—The weight of actually new busi- ness doing continues only limited in extent. The market though dull as regards business, is very steady so far as prices are concerned. For delivery equal to Manchester, Lancashire forge and foundry pig iron is still quoted at 465. less 21 per cent, with district brands, such as Lincolnshire, at 47s Gd. to 48s. Gd. and 495. less 21, and Derbyshire at 435. 6d. to 503. per ton less 21, but at these figures sales only in small quantities are as a rule being made. The finished iron trade is steady. The home demand is only moderate. There is not quite the same pressure of work in the engineering trades as was the case a short time back, but the various branches throughout this district continue well employed both on home and foreign orders—The condition of the coal trade of this district still shows little or no change. House fire coals only meet with a slow sale, any extra buy- ing f, r winter stocks, as the result of the recent reduction in the Manchester rates, being only to a limited extent. There is no material variation in the demand for the common classes of round coal for iron-making and steam purposes, and supplies of these continue abundant; burgy still meets with only a moderate inquiry, but slack is less plentiful, and at some of the collieries this class of fuel is now scarce. Quoted prices are unaltered, and at the pit mouth average about Bs. to 85. 6d. for-best coals, 64 to Gs. 6d. for seconds, 44. 9d. to 5s 61. far common, 4s. 3d. to 4s. 61. for burgy, 3s. Gd. `o 4s. for best slack, and 2s. 9d. to 3s. 3d. for inferior sorts. Shipping has been rather quieter. The wages ques- tion appears to be causing a somewhat uneasy feeling. The determined stand taken by the men in the St. Helens dis- trict, and the probability that the miners' conference in Man- chester next week may; tend to stimulate a more general movement, induce the belief in many quarters that with the approach of winter the wages question may become a seriously disturbing element in the coal trade.

div.head: LANCASHIRE ENGINEERING TRADES.
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE ENGINEERING TRADES.

,The engineering branches of trade throughout the various important Lancashire centres of industry continue generally well employed. Although there is not quite the same press- in, inquiry for men in certain departments as was the case a short time back, the monthly returns issues by the various local branches connected with the Amalgamated Society of Engineers show that the men are kept steadily employed. For some-time past there has been no appreciable variation in the number of men in receipt of out-of-work donation, which has been kept at an exceedingly low point, and in the Manchester and Salford districts the number actually out of employment continues at less than 2 per cent. of the total local membership of the Society. The iron ship- building trade continues in an abnormal state of activity throughout all the great shipbuilding centres of the king- dom c, , and shows no present sign of falling off. The com- plaint, however, in this, although perhaps to a less extent than in other branches of the engineering, is also that the results to employers .on the work taken are not financially. of a very satisfactory character, and the chief advantage which has accrued from the activity is that they have been able to keep their plant fully occupied,in the place of stand- ing idle at a loss, as was the case very generally twelve months bask.

div.head: TFIUNDERSTOIIMS.
div.p: TFIUNDERSTOIIMS.
A severe thunderstorm visited Carrick-on-Shannon on Monday. The lightning killed several cattle, and near Elphin a farmer was struck and has since expired.
During a severe thunderstorm on Sunday, a young man named Boardman, livinp.: at Dun Soy, near Belfast, was struck by lightning when retiring to rest, and instantly killed.

Telegrams from Coleraine and Thurso report that a severe thunderstorm passed over those districts respectively of Ireland and Scotland on Sunday-night, accompanied by heavy rain, and greatly damaging the crops. About seven o'clock on Sunday morning a thunderstorm passed over the Vale of Clwyd. A tree on the farm of Mr. Thomas Jones, Rhydycilgwyn; near Ruthin, was struck by lightning, and a valuable pony that was sheltering under the tree was killed.

At Portsmouth, lightning struck the brewery of Messrs. Allen, smashing a chimney stack and the roofs of the brewery and an adjoining house. The lightning was very vivid, and hundreds of persons flocked to Southsea to see it playing over the Solent. _ _

On• Sunday a heavy thunderstorm passed over Chester, accompanied by vivid flashes of lightening. There was but little rain. During the storm the lightning struck the roof of a house belonging to Mr. Briggs, in Garden-lane, but happily passed to the ground by the waterspout, which it fused all the way down. A house at Horwich, near Bolton, occupied by a widow named Elizabeth Ellison, was considerably damaged by lightning on Sunday evening. The electric fluid seems first to have struck the chimney, which .it shattered; then, partially stripping the roof, it entered the bedroom, hurling from the wall a clock. tt afterwards made ito exit through the window, the glass in which it smashed: Mrs. Ellison and several visitors were in the house a the time, but escaped uninjured. Violent thunderstorms, which had fatal and destructive consequences, prevaikt in various parts of the country on Saturday. William Jackson, a young farmer, near Tavi- stock, Devon, was killed by lightning while haymaking. The storm. coming on suddenly, the deceased suggested to. the others working with hint that they should protect themszlyes from the rain by holding some hay over tireir heads. He did this himself, and the lightning struck the pitchfork, and killed him instantaneously. Two of he others sustained slight injuries.

The rents on the extensive' Forfarshire estates a Lard Dalhousie were collected in Brechin on Tuesday, when an abatement of 15 per cent, was allowed on the crop of 1881. The rents on Lord Northesk's estates were also collected on Tuesday, when an abatement of 10 par cent, was allowed. Madame Sarah:Bernhardt-Damala, who was to have com- menced an enzagement at the Brighton Theatre Royal and Opera Howe on Monday night, was unable to appear in cons:quence of indisposition. The local legisla- tion is already in excess ot last yearorten the total was 219, and the public etatutes numbertd 77g. Prom all the-moors, whethcr in tgland, Wales, or Scot- land, satisfactary reports are to hand. The birds are reported to be numerous, hcaltlrjyand plump, and sport is universally t 3od. The weather was everywhere fine, but very hot. An expiction of gas occ-arret -at the Theatre Royal, Old- ham, on -Saturday evening. A portion of the floor of a dressing-mom was blown up, ,and Miss Rignold, an actress, had one tf her legs broken. At Clay Cross, Derbyshire, the other night, two brothers named 'Wray, miners, 'quarrelled, and one fetching a gun from is house took deliterate aim at the other, shooting him telow the knee. Amputation of the limb was found to be necessary, and the irilured man died the same night. Th-e murderer is in custody. A lamentable accident, resulting in the loss of four lives, octurred in the Grog*, Channel on Saturday night. While the schooner Agnes was lying at anclor, the Vera Cruz, onward bound to Enrto Rico, came into collision with her, ad the Agnes sank immediately, the captain, mate, and two •Ci the captain's acne being drowned. The Examinuni for the Co.bden prize (value 60) offered by the committer; of the Cobden Club for the best essay on some subject 'connected with political economy, have awarded it to sir. Foster Watson, M.A., London, for an essay upon °O.,Teasant Proprietorship." The next competi- tion will be in 1885.

It is considered doubtful whether Mr. Justice North wlll in the vacation proceed with the action of seques- tration instituted by the Board of Trade against the Sub- marine Railway Company. 'As was anticipated, the Anstralian.cricketers have-teen severely defeated by the }Plavers of'r ogland, the great match Which came to a close on Saturday having resulted in a score for the Australiansof a'S for the two innings, agtinst 1122 for the first innings of the 'Players. The Australians I have now played. 24 mildhes during their visit, and of these ! ' they have won 16 artilost '2, the remainder being untl!aished. I Their previous defeat,lt will he remembered, was' by Cam- bridge University. A terrible account •cf--shipwreck,and suffering is furnished by the arrival in lioerpool'of the-survivors of the crew of the Star of Brunswkkovhich was wrecked on the‘Fcilkland Islands, whilst Isonterward bound, &sing a heavy gale in May last. Five -of the crew were drowned or killed by falling spars, and thc rest endured :great hardships before they succeeded inTenthing the land,laving to remain by the stranded vessel thoughout. two days of a snowstorm. The ship was owned inr.Liverpool. The memh?rs. ,d 1 'the Salvation -Army an London held a great festival on 'Saturday to celebrate the acquisition of the Grecian Thectrs and the Eagle Tavern in the City-road. "General" Beotla-onnouneed that the Army had paid nearly £8,500 of the sum, required for the premises, £16,750 ; and he had no doubt they would be able to open them free from debt in September. The progress of the Salvationists through the streets‘was made the occasion of hostile demon- stration by au unruly mob, who threw bags of flour on the I "officer," and hustled and mobbed' the "sister," -without meeting with any iffectnal check from the police. 'For the presenttlae committee content themselves with presenting their voluminous eitidencetaken, and reporting that the case is not yet complete. • Th-er add that the condition of affairs has trade it impossible -Os vet to examine the 'Eub-Commissioners, about whom several points of controversy had been mical. THE CONING 'ROYAL VISIT TO IIf..NCASHIRE. —OD the occasion of the-Visit to Preston Guild of the •Dulsc and Duchess of Albany in September next, their 'Royal Eigh- nesses will be -the guests of the Earl and Countess of Lathom, at Lathoni House. The Duke and Ducbees are expected to arrivecfOrmskirk station- on Monday, Sei;tem- her 4, and a meeting of the inbabitanteb to be convened for the purpose -of•oonsidering what steps should be taken to accord to the. It is estimatedlEat about £3OO will'AA required, and no ,doubt is entertained that this sum will-be raised. AMALOANATIOI4 Or -LONDON AND MANC-SRSTER THRATmo. —An agreement has been entered -into between Mr.-,J. Hollingshead, 'Mr. C'Oyly Carte, Mr. 'Michael Guru; and Captain Bainbridge, by which the Prince's Theatre and Theatre Royal, Manchester, and the Court Theatre, Liver- pool, are to bounited for business purposes with the theatres already under the direction of the first-named gentlemen in London, Liverpool, and Dublin. It is said that the Savoy and the Gaiety in'London and the Gaiety la Dublin will be carried on as heretofore by Mr. Carte, Mr. Eisllingshead, and: Mr. Gunn respectively, but that the two Manchester theatres and the new' Court Theatre in' ,Liverpool will be under the joint-central of all the gentlemen mentioned.
