tHE MERSEI 4all.—Mr. H. C. Raikes.K.V., presided at the half-yearly meeting of the Mersey Rahway Company on Saturday. He gave a favourable report as to he progress of the tunnel, and•said that although their bill had not yet received the Royal assentit had passed through bah-Houses, and strongly criticised tile action of the Etirkonhes.d Corpora- tion as extorting the" fu-.I pound of flesh:" The directors, lie added, believed the time was rapidly approaching when they could call up the remainder of their capital, and obtain the quotation so nuchd&ired by some of thc sivlreholders. In reply to a question, Mr. Waddell, the contractor, enter- tained great hopes that the -andertaking would be catried out the end of next,year. The report and. statement of accounts were passed. _

PROFESSOR JEVONS ariOWNED.—Professor Jewels was ,droweed on Monday, at Bexhill, Sussex, while bathing. An 'ininest was held on Tuesday. Mrs. Jevons, wife of the \deceased, stated that they -were staying at Bexhill—She went out on Monday morning with her husband aud -chi:dren. The professor left them, andeehe did not see him again alive. Other witnesses stated that the body was seen -Eoatieg • on the water, life being, extinct. The clothes of the deccesed were lying on the Q.*. The sea was dangerous there for a person who was not a good ,cwimtner, especially at-ligh water. The jury teturned wverdict of " Accidentaleleath." Wm,. Stanley Jevons, MA., ILS., was the grandson of Win. Roscoe, of Liverpool, in .which city he was .born in laati. He was educated at University College, London, and fronel9s4 till 1859 held an appointment at the Australian Royal Mint, Sydney. He took the degree of M.A. at the London University in 1802, and -was made fellow of Lie college in 1864. He was appointed Professor of Logic, MentaLand Moral Philosophy, and Cobden lecturer in ,poli- tieal economy in Owens College,Xanchester, in 1866. 'ln' 1872 he.aras elected a fellow of . the Royal Society. In 1878 te=rezeived the honorary degree of LL.D. from the Edinburgh University, and in the,eame year he resigned his profeescrship in Manchester on being appointed Professor of Political Economy in University College, London. In recent years Professor Jevons hadtheen an indefatigable writer in the, various subjects which 'he had specially studied, and he hadlezen engaged in many controversies with the,, most ereinent.men of the day. Orn FRUIT. CROPS.—The Gardenene, Chronicle publishes its annual reports of the fruit crops of the year. These reports number 249, of which 40 represent Scotland, lc England, 10'Weles, 19 Ireland, and t+l the Channel Islands,. aed are summarised as follow :—"Apricots under an average generally, the best crops in eastern, midland, and western ; counties. Plums much under the average, and quality ; ' inferior. Cherries much under the average' as usual of • Morellos ; bee returns from Bedfordshire and Oxfordshire. Peaches and ntarinee under an average, exzept in southern and western counties. Apples very much under an Average. Pears teery,much under an average, and quality f4enerally reported aslikely to be inferior. Small fruits, a very good average generally and over average in eastern, smithere, and yea-tern .counties. Strawberries a good eve:age generally. Nuts .under average, except-in eastern, midland, southern, said western counties; walnuts, a thin crop generally." It thinks .those who advise the British farmer to try fruit growing saa remedy for agricultural dis- tress, should scan its annual records of the fruit crop ',before counseling locking up capital im fruit culture. Taking the last tee =years as a sample, it states :—" We find in 1870 that fruit crop of all kinds were generally abundant; in on• they were scanty and late; in t 1872 there was universal failure ; in ,1873 the crop was reported under average.; in 1874 the yield was over average; so was it , in 1875; 'but in 1876, 1811, 1818, 1879, 1880-6.ve years in succession—a poor crop was recorded. In 1881 the crop was a fairaverage' and now in 18e,2 we have another gen.ral deficiency." Taking apples for instance :—" In [B7O they were ,abundant, in 1871 partial, in 1872 very , scarce, in 1873 below he average, in 1814 fair, in 1875 abundant, in 1876 tearce, in 1877 below average, in 18781 much below average., in 1879 again much below average, in 1880 deficient, in 1881 they were abundant, and this year they are spoken of as below the average." These are thought to be conclusive facts against fruit growing as a eelief to farmers. As to the cause otthe fruit failures, it proceeds "To spring frost, more than a,n7 other single cause, must be attributed our deficient crops. Thus in 1870, 1875, and 1881 there was a general, or at east relative absence of frost at the critical periods, and in all those years the crop , was above the average. On the other ,hand, in 1871, 1872, 1873, 1877, 1878, 1879, and 1880 sprit:s frosts an 4 peat winds effected tho ilfctrrxtion of crops,"

Harvest work it progressing rapidly, rnd the crops are turning out much better than was anticipated aefew weeks I ago. Of 28 of the largest English towns, Halifax had the lowest rate of mortality last week. 11 9 per 1,000 per annum, and Sunderland the highest, 311. The death-rate in Liverpoolwas 23.8 per 1,000. At present many hundreds of rabbits are dying in Dum- friesshire, from enlarged livers. Numbers die in ordinary seasons from this cause, but this year it seems to have assumed the form of an epidemic. A meeting of the executive of the Halifax Liberal Asso- ciation on Monday night passed a resolution accepting with regret the resignation of Mr. Httchinson, one of the borough members. Mr. Thomas Shaw, J.P., woollen manufacturer, Allan-gate, was selected as the Liberal candidate. No con- test is expected: On Monday the Coroner's inquiry into the death of Wm. Riley, who was killed by the overthrow of a steam tram- way car at Blackburn some days ago, terminated in a ver- dict of manslaughter against the cardriver. It was stated that the speed was far in excess of the Board of Trade regu- lation and that the car was much overloaded, these condi- tions producing an unsteadiness which caused the accident. An exciting scene occurred at Hagley Railway Station on Monday morning. As an excursion train for Worcester was coming in a woman attempted to cross the line right in front of it. Painful cries were raised, as the woman's escape seemel almost impossible. Some men, however, gripped her arms just in time to pull her on the high plat- form before the engine reached her. The driver tried but could not stop the train. A gas explosion of an alarming and destructive nature took place early on Monday morning at the Everton Con- servative Club, Breckfield-road North, by which the keeper and his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Orrell, were injured—the former so seriously that he is reported to be in a precarious condition at the Royal Infirmary. Considerable damage was caused to the building by the explosion, which occurred in the smoke-room, and part of the structure has been con- demned by the city engineer. A Midland express from Derby to London has just had a very narrow 7escape. The driver, when near Leicester, saw a man with a waggon and team of horses leisurely come on the line through an occupation crossing. By great efforts, and by using the vacuum brake, the express was stopped Jest as it reached the waggon. The waggoner, on being remonstrated with, laughed at the driver aud guard of the -train, treating the matter as a lark. TIIE NATIONAL PoRTRAIT GALLERY.—The 25th annual report of the trustees of the National Portrait Gallery shows that the number of visitors to the institution during the first six months of the present year was 39,200, of which number 2,851 visited the building on Easter Monday, and 2,388 on Whitsun Monday. The total number of visitors to the Gallery from the commencement in Great George-street, West ninster, in 1859, to the end of last year, was 1,053,103. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL WonKs.—An application on the part of the Crown to sequestrate the South-Eastern Railway Company's property, in consequence of the company's diso- bedience to the order made by Mr. Justice Kay forbidding further boring in the Channel Tunnel, came before Mr. Justice North, in Chancery, on Wednesday. On the defeu- dents undertaking that the works should be entirely stopped, the motion was ordered to stand over -sine die.

ESCAPE AND CAPTURE OF CONVICTS. Two convicts, named James Fowler, under sentence of five years', and James Campbell, sentenced to eight years' penal servitude, were at work at the Portsmouth Dockyard extension works on Monday afternoon, when they managed to put on canvas suits, which they bad secreted near the works, -and walked out of one of the gates. When the warder ordered the gang to leave off work he found that the two men were missing. The police were placed on their track, and the singular dress and cropped hair of the men led to their detection and subsequent reconverance to prison. Tns MIDLAND Ran.wkr.--At the half-yearly meeting of the Midland Railway Company, held on Tuesday at Derby, the dividends recommended by-the Directors in their report recently published were declared payable. The Directors were authorised to borrow £696,000 on mortgage. In answering some questions that were put by shareholders, the chairman (Mr. M. W. Thompson) combated the assertion that the Midland Company was keeping down dividends by pursuing. a "spirited policy of encroachment." It was not. the Midland, he mairrtiined, but the London and North- Western and the Great Northern Companies that were encroaching. TIIE WEST STANT:EY COLLIERY EXPLOSION.---The report of Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P., upon an inquiry into the causes of a fatal explosion which occurred on the 19th of of April last in the Busty seam of the West Stanley Col- liery, by which 13 fives were lost, was issued, in the form of a parliamentary blue book, on Wednesday. Mr. Morley finds that the explosion cannot be said to have been caused by the absence of a sufficient control in the matter of aftept- ing precautions against naked lights being used, or careless firing: of shots; but thinks greater care should be taken to carry out strictly the provisions of the Mines Regulation Act, and the speckil rules which were supposed to be in force in the mine.

SALVATION ARSTV DISTUBBAICZX 'IN THE POTTERIES.— At a late hour on Monday night, after trying in vain to gain a hearing, or Fawcett and a female captain, who have been sent to Henley to take charge of the Salvation Army contingent there, had to be e.scarted to their lodgings by a body of 12 policemen as a protection against the fury of the mob. The proceedings at•the meeting were of a most uproarious character throughout, there being over 2,000 persons present, who went for .the avowed purpose of pre- venting General Booth's officers from bolding the service. The name of General Booth 'was receiKed with hisses, groans. catcalls, and-other deafening noises, Nearly all the local Salvationists have joined the opposition army under Captain Gipsy Smith and his lieutenant, who were dis- charged by the general for receiving presents.

ATTEMPTED litlftlYEß ET A SERGEANT.—At Birmingham, on Monday, Thomas Downes, a sergeant in the 38th-Regi- ment, at present stationed at 'Lichfield, but under orders to sail this week for Egypt was committed for trial charged with maliciously wounding George Bruce, a brass founder. lon the 23rd July The prisoner met the prosecutor isp a public-house, and told him he meant to give him something before going to Egypt, for sending to prison a comrade who had fractured Bruce's skull. iriter•on the prosecutor was -enticed into a neighbouring house. the door was locked, and he was murderously attacked 'by the prisoner with a hatchet. He would havebeen killed had not a crowd broken the windows, and entering the house rescued the prosecutor, who was streaming with blood. 'THE HOP PLATITATIONS.—During last week the Kentish hop plantations progressed as satisfactorily as was expected. Iconsidering the condition they are in this season. With a continuance of the present weather the early grounds whicjl I have escaped the blight will be ready for the pickers at an I early date. At Cranbrook one planter anticipates a yield of 114uite.10 cwt. per acre, two others will get froms to 10 per I acre ;'but the hulk of the grounds will not produce an average of 2 cwt. At Littlebnurne, in East Kent, a large grower ex- pects a. yield of 7 and 8 cwt., and tile Isle of Thanet gardens promise an average of about 8 cwt. Around Maidstone the crop n'lli he exceedingly small, and the celebrated Ashford district will do but little. At Ticehurst, in Sussex, prolifics will be ready for picking in a fortnight. Mould is spreading in the Sussex plantations. From Ito 2 cwt. will be the pro- I duce of the Surrey grounds. CRTYWANO'S NAMESAKE.—An inquest was held at Plum- stead, on Monday, on the both, of a child named Cetywayo Kitchingham, aged two years and seven months, who, while playing in a garden, was seized with vomiting and died from the effects of some irritant poison. The child, it appeared, was seen with somerflowers and weeds in its hand, which niast have been plucked from the next garden through the fence. When the jury viewed the body they also inspected the next garden, and among some scarlet runners the coroner drew their attention to some deadly night shade, orbelladonna, the berries of which were green. Dr. Ingledevr said the weed produced was nightshade, and from a post-mortem examination he attributed death to the dectased having eaten some of the berries. Mrs. Hender- son, the neighbour, produced some of the weed, and said she had since cleared her garden of it. The jury returned a verdict of death from accidentally eating berries of deadly nightshade.

POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE BRITISH FORCES IN -EGYPT.— For the convenience of Her Majesty's forces serving in Egypt the Postmaster General has established an army post-office, which will <undertake all duties connected with the receipt and dispatch of mails, the sale of postage stamps, and the issue and payment of money orders and postal orders. Mails for the forces in Egypt will be made up in 'London three times a week—viz, on Monday evenings, on Wednesdiy mornings, and on Friday evenings. The rates <of postage will be as follows:—Letters, 21d. per •oz.; post cards,‘ld. each: newspapers, id. each not exceeding 2ot. in weight, and Id. for every additional 20z.; printed papers and books, id. per 2oz. But in exception to the above rate on letters, those addressed to or sent by non-commissioned efficers,soldiers, and seamen In Her Majesty's service will he privileged to pass for a postage of Id. each, provided the letters do not exceed ioz- in weight. To enjoy this privi- lege the senders must in all cases comply with the regula- tions specially applicable to such letters, as detailed in the Post-office Guide. Money orders and postal orders will be issued at the same rates of commission as inland money orders and postal orders. COME-FIGHTING IN NORTH WALES.—An extraordinary case of cock-fighting is being investigated by the police authorities in North Wales, and already about a dozen sum- monses have been issued against the principals implicated in the affair—these being gentlemen occupying prominent positions and moving in good society, some being resident in Shropshire and others in the Principality. The scene of the encounter between the spurred birds was near Althrey Hall, Bangor Isycoed, soma six miles from Wrexham, and the dis- covery was effected in this way. It seems that one of those in the secret, desirous of " having a lark" with his brother " cockers," went to the house of a local policeman, who was absent from home on duty, and obtained the loan of a helmet and tunic. Donning these, be proceeded as near to the scene of the battle as HA shelter of a friendly hedge would permit him to do unseen, and, after allowing his friends to proceed with the business on which they were so intent, he suddenly popped his head above the hedge and gave an alarm. Per- -ceiving and hearing these warnings, the "noble sportsmen" at once skedaddled, leaving palpable evidence of the illicit sport in which they had been engaged behind them. The escapade of the practical joker coming to the knowledge of the chief constable of the county, an inquiry was set on foot which resulted in proceedings being ordered against as many of those who took part in the "cocking" as were known or could be discovered. As already stated, about a dozen summonses have been issued, and among the witnesses who iove been subpoenaed are an ex-mayor and others hold- -sngptiill pore exalted positions in society.

The Queen, on Thursday, at Cowes, presented new colours to the 2nd battalion Berkshire (66th) Regiment in place of the standards lost at the battle of Maiwand. in which the regiment suffered heavy loss. The Ist bittalion is now on service in Egypt under the Duke of Connaught. A labourer, named Jepson, had been committed for trial for the manslaughter, at Pocklington, Yorkshire, of an Irishman, named O'Halleran. The prisoner knocked O'Halleran down and kicked him so savagely that he expired on the spot. A further experiment was made on Wednesday, at Chatham, by the Explosives Committee, on board Her Majesty's ship Bullfinch. One gallon of xerotative siccative was laid over a magazine containing powder, and the bulk- head heated, but the powder remained intact. A fisherman, named Richard Abram, together with his son James, aged 14, went out from a small village on the Ribble named Banks, on Wednesday morning, to fish in the , estuary. As they did not return that evening search was made, and on Thursday their dead bodies were found on a sandbank near Southport, the capsized boat being aground some distance up the river. On Wednesday morning. at Boston, Lincolnshire, a chemist's assistant, named Frank Alltoft, was proceeding with a lighted lamp into a cellar where benzoline and paraffin was stored, when an explosion occurred, blowing out the shop windows and dreadfully burning Alltoft. He was removed to the hospital, but is not expected to recover. An outbreak of fire followed the explosion, but it was speedily subdued.

On Wednesday night, a singular scene was witnessed in Birmingham. A man named Francis O'Hara, who was masquerading in the streets in female attire, was mobbed by a crowd of persons, and obliged to take refuge in a house. Et great disturbance ensued, and the windows were smashed by the crowd, O'Hara being rescued from ill-usage by a con- stable, who took him into custody. The prisoner was on Thursday cautioned and discharged. • A Paris telegram states that General Ducrot died on Wednesday, in his sixty-sixth year. The deceased general greatly distinguished himself in the Franco-German war. When MacMahon was wounded at the battle of Sedan, Ducrot received from him the command-in-chief. After the surrender he was arrested, but escaped to Paris, where he participated in the great sorties from the beleaguered city. After the capitulation he was elected to the National Assembly, but resigned in 1873, An important action against Earl Granville, under the Employers' Liability Act, waB concluded at Hanley County Court on Tuesday, the plaintiff being Ellen Kelly, who claimed £124 for the death of her husband, at his lordship's iron works at Hanley. Whilst assisting to take down an engine-house, the deceased, under threat of dismisSal, was sent by his foreman into danger, and received such injuries as resulted in his death. The judge reserved his decision. THE MURDER OF AN OLD WOMAN.—Robert Sellers, aged 21, was on Thursday committed for trial by the Fareham magistrates on a charge of wilful murder. On Bank Holiday the prisoner was drinking in a public-house with several men, and all were more or less intoxicated. The prisoner subsequently led a woman, named Harriet Ford, aged 64, who was nearly blind, deaf, and dumb, to a waste piece of ground, and next morning her lifeless body was discovered. There were marks of a struggle having taken place, and the prisoner's hat was found on the spot. On the arrival of the express from Carlisle at Preston, on Tuesday, a woman's hand with sinews attached was found fast to the brake gearing of one of the vans. As the train was coming down beyond Shap at the rate of nearly sixty miles an hour, the driver saw, about one hundred yards ahead, a woman with an umbrella up near the metals. She was struck, run over, and frightfully mutilated. Part of her skull fell off the engine at Grayrig. The train was stopped at Teebay, and the body removed. The nomination for the Haddingban Burghs took place on Thursday. At the last moment the Conservatives have I found a candidate to oppose Mr. Craig Sellar. TAeir candi- date is Mr. Seton-Karr, of Bargally, who has twice unsuc- cessfully contested Rochester. The Conservative candidate .comes out generally on party lines—where they are at pre- sent descernible, and expresses his readiness to support " any measures of Conservative progress and Constitutional reform which time may render imperative or which any large class of Her Majesty's subjects may demand," a clause wide 1 enough to admit Home Rule itself. The poll will take place I on Tuesday. FATAL MILL FIRE.—A great mill fire occurred on Wed- nesday afternoon, in the Persian Cotton Mill, Bolton, by which damage to the amount of £60,000 was caused. Many of the operatives were imprisoned in an upper storey by the fire, their only means of escape being the hazardous expedient of jumping from the windows. The injuries sustained in this perilous descent produced a melancholy result, one woman being killed on the spot, whilst several other persons were conveyed to the Infirmary suffering from fractures of , limbs, and general contusions. The flames spread so ' rapidly that the fire extinguishing apparatus kept in the building was of no avail, and the mill was totally destroyed. THE NEXT-OF-KIN FRAUDS.—The magisterial proceedings instituted by the Public Prosecutor against Albert Edward Beeton, the Birmingham manager for the International Law Agency, for complicity in the "next-of-kin" .frauds, when continued on Thursday before the :deputv-stipendiary of Birmingham. A serious of extortions were revealed by one of the witnesscs, who stated that no less than 35 members of . her family paid half a guinea each to the prisoner and his association for prosecuting their claim to large estates in Scotland and Gloucestershire. At a second meeting of the members of the family, convened by circular, a fnrther con- tribution was levied upon all present.—The prisoner was committed for trial at the Warwick assizes. On Thursday morning, Lord O'Hagan opened a Catholic bazaar in the Mechanics' Institution, Burney, in the pre- &lnca of a large assemblage. The object of the bazaar is to receive funds to build new Catholic schools in Fulledge, Burnley, in connection with St. Mary's Church. The schools will cost £2,000, and it is hoped to raise £l,OOO by the bazaar. Lard O'Hagau said the bazaar had been supported by Protestants, which did them the highest honour, and ought to receive the warmest recognition. Burnley was a 'remarkable community, which had progressed rapidly, and he believed it was destined to be a powerful and influential community, and therefore required such charitable institu- tions as that they were met to support. A revolting story of a husband having gone to sea, leav- ing the body of his wife lying at the mortuary of the Bootle Hospital, was told in the Bootle Police Court, on Wednes- day. About a week ago the deceased woman attempted to strangle herself, and she died in the hospital from the results of her effort. In due course an inquest was held, and the coroner gave to the husband an order for the burial of the body. The man also obtained an order for interment from the relieving officer, but he then went off to join his ship, telling the neighbours that his wife had been buried. The body was, however, still lying in the mortuary, and the magistrates were on Wednesday appealed to, on zanitary grounds, for an order for its immediate interment, which, of course, they it once granted.

BEHIND THE SCENES.—A novel scene " bahind the scenes" of the The'atre Royal, Birmingham, where" Youth" is now being played, occurred on Monday and Tuesday evenings. On the former evening the whole of the super- nurneiaries, numbering between 100 and 200, declined to go on the stage, " striking " for payment .for the time spent in rehearsals. Many of the "supers" never having previously "trod the stage," may have been unaware that it was the custom not to pay for rehearsals, but a number who had "played" before were fully aware of the Practice. The con- sequence of the "strike" was that in the great sensational scene, instead of " regiments of soldiers" appearing, there were only three persons in the "army," one being the call boy. On Tuesday night, most of the "deserters " were begging to be reinstated, but their places had already been.l filled up, and only those who had been intimidated were allowed to again don the buskin. THE ALLEGED GREAT MINING FRAUDS.—A remarkable eharge of fraud has been investigated by the Bristol magis- trates. A notorious person named Edwin Harvey Wedge, having bought the abandoned workings of an old tin mine in Cornwall for £5OO, floated the "Cornwall Great Consols Mining Company," representing it as a valuable under- taking, the shares in which were chiefly held by a "wealthy syndicate." On these representations he obtained several thousands of pounds from residents in Manchester, Liver- pool, and elsewhere. From the rcine only £3OO worth of tin was ever extracted, and it was subsequently ascertained, as alleged br the prosecution, that the " company " was Wadge himself, the other members of the "syndicate being his clerks and office boys some of whom figured as holders of many thousand pound; worth of shares. Wedge was on Thursday committed for trial. At a meeting of the Liberal electors of Halifax on Thurs- day evening a resolution was passed expressing deep sympathy with Mr. Hutchinson, who has Wen compelled through ill-health to retire from the representation of the borough, and gratefully acknowledging his services to the town and to the Liberal party. Mr. T. Shaw was, by another resolution, unanimously accepted as the Liberal candidate to succeed Mr. Hutchinson. He addressed the meeting on current political topics, and was warmly re- ceived. He said he gave his cordial support to Mr. Glad- stone's Goveinment, and should earnestly support such measures as the procedure rules, household suffrage for the counties, the extention of local government, and the adoption of the principle of local option. He believed the troubles in Ireland were coming to an end. Mr. Shaw's election will not be opposed, the Conservative party in the borough having resolved that it is inexpedient at the present time to force a contest.

On Thursday morning, Thomas Alexander Heyes Robin- son, described as a gentleman of independent means, was brought up in custody before the Wigan county magistrates charged with shooting at two police-constables with intent to murder. Last week Mr. Justice Chitty committed Robin- son for contempt for assault on" a process server, and on Taesday night the deputy Dipstaff and two constables attempted to arrest him on the judge's warrant. Robinson presented a pistol at them, and threat- ened to shoot them if they approached. The men tried to obtain an entrance to his room, whereupon Robinson took up a gun and fired at them, the bullet smashing the door panel, one of the constables being struck by the splinters of the door. They retired for reinforcements, and on Wednes- day night seven officers proceeded to Orrell-mount, prisoner's residence. Constable Stead was first, and on ascending the staircase Robinson appeared on the landinq, and, presenting a revolver, cried out he would shoot him if he approached further. Stead made a rush forward, whereupon Robinson fired, a bullet striking the wall at the bottom of the stair- eise.; The prisoner was then secured. A revolver with four chariibers still loaded, and a double-barrelled gun were pro- ducild in court. Formal evidence having been given the prisdner was remanded till Monday. The case excited con- siderable interest,- the prisoner being well known. The chancery proceedings have arisen out of matrimonial differ- URA.

div.head: WAR IN EGYPT.
div.p: THE WAR IN EGYPT.
ARRIVAL OF Sin O. WOLSELEY.

Sir Garnet Wolseley and the leading members of his staff arrived, on Tuesday, at Alexandria; and the steady arrival and the martial appearance of the British troops is greatly depressing the natives—so much so that an entire infantry battalion has offered to surrender as prisoners or submit to the Khedive. But Arabi shows no disposition to run away. On the contrary, he continues to spread marvellous stories of British defeats, and, while managing to keep order at Cairo and elsewhere, continues to strengthen his position, and is even said to have obtained a proclamation from the Ulemas deposing the Sultan from the Caliphate and elevating the Cherif of Mecca in his stead. The Sultan, on the other hand, is understood to have telegraphed to Arabi peremptorily ordering him to submit, in peril of being left to be dealt with by the English.

THE PROCLAMATION -AGAINST ARABI.—THE MILITARY CONVENTION WITH ENGLAND. The military convention between England and Turkey makes slow progress, and the issue of the proclamation declar- ing Arabi a rebel is still delayed. The negotiations progress, or, rather, stand still, as though the Porte were undecided what course to purse; but it is prebable that the delay is not owing to vacillation so much as to the inveterate habit of the Turk to haggle, with a view to making the best bar- gain possible. The terms of the proclamation regarding Arabi are understood to have been settled, but the exact lines of the Military Convention are still under discussion, and it is quite in accordance with Oriental diplomacy to hold back the issue oi the proclamation in the hope that Eng- land may thereby be induced to make some concession in the arrangements under which the Tnrkisil troops are to enter Egypt. The Sultan knows well,that England desires Arabi to be denounced as a rebel, but does not particularly wish for Turkish intervention in Egypt; but he is mistaken if he thinks the British will purchase his proclamation of Arabi at the expense of impbrtant,military concessions.

THE ACTIVITY OF THE KHEDIVE. While the Sultan thus sits between two stools there is no longer any indecision in Egypt. The Khedive has issued another proclamation formally authorising Admiral Seymour to prevent the importation of coal or munitions of war into Egypt, and he has also issued notices empowering the Ad- miral to occupy the Isthmus of Suez, or any portion of it. This final permission to land troops along the Canal dis- poses of all criticisms that may be raised by the Powers as to England's actions there, the Canal being under the Khedive's authority. Appearances indicate that active steps for the preservation of order in the Canal tcwns cannot be much longer delayed. At Port Said a semi-panic prevails, and an outbreak appears to be so imminent that the ships there are kept ready for action.
RECONNOITRING THE ENEMY'S POSITIONS. DARING CONDUCT.

A somewhat hazardous attempt of a young officer to reconnoitre the enemy's position without any escort, and accompanied only by one comrade, though interesting enough as an adventure, has not been productive of any substantial advantage. It was Lieutenant Smith Dorrien, of the Invincible, who conceived the idea, and Sub-Lieu- tenant Hamilton, of the Helicon, was his only companion. Going out, after dark, on Monlay night, they crossed the edge of Lake Mariout, floundered through the mud for a mile, and getting on to firmer ground, succeeded in reaching the enemy's outposts, 16 miles off, by half-past two on Tuesday morning. Before there was light enough for them to reconnoitre the position, however, they were dis- covered by the Arab picket. Immediately a bright signal light was flashed out, and answered from end to end of the line. Finding their presence thus discovered, the two lieu- tenants make a bolt .for the lake, followed by Arabi's cavalry, whose horses, however, would not face the water. After lying for some time in two feet of water, they suc- ceeded in evading the vigilance of their enemy, and making a wide detour towards Mex, got back to the English lines by daybreak, with nothing to show for their pains but wet jackets. This independent reconnoitring is more creditable to the courage of those who undertake it than to their dis- cretion. Only on very exceptional occasions, and in the case of men especially constituted for such under- takings, do they succeed. A wise commander gener- ally discountenances them as likely to do more harm than good. A reconnaissance by colonel Gerard on Tues- day, though not quite so exciting to those who took part in it, was carried to a more successful issue. With a detach- ment of mounted infantry this experienced officer of the Bengal Staff penetrated nearly to the enemy's second line, and seems to have stayed there long enough to make mental notes of facts that may be found vtry useful hereafter. When the enemy's cavalry swept down upon them, this little band retired in good order, dismounted to give their pursuers a well-directed volley that emptied several saddles, then mounted again, and rode back to our own lines unhurt. In the absence of more stirring events these small affairs, if they do nothing else, help to keep the men in good beart. Before many days have passed, however, there will probably be work of much more serious importance on hand.
A SKIRMISH BEYOND MEX : THE FORCE OF THE ENEMY.

A skirmish has taken place beyond Mex. The Arabs appeared in some force, with two cannon. Our sailors and marines drove them back without loss on our side. The enemy it is thought sustained several casualties. The Daily Telegraph's Alexandria correspondent says the latest infor- mation respecting the enemy's force round Alexandria gives it at over 12,000, including 2,000 cavalry and 40 guns, most of them Krupp. Mahmoud Samy's force near Ismailia is reported to consist of nearly 20,000 men, chiefly undis- ciplined hordes, and it is said that the Bedouins therabouts are also at his disposal. Many of Arabi's gunners are Turks by birth or extraction. The enemy is still multiply- ing obstacles to our advance, chiefly earthworks. which are visible in several places. The Egyptian General is said to be specially strong in artillery. Another correspondent says the preparations of Arabi bear no proportion to ours, and that we are gaining upon him with terrible rapidity. Nevertheless he is said to show a bold, defiant spirit, and to keep up the courage of his fol- lowers by wholesale inventien. Just as massacres up-country were a favourite tonic with alarmists in Alexandria, so vic- tories over the English have been the staple of Cairo

Other accounts from Alexandria show there is apparently some doubt whether Arabi after all has succeeded in making ; his position at Kafr Dowar much more formidable than it was a week ago, notwithstanding the great show of ceaseless activity kept up by his working parties. A special corres- pondent, telegraphing at a late hour on Tuesday, says : "It would almost seem that he is doing nothing serious, but trying to impress us with an idea of -his strong entrench- ments; for though the Arabi are working every day their labour produces small results. Very little has been added by them to the shelter trenches they had a week ago." These words, it should be explained, do not apply to the Aboukir forts and earthworks connecting them with Rosetta, which have no doubt been armed with heavy ordnance of most effective patterns. Arabi knows well enough the value of those forts, and has done all in his power to make them towcrs of strength. Presenting as they do the only obstacles to a landing along the shores- of Aboukir Bay or the passage of gunboats up the Rosetta mouth of the Nile, and at the same time menacing the dank of a force advancing by land from Alexandria, these works are of considerable importance to Arabi's system of defence, whether he chooses to make his stand at Kafr Dowar or to fall back on some other posi- tion nearer Cairo.
THE BRITISH FORCES.: THE INDIAN CONTINGENT.

The British forces, it is said, are now strong enough to do whatever Sir Garnet Wolseley may decide upon doing, and the officers and men are impatient to be led against the enemy. The Scots Guards and Grenadiers have landed, and are now encamped at Ramleh. Their fine healthy appear- ance was much remarked ag they marched through the European quarter of city. The camping ground is a magni- ficent situation as to health. The sea breeze sweeps over the sandy ridges where the tents are pitched, and there is sea bathing close at hand. The men seem to take kindly to camp life in Egypt, and have got everything into excellent order, but are rather closely packed. The Duke of Con- naught has applied to have the Marines brigaded with the Guards, and this is taken as a compliment by the Marines. On Monday, the transport Hoiland landed 250 horses of the Life Guards and Blues. She did not havea single loss during the voyage. The horses, after neatly a fortnight on board ship, were soon quite at home on shore. On Tuesday, the ttehsronagnd marched of curious t7h9rtohuHghigAhileaxnadnedrerialeft Tthheeytrpoaospasehdiapmo4oan spectators, and were much admired: Reinfordenlents now arrive daily. A Times Calcutta telegram says :—The main body of the Indian contingent has been despatched from Bombay, and is now en route for Suez, where that splendid regiment the Seaforth Highlanders is already awaiting its arrival. Great satisfaction has been expressed by the authorities at the promptitude, energy, and ability which have been evinced by the Bombay officers in the equipment and despatch of the contingent. Definite orders for the despatch of the force were only received on Tuesday, July 25. In the course of the next day 21 steamers were surveyed and chartered. These were inimediately placed in the hands of the dock authorities for equipment fer troops. Many of these trans- ports were cargo boats, and their conversion into troopships necessitated very extensive and serious alterations, and yet in a week all these preparations were completed. Every endeavour has been made, too, to consult the health and comfort of the troops. It is generally believed that the Government will find:it necessary to raise the number of the force to 10.000, and to strengthen its constitution very con- siderably in artillery and other war equipment in order to effect its complete organisation. SIR GARNET WOLSELEY'S MOVEMENTS. Sir Garnet Wolseley's first act after landing was to issue, with the sanction of the Khedive, a proclamation which would no doubt be very effective and productive of good results, if it could be disseminated widely enough. A de- claration is made that the British army fights only against those who are in rebellion against the lawful ruler of the land, and promises are given that "all peaceful inhabitants will be treated with kindness, and no act of violence will b.) committed against their religion. Their mosques, their families and their properties adwyliloloplbneeerlnsyreedostnphf eoecrtstietieerdta.hdpi inneAglgt l csosouruuppl supplies alongll iibeeses which may be wanted will be paid for, and the inhabitants ral grai cnt udh let: lu aretmhae di esn linet oe dwyntaol t ol Valle yr ai gn would undoubtedly come in quickly enough to the English camp, for these peaceful tillers of the soil are probably by this time weary enough of the requisitions made upon them by the self-constituted dictator. On Wednesday, after visiting the Khedive, Sir Garnet,

ecompanied by Generals the Duke of Connaught, Sir John Adve, Sir Archibald Alison, Willis, Hamley, Graham, Sir Evelyn Wood, and otter otfic,rs, inspected the positions a our outposts at Ran.leh. From personal observation during& this visit they were not enabled to learn much of the enemy's movements, but on that point they could gather valuable information from Colonel Gerard, who made successful reconnaissance in company with Captain Parr anal' the mounted infantry. These adventurous scouts not only got quite on the right flank of Arabi's lines, but succeededi while there in making hasty sketches of much value, ancV". notes of the enemy's dispositions. They ascertained beyond'l dopbt that the Arabs are strong in regular infantry. "The tents of at least 8,000 men were distinctly -counted." A duty of this`kind bravely undertaken an skilfully carried out by a mere handful of intelligent soldiers must necessarily be productive of more valuable results than any recon- naissance in force, and where practicable is always to be preferred, especially when dealing with foes who are not duly impressed with the moral effect of more imposing combination i that apparently end in no material advantage for the attacking side. The authorities lave decided to send out one or more ball ions which might have been used with much effect for reconnoitring at an earlier stage. SIR G. WOLSELEY'S PLAN OF ATTACK. A Renter's telegram fron, Alexandria, on Thursday, at 12.40 says :—Sir Garnet Wolseley has decided that the British advance shall not be made from Ramleh, bet from Aboukir. The troops will embark on Saturday, and land and attack the Aboukir Forts on Sunday. The Khedive paid a second visit to Sir Garnet Wolseley on board the Salamis this morning, and remained nearly an hour with the Commander-in-Chief.

Another telegram from Alexandria at noon on Thursday, per Exchange Telegraph Company, states :—Sir Garnet Wolseley will, it is believed in Alexandria, attack Arabi to- morrow night or Saturday morning in two columns. 01-4 e along the route of the last reconnaissance, the other by way of Aboukir Lake and Nechon, taking Arabi at the point where his right rear rests on the Mahmoudieh Canal.
NEGOTIATIONS FOR A SURRENDER. A Central News telegram from Alexandria, at 10-20 on

Thursday, states :—Negotiations are proceeding between the , Colonel of the 75th and one of the Khedive's officers on the one hand, and the Bedouin Sheik, near Meks, on the other, for the surre,nder of 2,000 Bedouins. The Sheik is expected at Meks at 11. o'clock to arrange terms. Sir Garnet Wolseley will inspect the Meks fortifications to-day.

RUSSIAN INTRIGUES AGAINST ENGLAND. An Exchange Telegraph Company's telegram from Con- stantinople, dated Thursday, says :--" Russian intrigues against England, instead of diminishing, as has been asserted, are increasing, and a general cry against England's policy as formulated by Mr. Gladstone is being raised and maintained. There is little hope that the Porte will yield another inch to Lord Dafferin's suzgestion as to the Con- vention, and some Russians openly state that they will take the Bosphorus under their protection if the English seize the Canal.
MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS. Th 2 Central Union of the Land League in Philadelphia Las disapproved of the proposal to send assistance to Arabi

The last of the troops included in the first army corps ordered to Egypt embarked on Monday in the Lydian Mon- arch, at Albert Docks, and in the Teviot, at Woolwich. Intelligence has been received at Port Said of varim;s movements of Arab troops in the neighbourhood of Kantara. One of Her Majesty's gunboats has entered the Canal.

A droll incident is reported from Ismailia. A British captain, "landing on business," with his boat's crew fully armed, was received by Arabi's soliPers with the usual military honours. A captain of the Egyptian army, supposed to be the bearer of despatches to Arabi, has been arrested at Suez, coming ' from the Red Sea, A number of documents in Arabic r thought to he important, have been found on him. Lake Mareotis near the railway junction of Malahla, is drying up fast, there being no infiltration from the Canal to. counteract evaporation. People are thus enabled to go to. and from Kafr Dowar beyond reach of the guns of our out— posts. The Press Association is informed that a major-general on the active list of the Royal Marine Light Infantry will very shortly leave for Egypt. It is considered advisable that the 3,000 men of marines in that country should have a briga- dier of their own. On arrival of the officer the mariues will be massed as an entirely separate brigade. Tuesday, being the last day of Bairam, the Khedive held a reception at the Rasel tin Palace. His Highness showed won- f derful tact and coolness in the way he received big guests. a He did not avoid mentioning passing events, but just 4 touched on them with happy lightness. He told some of the incidents of the anxious hours at Ramleh during the bombardment, and expressed hfs satisfaction at the arrival of such strong reinforcemen's. The foreigners in Alexandria, now that the immediate danger has passed away, and that they are safe behind British bayonets, begin to grumble and snarl at those who protect them. They have even formed a Vigilance Com- mittee to watch over European interests, and will be a source of trouble to Sir Garnet Wolseley if not firmly taken in hand.

A Stan(larl telegram says that Captain Ewart, late of the 78th Regiment, is now endeavouring to organise a corps of Bedouins for reconnoitring. purposes. He himself has made a plucky reconnaissance from Fort Melgs. He started at one in the morning, accompanied only by an interpreter, and by daybreak had ridden ten miles into the country. He estab. lisbed the fact that all the reports of large bodies of the enemy being established in that direction are wholly untrue. Preparations are being made by the War Office authorities for the shipment of a further body of men to Egypt, should Sir Garnet Wolieley require -reinforcements. It is not deemed probable that a second army corps will be despatched, but a few regiments of infantry from this country and a further contingent from India have been arranged for should Arabi's army show a stubborn resistance. In this case it is expected that the Government would ask Parliament to grant a further supply for the calling out of more reserves.

div.head: CETEWAYO IN LONDON.
div.p: CETEWAYO IN LONDON.

Cetewayo has recovered from his indisposition. On Satur-- daY morning he rose early, and after breakfast proceeded, in company of his attendant chiefs and Mr. Shepstone, to Regent-street, fctr the purpose of being photographed.. Shortly after ten o'clock on Sunday morning, Cetewayo, accompanied by his chiefs and his Interpreter, Mr. Dunn, proceeded to Wellington Barracks, on the invitation of Lieut.-Colonel Jones, to witness the church parade of the • regiment. The King was received on his arrival at the blacks by Colonel Jones, who entered into conversation. with him through the interpreter. He was conducted along the lines and seemed pleased with the Smart appearance of the men. He also expressed great pleasure at the perfor- mance of the band. After parade,the party were entertained to lunch in the officers' mess, returning to Melbury-road shortly after two. The remainder of the day was spent indoors, many visitors calling in the afternoon. During the day the crowd increased around the house to such an ex- . tent that the services of extra policemen were called in. In the evening, after-dinner, the King and party showed themselves at the door, the crowd soon after dispersing. At half-past eight on Monday morning, Cetewayo, attended by his cousin and chiefs, left London, accompanied by Mr. Shepstone and Mr. Dunn, to visit the Queen at Osborne. The party included the Earl of Kimberley. The train arrived at. Portsmouth at a quarter past eleven, and at the Town Hall a large crowd had assembled to see the -7Alln - King, who seemed rather pleased at the interest manifested by the people. On arriving at Cowes, the King was driven in a Royal carriage to Osborne amid the plaudits of the people, the crew of the Royal yacht 'Victoria and Albert forming a guard of honour. Cetewayo was introduced to Her Majesty by the Earl of Kimberley, and a long conVer- sation took place through the interpreter. The party re- -. turned to EastCowes at 3 p.m., and on reaching Portsmouth Cetewayo was loudly cheered from the beach. Shortly before noon on Tuesday Cetewayo left his residence, Melbury road, and, accompanied by his cousin, his chiefs, and Mr. Dunn and Mr. Sbepstone, drove to the Colonial Office, where he had an interview with lord Kimberley. Some time before the party reached Downing-street a considerable crowd had assembled, and as the carriages drove up the ex-King was gseeted with quite a popular ovation. Cetewayo was evi- dently much pleased wits his reception, and bowed his acknowledgments to the crowd. Mr. Shepstone had a pri- vate conference with Lord Kimberley before the sable monarch was shown into the reception-room of the Colonial Office. At one o'clock Cetewayo and the chiefs were ushered in to the presence of the- Colonial Secretary, with whom Cetewayo had a' private interview which occupied about three-quarters of an hour. Lord Kimberley explained to the ex-King the conditions upon which the Government would allow him to return to Zululand. With these Cete- wayo is believed to have expressed his satisfaction. Upon leaving the Colonial Office the distinguished visitor was again cheered, and his carri ige was followed by a demons strative crowd on driving off from Downing-street. On Wednesday afternoon, Cetewayo drove in a closed carriage to Marlborough House, where a call was made upon the Prince and Princess of Wales. Their Royal Highnesses, with whom were also the young princes, princesses, and suite, gave the Zulu King a very cordial reception. The Zulu Kina, with his chiefs and interpreter, again. visited the Colonial Office on Thurs4ay, and had an intervi-Aar with Lord Kimberley of about an hour and a half's durs';ioe, the conversation referring almost exclusively to a* range- ments for the King's restoration to the Zulu throne. Paring the afternoon Cetywayo remained at home and received several visitors.

THE RESTORATION OF CETEW,Ayo. A Durban telegram lavS :.--6‘ The report' hat the Governs ment intend to restore betevrayo cause,- . 4 consternation at such'reekless disregard of the peace colonists and natives— itemorials. an., ' And welfare of the , meetings are being organised. The ex-Ring's return i.s generally regarded as a certakn prelude to war, for which he English Governmat is iioiely responsible,"
