div.head: SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882.
div.p: SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882.

SIR GARNET WOLSELEY arrived at Alexandria on Tuesday, and the major portion of our expedition against the rebel forces having found a footing on Egyptian soil, in the course of a very few days— probably only a few hours—we may hear of an ad- vance movement from the British lines. The com- mander, happily, is in excellent health, havints quite recovered from his attack of fever; the officers and men are also said to be in capital spirits, and only eager to be led against the enemy. Our force is now believed to be strong enough to do what Sir Garnet May decide upon, and whatever that may be it is of course desirable that it should be done at once, while we are as yet unhampered with the presence of Turkish troops. No one con be more keenly alive to the ad- vantages we now possess in that respect than the Commander himself, and he may thereiule be trusted to make the most of them. Turkish duplicity and procrastination have on many occasions worked in- calculable mischief ; they have been the cause of much annoyance to our own as well as to other Governments from time to time, but on no occasion have they, as they are doing now, combined to further the very end which we are so anxious to attain.. If the Sultan will only continue hit shuffling movements we doubt not that before he has made up his mind what to de a blow will have been struck by the British Commander and his gallant army which will cause Arabi and his rebellious followers to submit. Though it was announced last week that at the re-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882.

!quest of Lord Dufferin the Sultan was prepared to issue a proclamation declaring Arabi by name a rebel, the signing of that important document ,is still delayed ; and the military convention between England and Turkey makes extremely slow progress, for the reason that the stringent terms which England insists upon do not commend themselves to the Oriental mind. The signature to the proclamation is supposed to be withheld in the hope that Ragland may be induced to modify the terms under which she will permit Turkish troops to co-operate with her in Agypt ; but if that be so the Sultan will find himself trusting to a broken reed. English diplomatists are wideawake enough to know that Turkish troops will be a greater hinderance than help to our military operations, and they are not, therefore, likely to be by any means betrayed into the purchase of the pro- clamation, much as they desire that Arabi should be proclaimed. If, however, the Sultan is trifling with us at Constantinople, the Khedive is giving us his active support in Egypt. Two decrees have this week been promulgated by his Highness, both being of immense importance, and rendered absolutely necessary by the work of pacification which we have undertaken. By one of these decrees the Khedive informs the military authorities in the Isthmus of Suez that Sir Garnet Wolseley and Admiral Seymour are authorised to occupy all the points they may consider useful and necessary for their operations; and by the other decree Admiral Seymour, as well as any officer acting under him, is empowered to take whatever measures may be deemed expedient to prevent t,he importation of coal and munitions of war along the whole extent of the coast between Alexandria and Port Said. This latter order is one which the governors of Port Said, Aboukir, Rosetta, and Damietta wilt be bound to respect and observe. The power which these decrees confer had already been practically assumed by us in order to safeguard our own interests, but the co-opera- and assistance of his Highness the Khedive is none the less acceptable; and the influence these proclama- tions will exercise in a moral sense on the native population as showing that we have the concurrence of the ruler of Egypt in our enterprises must be con- siderable. Though matters are progressing quietly but satisfactorily at the scene of future operatfteaseit is astonishing to find politicians of the Ashmead- Bartlett stamp--who are never tired of boasting of their patriotism and loyalty—doing all they can to discredit and embarrass the Government at home: In his usual bungling and blundering fashion the-mem- ber for Eye, on Tuesday, and again on Wednesday, attacked the Egyptian policy of the Government, in which, of course, he cannot expect to find any good point. This hon. member- naturally thinks—for what reason he does not 83y—that when the campaign is over the Government will only be at the beginning of their difficulties; and wilfully ignoring the part. wLich his own party has played in Egyptian politics, complains of our having for a time acted in concert with France, thus causing this country, he alleges, to lose the alliance bf Austria and Germany. The hon. member conveniently forgets that we were bound up to a certain point to act in con junction with France, that, in fact, was the policy of the joint Control handed down to us by our Conservativnpredecessors ; and as to the alliance of Austria and Germany, .we have the assurance of the Under. Secretary for Foreign Affairs that at no time were the relations between these countries and England more cordial than they are at the present moment. Sir Charles charactetised the statements of the member for Eye as "moonshine and nonsense," and when we read in well- informed quarters that "the Garman Govern- ment places full reliance on Mr. Glad- - stone's policy," and further that the Austrian press unequivocally approves it, we are not surprised at the blunt and expressive language which Sir Charles uses. Again, Mr. O'Donnell, who ought rather to be a friend of the Government, adversely criticises our Egyptian policy at every opportunity. Notwithstanding assurances again and *again repeated to the contrary, this hon. member will have it that out only object in going to war is to protect the bond- holders. He is continually endeavouring to damage. Mr. Goschen's aCtion in Egypt because he was at one time a member of the firm of Messrs. Pi-killing and Goschen, who negotiated several loans for the Egyp- tian Government, and he insinuates that the hon. mem- ber in going to Egypt on behalf of the Government of the day, and in order to extort money from the Egyptian people for his firm. and other "money- lenders," had been a party to oppression. There should, however, after the statement of Mr. Goschen on Tuesday, be no,longer any misunderstanding with reference to his conduct, if, indeed, there need have been any previously. He has not been in any way connected with Egyptian loans since the year 1866, the year previous to which he had retired from all connection with the firm; whilst it was not till 1876— ten years after—that he went to Egypt, and then only in, a perfectly honorary capacity. He had no pecuniary interest whatever in the country, and he went there solely to make the best arrangements that were possible in the interests of the tax-payers and the creditors. Mr. O'Donnelt's charges are. conse- quently groundless, and though their reckless repeti- tion may tend to blind the ignorant, with those whe know better they can have no weight whatever. According to the speeches of Sir Wilfrid Lawson and Sir George Campbell, on Wednesday, there is in the opinion of these hon. members even now an opportu- nity for equitable compromise in order to save blood- abed, and they would have England humiliate herself at the feet of Arabi. Depend upon it unless we strike the blow which Arabi has invited, and unless Ihis army is made to feel the full effects of our power, our influence in Egypt will be gone. The sooner this has been done, the better for all parties con- cerned. It is a mistake to suppose, as seems to be inferred in some quarters, that we have not the sym- pathy of .Europe in our work; for according to the latest utterances of the Foreign Secretary and his subordinate, our policy has the approval of all the continential Powers, by whom it is admitted thei e is no course open to us other than that we are pursuing. The position of England is one at the present moment certainly of unprecedented gravity, but it is one from which her army and navy will safely and honourably I deliver her, and in doing so we arc sure the aspira- tions of the National Party, if such there be in Egypt, will not in any way suffer. These aspirations for liberty the Government will do their utmost to foster and promote; and in rescuing the Egyptian people from the system of tyranny by which they have been crippled and oppressed, we are only obeying the dictates of humanity.

trict known as the Duke's Field. Ido not know how this could be brought to pass, but suggest that the Commis- sioners, as the representatives of the inhabitants, migh bring it before the Postal Authorities in London. How invigorating to the wearied frame are the breezes of " native air !" How they dispel lassitude and make vigorous the weak! And how often is the last prescription of a doctor to his patient away from childhood's home—" native air!" Even the murky, stench-laden, fuming, "native air " of Widnes has its virtues; unsuspected, it may be, by its gas- inhaling inhabitants; but still so it is. But what enterprising Widnesian ever thought of setting it up as a rival health resort to that salubrious spot, Southport—of pitting Widnes stinks against Southport ozone—West Bank against the Promenade—the muddy Mer3ey against the Irish Sea? Is this improbable? An incredulous smile perhaps greets the question. But do not more remarkable things occur in this electric, dynamitic, torpedoiticnineteenth century? What if already Widnes gas has proved more health-giving than Southport breezes? I will relate an instance. A. gentle- man who had lived Ole greater portion of his life in Widnes retired to Southport. He became ill, and not recovering very quickly, Be came to Widnes to inhale his " native air." In a fortnight he was, to use a " quack " phrase, completely restored. Who, after this, will attempt to stop the chimneys belching forth their black vapours to form an impenetrable fog in winter, an almost invisible scourge in summer? •

It will occasion no surprise that the Government have decided, under certain limitations, to restore Cetewayo to Zululand. He has been described by Lord Salisbury as "one of the most dangeroas and most bloodthirsty tyrants of the century ;" but if the noble Marquis were asked for proof of such a reckless assertion he would have a difficulty in producing it. Cetewayo is certainly not the most humane of monarchs, neither is he the most brutal ; but if in returning to his people he could take Lord Salisbury with him, his lordship's presence would doubtless have a very civilising influence, while a lo.lef sojourn in Zululand might not be without corresponding advantages to Lord Salisbury. Some portion of the now deposed King's country is to be reserved in order to meet obligations towards those cf the appointed chiefs and people who may not be willing to return under Cetewayo's,rule. Nine, however, if not ten, of those chiefs have already expressed a desire to have Cete- wayo restored ; so that if the remaining four, with their people, be reckoned as opposed to Cetewayo—of which by the way, there is no evideace—the opposition is not very formidable. A British resident is to be maintained in Zulu- land, and Cetewayo is to be required to enter into engage- ments similar to those by which the thirteen chiefs are now bound, which specially inolude a prohibition to revive in any form the military system which formerly prevailed. It is gratifying to learn that no portion of Zululand will be annexed to British territory. This, to my mind, is the best feature in the arrangements for Cetewayo's restoration. Lord Salisbury is very much concerned that all this means a reversal of policy, hut surely it is much more honourable 'to boldly reverse a policy than for the Government to main- tain one which they believe to be wrong.

There are very few,tit any scholars who would be prepared to draw a distinction between a " falsehoo4" and a'" false statement," yet this is what Mr. Callan, the member for Louth, endeavoured to do the other evening. In committee of the House the hon. member frequently characterised the state- ments of the Home Secretary with respect to certain Irish members as false, and when cllled to order refused to with- draw; rather did he propose to exonerate himself by a species of reasoning not very clear. The chairman of the committee, Dr. Playfair—hitnself by no means an ignoramus —refused to he gulled by Mr. Callan's display of erudition, and the member forLouth had in respect of his interruptions to again undergo the penalty of suspension. This is the second occasion Mr. Callan has been suspended this session, and the result of a third suspension would have been that his constituents would have had to suffer, as well as him- self, inasmuch as he would not have been allowed to take his seat again during the remainder of the session. Would it not be well for constituencies to weigh v; ell the con- sequences before they return representatives of Mr. Callan's calibre? and on the other hand, it seems to me advisable that members should be , a little more respectful and gentlemanly in their behaviour in the first Senate of the world.

I think we have been altogether too lavish in our praises of the conduct of. Admiral Seymour and the Britieh fleet before Alexandria, and it would appear I am not alone in this opinion. I endorse, and lam sure many of my readers will endorse, every word of the following passage, clipped from the St. James's Gazette:—" To every deserving man his due reward, and a word of approval for him who does his duty well. But, for a great nation, are we not becoming a little too much excited about the valour and the skill of our forces at Alexandria? The born')ardment, was very well done, but surely the reduction of the Egyptian forts, manned as they were, was not a wonderful achievement— nothing for the 'greatest of naval Powers to brag about ; nor are we aware of anything that has since happened which. justifies the use of large and boastful language. The truth seems to be that a rather unpleasant change has passed over the national temper in this respect. There were times when the soldier or the sailor who did his duty on ordinary occasions in an ordinary way, neither sought nor received any particular recognition of his services. He was ex- pected to do his duty; be did it, and there was an end of the matter. It was only when exceptional dangers were met with exceptional skill, steadiness, and daring that re- cognition and reward came in ; and they were the sweeter because they were known to be shared only by the doers of really great deeds. All that is changed ; and at this rate we shall soon see every officer who does a good piece of outpost duty imitating the demeanour of the popalar danseuse when she trips to the footlights at the end of a graceful fling." FLACCU3.

APPROACHING REVISION OF VOTERS AT WIDNES.—We understand that the Liberals have made 50 claims and the Conservatives nine claims for owners of property in Widnes to be placed on the Parliamentary register. In Ditton, Bold, and Cronton each party has made 10 claims. It will thus be seen that the Liberals are far in advance of their opponents.

WIDNES DRUNEARDS.--At Widnes Petty Sessions on Mon- day, the following persons were fined ss. and costs by Mr. John Brock, the magistrate :—Patrick Harvey, Moses Rowell,. Thomas McKenny, Martin Egan, Susan Laing, Eden Nolan, Ann Gibson, Thomas Kelly, Stephen Quigley, Joseph Smith, Joseph Croft, and Mary Ann Tobin.

STAR OF WIDNES LODGE 1.0.G.T.—8r0. J. Nelson Jones, of Crewe, gave an address on the benefits of temperance to the menA)ers of this lodge on Wednesday, the meeting being presided over by Bro. H. Hutton, W.C.T. He also gave several recitations Ond songs, including "The badge of blue." Bro. J. Reay, of the Hope of Appleton Lodge, gave an address and recitation; and Bro. Boardman, of the Port- land Oregon Lodge, U.S.A., sang "The sailor's grave." A FORGIVING WIFE. Jeffrey Waring was summoned by his wife before the Runcorn bench of magistratps, on Monday, for assaulting her on the 9th mat, and he pleaded guilty. Mrs. Waring said she did not want to press the case; all she wanted was quietness and peace. He had pro- mised her that morning that he „" would never do it no more." She had been married 30 years, and if he would promise to mend she would withdraw the summons. Mr. Bankes (one of the magistrates, to defendant): Will you do so? Defendant (unconcernedly): Oh, yes. (Laughter.)— The summons was withdrawn..

WIDNES (No. 429) INVINCIBLE ORANGE LODGE has passed a resolution expressing condolence for the wife and family of the late Mr. James Clunie, who was master of the local Orange lodge. A vote of thanks was also accorded tsi the Star of Temperance Lodge for their services at Mr. Clunie's funeral. About 80 members of the ledge, accom- panied by representatives from Liverpool, Warrington, Penketh, and St. Helens, on Monday atteniled.Divine service at Widnes Parish Church. They wore the regalia of the order. The vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, preached a suitable sermon to the brethren.

TIIE POLICE A SS&IILTED BY A WOMAN AT RUNCORN.—At the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, a young woman named Catherine Kenealy was charged, before Mr. Banks and Mr. Chadwick, with being drunk and disorderly early that day, and also with assaulting P.C. Finney.—lt ap- peared that about half-past one the prisoner was creating a great disturbance in Cooper-street, where a large number of sailors were congregated. • The officer ordered her to leave the street, but she refused to do so, and struck him a blow on the eye.—P.C. Burkhill stated he saw a stone in the prisoner's hand after she had struck Finney.—The prisoner told the magistrates it was all through drink, and Superin- tendent Williamson produced a very black list against her. —Mr. Bankes said she was going from "bad to worse." and for being drunk and aisorderly she would be fined 20... and costs, or a month ; and for the assault go to gaol for two months.

WILFUL DAMAGE TO HAY AND CROPS. - Patrick' McCabe, James Keating, Thomas McManus, Robert Brown, and William Wright, boys, were at Whines Police Court on Wednesday, each summoned for doing damage to the extent of Is. to a certain crop of growing corn belonging to Eliza- beth Hulme. McManus did not appear. It appeared that on Sunday last, about half-past five, the defendants were bathing in a pit close by the corn field in question. When they came out of the water, they ran through the field, and trampled down the corn. The manager of the farm stated there had been much damage done. The boys bad no right to go in the pit. Each defendant was ordered to pay Sc. 3.1. —A boy named Joseph Caffey was summoned for doing wilful damage to a hay stack, the property of Mrs. E!iza- beth Huhne. Peter Spark, cowman, said the defendant climbed upon the new bay stack and pulled down four or five cwt. of hay, doing damage amounting to 2s. There were other boys also on the stack, but made good their escape. Mr. Hall said this was down right wilful damage, and fined defendant 29. di., pay the damage and costs, al!ogether 10s. •t3J ,

THE ATTEMTED HORRIBLE OUTRAGE ON CHILDREN AT WlDNES.—Jarnes Moran, a tailor, living in Wellington- street, was brought up on remand at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, charged with attempting to commit a rape upon Elizabeth Holden and Catherine Riley, girls nine years of age. The case was beard privately by Mr. John 'Brock, as the details were of a most atrocious nature; and after the evidence had been given, the prisoner was com- mitted to take his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

ASSAULT ON THE Poiicr..—On Wednesday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Messrs. H. S. Hall and John Brock, Thomas Burke was brought up, on remand, charged with assaulting P.C. Hargreaves whilst in the execution of his duty.—The officer stated that whilst P.C. Thompson and P.C. Laing were bringing a female prisoner along Victoria- road, on Saturday night, the prisoner took hold of Thompson's arm and attempted: to rescue the woman. Witness went to him and informed him that he would have to go to the police station to explain his conduct. The prisoner resisted, struck the witness in the face with his fist,. knocked him to the ground, and kicked him several times. —The Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for a month. with hard labour, without the option of a fine. THE REV. THOMAS HUGHES, OF WIDNES.7-ThiS gentle- man, who is the pastor of the Welsh Wesleyan Church, has been appointed to the Carnarvon circuit, and in the course of next week will depart from Widnes. He will he succeeded by the Rev. D. A. Richards, of Ruthin. During his brief sojourn of twelve months, Mr. Hughes has been the means of putting in a fair way for accomplishment the project for a new chapel, which, with his other untiring labours' has won for him the respect of his congregation. while his unfailing courtesy has won for him the good opinion of all with whom he came in contact. He took a pro- minent part in all temperance matters, appearing before the public on several occasions to give the cause his warm advocacy. Not only the Welsh Wesleyans, but the public generally, will regret his departure, and their hearty good wishes for his success will follow him to his new sphere of labour.

THE IRISHMAN AND THE COAT: THE CONFIDING RUNCORN TAILOI2.—On Monday, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, an Irish labourer, named Thomas Henry Gibbons, was charged in custody, that he being bailee of a Coat, value 303., the property of James Littlemore, did ap- propriate the same to his own use, thereby feloniously, stealing the same. The prosecutor is a tailor, and keeps a shop in Greenway-road, Runcorn. 7 On Saturday, the sth inst., the prisoner called at the shop, and asked the prose- cutor to make him a suit of clothes. The prosecutor re- plied that before he could do so the prisoner must deposit Not having that amount upon him, the prisoner asked for the loan of an overcoat for half an hour, and pro- rnisd to pay the in the evening. He was lent the coat, and did not return to the shop again until Saturday last, when he inquired if the suit which he had ordered was ready, and not only did he refuse to pay the promised de- posit of £2, hut also to return the overcoat until the suit was wade. Information was given to the police, and it transpired that the prisoner had sold the coat to Mr. Patrick Collins, clothitr, Church-street, on the same day on which he had obtained it, and for the small rum of ,23. 6d. He "was in drink, but not drunk" at the time. On Saturday he again went to Collins's, and wished to buy the coat trick for 7s. 61. He was apprehended by P.C. Morris. The prisoner informed the Bench that he was drunk when he sold the coat, and "did not know what he was doing any more than a toel."—Mr. Bankes said drunkenness tY,.AS no excuse, but the Bench thought he did not intend to steal the coat, and would deal leniently with him by Going him only 103., and £1 is. costa. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE RAILWAY COMPANY AT FARNWORTM—An elderly woman named Elizabeth •Clare was brought up at 'Widnes Police Court, before Messrs. S. 11. Hall anl John Brock, charged with riding on the Cheshire Lines Railway, on the 17th July, without previously paying her fare, with intent to•avoid payment thereof—From the evidence it appeared that the defendant was on Warrington Central station when the 11-33 train for Liverpool was about to depart. She informed the foreman porter, named Edward Hughes, that she wished to go to Farnworth. She, however, stated she had no ticket, hut would pay when she arrived at Farnworth. As she was an old lady, and that the , last train, he placed her in a carriage, and told the guard of the circumstance. When the train reachPd Farnworth the defendant alighted, and when asked for her fare she alleged that she had given a porter is. to obtain her a ticket, hut he had neither given her the ticket nor the change. Mr. Nutter, the stationmaster, said he could not accept that statement, when the defendant commenced to use bad language, and declared she would not leave the station until she bad received 6d. A threat to put her in charge of a policeman made her rather calm, and Fdp, On offered !o pay the far. Under the circumstances the railway oMcials refused to accept it, and the case was reported to the manager.—Defen- dant told the Bench that she had travelled for 33 years, and had never been in such an unfortunate position before.—She , was fined 53. and costs. .

A Row AT WEST BANK WIDNES: PROPERTY DEMOLISHED. —Henry White and Mary White, husband and wife, were summoned to Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, to answer a charge of committing wilful damage to the property of Elizabeth Jones, livinc, in West Pak-street.—Mr. T. J. Peters appeared for the defendants.—The Complainant said that on Saturday the 12th inst., about 9-39 p.m., the defen- dants created a disturbance in the street, and sent a number of stones through the window, damaging very much a chest of drawers, and smashing all the ornaments upon it. Then they broke a large washing tub, and sent the pieces through the window. The damage amounted to £1 10s.—Ann Curtis a young woman, who lived with the complainant stated that ' on the day in question, she was standing at the door when the defendants came up. Mrs. White celled leer a "fearful name," and gave her a push, and she went in. Mr, White followed her and the 'lodger put him out, and load the itico,, With her arm, Mrs. White then smashed two panes lof glass, and Prat stones and pieces of timber through the window breaking the sash. Eleven panes of eass were mashed ; six of them by Mr. White.—Corroborative evi• -aenca was given by Ellen Jones.—Mr. Peters addressed tl Bench for the defence, and called David Hall, who lodged with the defendants. He alleged Ann Curtis commenced the disturbance, and emphatically stated Mrs. White did not leave the house during that night.— The Complainant said the witness was keeping ! " nicks " for the defendants.—Mr. Hall said the Bench considered the case proved, and fined each defendant • 55., and Bs. 6d. costs, and pay the damage. Altogether each defendant had to pay £1 18s. fitl.,!or in dzfault one raonth's hard labour.

• I ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM TIIE PERSOM AT WIDNES.— At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a man named Matthew Cassin was brought up on remand from Monday charged with stealing 18s. from the person of Mary Inge- hart, living in Charlotte street, at Widnes. It appeared that the prosecutax, on Saturday night, received 18s. from Mr. Cassin, a relative of the prisoner. About eight o'clock she went to the prisoner's house in Water-street, but as he was not at home she, with her sister-in-law, went in search of him. They found him, and stood talkine, with him for some time in an entry near a house which the prisoner had left shortly before. On leaving him the prosecutrix missed the money, which had been loose in her dress pocket, and at once suspected the prisoner. She then went to the house where the prisoner was, and said "Matt, give me my money, you have taken from my pocket." He replied, " What! me take money out of your pocket," and laughed. Prose- cutrix said she was sure he had taken it, but the prisoner refused to return it, and wanted her to have some drink. She gave information to the police, and the prisoner was subsequently apprehended.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Husband, who appeared for the prisoner, the prosecutrix said she had walked through a very crowded thoroughfare before she saw the prisoner —Kate Cassin, .sister of the prisoner, and who was with the prosecutrix on the night in question, stated she did not see the prisoner put his hand into the prosecutrix's pocket and he could not have done so without her seeing him—P.C. Almond stated that the prisoner, when apprehended, pulled out of one pocket 18a.— one two shilling piece and 16 shillings—exactly similer pieces to those stolen from the prosecutrix. He bed also money in other pockets.—Mr. Husband having spoken for the defence. the prisoner was committed to take his trial at Liverpool Sessions. IMPURE' LITERATURE AT RUNCOUN.—EXEMPLARY PuNrslietEerr.—A young man named John Woods was brought up in custody at Runc)rn Police Court, on Mon- day, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. Henry Reynolds, charged with offering an indecent publication for sale in Bridge-street, on Saturday night.—Prisoner pleaded guilty. —Mc. Superintendent Williamson said a little before nine o'clock he became aware of a large cro.vd on the Market ground, and went there to discover its cause. Seeing the prisoner there selling a piece of paper for 2d., and giving away a book as he alleged, he (the superintendent) caused one to be purchased. At that time the prisoner was selling them indiscriminately to old and young, and was doing plenty of "business." . After obtaining the book he ad- journed to the oflice•and perused it, and then came to the conclueion that it was certainly indecent. The Superinten- dent then arrested the man. anil in his possession was £1 is. and about 18 books. The prisener's manner of selling the book was this. He said, "I dare not sell these books as they are, but I have to turn the leaf down so as not to dis- close the name, and I sell you this piece of paper for two- pence and give you this book." The Superintendent said it was an abominable work, and ought to be suppressed.—The prisoner, who had pleaded guilty, said he did not sell the book to boys, only to men, and he was given to understand by the publisher, and also the agent at Manchester, that the work was not indecent in a legal settee. They were sold on the book stalls in Manchester, and also openly in the street. In the daily newspapere, of the day he could find phrases as bad as any in the hooke—The Superintendent remarked that Inspector Hollingworth had seen the prisoner supply boys from 12 to 14; although be was continually saying, "I won't sell them to boys and girls under 14." As to the statement that the work could be purchased anywhere in Manclieser, he was sorry to say that there were many publications sold in Manchester and ether towns which would not be allowed if it were known .—lnspector Hollingworth was called, and proved the sale to boys under 14.—Mr. Bankes said the Bench con- sidered the book was a most indecent one, and ought never to have been sold to the public on any pretence whatever.— The prisoner was fined 40e. and co.ets, 6e. 41, or in default, 14 days' hard labour,

THE WELSH WESLEYAN BAZAAR.—The total sum realised at the bazaar, which was open six evenings, was £173. Ruxconx CO-OPERATIVE SocIETY.—A trip in connection with this society went to Blackpool on Mouthy last, and was largely patronised. The day was fine, and the many amusements of the Brighton of the North were fully enjoyed. TEMPERANCE 'MEETING AT RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance, an open-air meeting was held on the Market Ground, Runcorn, on Wed- I nesday evening, and there was a large attendance, composed I mainly of working men. The speakers were Mr. C. H. Murray, of Preston. and Mr. J. Paton, of Barrhead. The addresses were listened to with great attention. RUNC,ORN COMMISSIONERS OFFICES.—A refel ence to our advertising columns will show that the Commissioners invite offers for the occupation of the Public Offices, which comprise three rooms. The board-room is very spacious, and the secretary's and surveyor's offices are of moderate size, and conveniently fitted up. They also occupy a very central position- in the town.

NELSON STREET SCHOOL, RuxcaßN.—Oa Saul ly the anniversary sermons in connection with this church were preached in Camden School Chapel, morning and evening, by the Rev. Geo. S. Weston, of Liverpool. In the afternoon, Mr. J.R. Frith gave an address to the schelars. Tile; collec- tions amounted to £l6, an increase of £3 on last year. It may be interesting to state that there are now 180 scholars attending school, while the teachers' roll contains 16 names.

I. O.G. T. HOPE OP Rtrivoonx LODGE. —Th e ordinary meeting of this lodge was held on Friday night week. After the business had been transacted, a fruit banquet was held. Flowers and ferns, judiciously displayed, imparted to the room an attractive appearance and the tables were plentifully supplied with fruit of various kinds. Sisters Mcßride, Heald. Jones, and Foster had carried out the arrangements. The proceedings were rendered additionally pleasant by a humorous recitation by Bro. Jones, of Crewe, and readings by Bros. J. Coventry and Jno. Faulkner. The Rey. Geo. Hack delivered as hort and appropriate address.

WIDNES PA.RISH CHIJECII PIC•NIO TO CHESTER.— I Once a year it is customary to give the choir of Widnes Parish Church a pc-nic, and this year it was decided to ' combine with it a trip in which the congregation could par- ticipate, Chester being the destination fixed upon. The project was very successful, ever 300 persons booking by the special t:ain which conveyed the party from Widnes at 8-30 on Saturday morning, arriving at 'Chester about ten o'clock. The route taken was via Ditton, Runcorn, and Friodsham. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar; the Rev. G. Bond, vicar of Farnworth and party •, Mr. W. Treacv, senior, churchwarden; and Mr. Crawford, organist and choir- muster, were among thosa who accompanied the excursion. Favoured with beautiful weather, ample time, and pleasant company, the beauties of the interesting and ancient city were vit.‘,,ved to advantage, and greatly appreciated by the Widnesians. The choir, accompanied by the vicar, Mr. Treacy, senior, and Mr. Crawford, paid a visit to Eaton Hall during the day. The excursionists arrived back at Widnes at 9-30.

ENTERTAINMENT AT Sr. MARY'S CATHOLIC SCHOOLS, DITTON.—A musical and dramatic performance in aid of the ! school funds was given at the above schools on Thursday evening, before a large and appreciative audience. The first, part of the programme included a humorous farce entitled, The fatal bet," and the various parts were creditably sustained by the boys. The. caste was Mr. Kerr, the inn- keeper, J. Moran ; Mr. Allright, the physician E.'Fazacker- ley •' Mr. Perchance, J. Devine ; Mrs. Pick, H. Devine; Mr. Rock, J. Connolly ; Mr. Watch, W. Hull; two thieves, J. Walsh and T. McCann. "The Magic Wand," a pantomime, was next performed, the characters being sustained by W. P. Martin; J. Devine, E. Fazackerley, J. Moran; W. Con igan, H. Devine, J. McHugh, W. Hull, J. T. Beesley, J. Walsh, sod J. Connolly. The second part of the programme con- sisted of selections from the Cantata, "The Flower Queen," and they were very sweetly and expressively rendered. S. , A. McGrath sing " Here would I rest," M. Bailey the solo , "Crocus," A. J. Long and IT. Walsh the duet "-Lily and rose," K. and W. Brandreth "Violet and primrose," E. Darlington "Holly-bock," W. G. Martin" Dande!ion," and E. Wakefield "Touch-me-not." Selections were also sung by M. Greathanks, M. Longton, M. Walsh, A. J. Corrigan, and E. Rimmer. Father Evers performed the duties of accom- panist with his usual success. DAIIIGING A CORN FIELD AT RUNOolol.—Thomas Williams, senior, and Edward Ceskey, were summoned at the Runcorn Police Court, on :Clonday, for having, on the sth inst , unlawfully committed damage to corn then grow- ing in a certain field recopied by Joseph Ashley, by tramp- ling upon and breaking down the same. The prosecutor said he .had suffered greatly through his corn being trampled , down, and he had been obliged to mow several lots owing , to the damage done to it. The damage in this case amounted to 2s. 6-I.—The son of the proseco tor deposed to seeing the defendants in the oats. He ran towards thsm, when they tried to escape over the wall. He, however, caught Caskcy, and said to Williams " All right, Tom," who, discovering he was known, stopped.—Defcndants contended that two men and two women had done the damage, and denied that they were among the cereals.—A witness named Mary Jolley stated CasLev only got over the wall, which was mounted by Williams, who threw a bucket of water on the persons on the other side.—Pt osecutor's son, recalled, per- sisted in his statement that the dehndants were in the corn. There were other people also in, but these ha could not c stela—The Chairman said the Bench were quite satisfied the defendants had committed the offence, and would each be fined is. and costs, and must pay the damage.—Thomas Williams, jun. (son of the defendant in the last case) and i Alfred Ellis were brought up on a similer Oleo, me, Asbiey 5.11..1. he had previomly bad to complain of Williams, and Ellis had been before iaie Bench. For the defence, it , was alleged that a calf had done the damage; but Harriet Ashley, prosecutor's daughter-in-law, deposed to seeing the defendants in the field. Williams was ordered to pay a tine of is. and half the costs, and half the damage is. 3d. Ellis was ordered to pay a fine of 2s. 61. and costs, and half the damage is. 3d. MILK ADVLTERITION AT WIDNES. The chargd .01 selling milk not of the "nature, substance, and quality delnanded, which was preferred against Mrs. Ann Board- men, milk dealer, Widnes-road, a fortnight ago, was finally adjudicated upon at the Widnes Police Court, 6il Wednes- dav, The magistrates on the Bench were Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. John Broek. From the statement of Mr. Superin- tendent Barker, it appeared that on the morning of the 14th of July, he entered the shop of the defendant, where he saw a mug of milk on the counter. He enquired of the young woman in attendance, who stated her name was Boardman, what kind of milk the mug contained. She replied "new milk." Thereupon the Superintendent purchased a quart for which he peid 3d., and having informed the attendant of , the course he intended to take, he sent it to the public analyst, Mr. Campbell Brown. That gentleman had for- warded a certificate which stated the milk contained 3 2 parts of fat, 77 parts of other solids, and 15 parts of water to every hundred parts of milk.—Mr. G. T. Moore, of War- rington, who appeared for the defence, submitted that though the defendant might be legally guilty of the offence with which she was charged, sne was not morally so. She was a woman of most irreproachable character, and euring her long residence in Widnes no breath of suspicion had attached itself to her. Mr. Moore produced a large bundle of testimonials, including one from the Vicar of the Parish, who spoke in high terms of the defendant's character, and expressed his conviction that she could not be intentionally guilty of fraud such as that with which she was charged.— Mr. Superintendent Barker said he had nothing whatever to say against the character of the defendant—Mr. Hall, in fining the defendant £2 and costs, remarked that the Bench were bound to protect the public in this matter, but they had taken a lenient view of the case.

REFUSING THE OATH AT WIDNES POLICE-COURT.— On Wednesday, at the Widnes Police-court, an Irishman, named Patrick Lynch, was brought up on remand, charged with committing an aggravated assault upon his sister, Ellen White. On the sth inst. the prisoner was given into custody by the prosecutrix on a charge of unlawfully wounding her. At that rime she had a most severe wound on the bead, which was bleeding profusely, and according to the statement of P.C. Almond she was "dripping." She alleged her brother had made a savage attack upon her with 3 piece of iron. When, however, the prisoner was brought before the magistrates on the Monday following, the prose- cutrix was missing. The case was consequently remanded two days, and the prosecutrix was warned to attend, but she again failed to appear and a warrant was granted for her apprehension. On Saturday, the 12th inet , she was taken in custody, and was remanded in gaol until Wednesday last. She then, however, refused to be sworn, and Mr. Superinten- dent Barker asked the Bench to mike an example of her. Pro- secutrix asserted that the prisoner had not struck her, and hinted that she hid got her wound by falling on her back.— Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) remarked that she was only doing her brother's case harm by her obstieate refusal to be sworn, and &aid he would only have to be remanded and re- remanded.—Prosecutrix (doggedly): If he his remanded all his life, I refuse to take the oath ; (and she jumped from the bax).—An officer : Stand in the oox.—Prosecutrix : I won't take the oath. She was proceeding to make some statement when Mr. Lewin interposed and said: You can tell that when you are sworn.—Prosecatrix: I will not be, sir.—Mr. Lewin: Then the magistrates will keep him until your swear.—Prosectitrix : I will not be sworn if they keep him for ever.—Mr. Lewin asked her if she would affirm, but she exhibited as great a repuguance to affirming as she did to taking the oath, and she was ordered to "stand down." At the conclusion of the business of the court she was again tolaced•in the box, and Mr. Hall asked : Do you still refuse to be sworn and give evidence in this case? Prosecutt (with a curtsey): Yes, your worship. (Wildly) I won't take the oath if you hang me by hooks to the ceiling. Aftee a short consultation the Beach committed her .to gaol for seven days, and remanded_ for the same period the prieimer, who murmured it was "hard upon him." Both the prisoner and prosecatrix were then removed.

I was pleased to read, the other day, that Widnes Local Board is still working to have the crossing nuisance on Waterloo-road removed. Their efforts, however, do not seem to meet with a very ready response from the railway company, which seldom exerts itself for the convenience of the public unless compelled. The nuisance at present is not so bad as it was some months ago, but the crossing ought to be dispensed with altogether. Sometimes I have the misfortune to have to stand looking over the gate while a train passes, and from what I then hear it would appear to be the cause of more blasphemy than the Salvation Army can "wash over" in a few months. The Board, however, is determined to have the matter remedied, and threaten to apply for powers to compel the company to do so, if the company will not quickly take action without. I have often thought that Runcorn is behind the times as regards postal facilities. Many towns of the size of Run- corn have a receiving box for the collection of letters at the local railway station. If 'one was placed in the Runcorn railway station it could not fail to be a great boon to travellers, merchants, captains of vessels, and. sailors, as well as to the large population of Newtown and Higher Runcorn. If this were done the pillar box at the lower corner of Waterloo Bridge might with great advantage be removed to the corner of Lord-street so as to meet the con- venience of the rapidly increasing inhabitants of the
' MIDNIGHT EPISODE AT FA RN WORTH'
STATION.

Yesterday, at the Widnes Police Court. before Mr. John Brock, a youn,4 woman named Mary Agnes Smith was charged with wilfully and maliciously breaking a pane of glass, of the value of 10s., the property of the Cheshire Lines Railway Company.—lt appeared from the evidence of Mr. Nutter, stationmaster, Farnworth Central, that the prisoner arrived at that station by the 11-43 p.tn, train on the previotts night. She presented a return half from Warrington to Widnes, niul demanded . that she should be conveyed to that place. She was told that it was only by an act of kindness that she had been permitted to travel to Farnworth, when she com- menced to use vile language, and becime very boisterous. As she was under the influeuce ,s.,f liquor, she was expelled from the platform. No sooner was she outside than Mr. Nutter heard the crashing of glass, and discovered that the, office window bid been smashed. He went in search of the prisoner, but was unable to find her. Two hours after- wards, however, he saw the prisoner emerge from a field of oats, and as rain bad been falling very heavily she was in -a wet "daggled " condition. She was given in charge of a police constable, and conveyed to the Widnes Folic, swion.—lospector Barnett said the prisoner was a stranger to the torin.—Mr. Brock remarked that it was doubtless through drink that the prisoner found herself in that position, and third her ss. and costs, and ordered her to pay the damage, or go to gaol for seven days. She went to gaol.

A STarcGLE WITH A DRUNKEN MAN.—At the Occasional Court House, Bank-street, Warring on, on 3lon lay, before Messrs. E. Greenall and James Mirson, John Regan was charged with being drunk and disorderly, at Whitler Superior, on the 13th inst.; and he was farther charged wi h assaulting. P.C. Speed whilst in the execution of his duty.—Prisoner commenced to assault the constable, and dealt him a blow on the face. During the struggle which ensued, both the prisoner and c•lnstable stumbled against some railings, whicla gave way, and thoy were precipitated into a clay pit, a distance of about six feet, but fortunately they recceived no serious injaries.—The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs.

THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE PRODCCTIVE SOCIETY: IN LIQUIDATION.—On Saturday meetings of the loan and shareholders in this society were held at Little. borough, when the liquidator submitted a report and balance sheet for the quarter ending July 8. The report states that the flannel trade continues in the same languid and un- profitable condition that has marked it for some time past; and that there are no signs of immediate improvement. The sales for the quarter have reached £3,428 ss. id., being £B7B 13s. sd. more than in the previous quarter, and £1 054 18s. 7d. more than in the corresponding quarter of last year. The share capital is £2,640 and loan capital £10,145, and after crediting this last sum with interest at the rate of five per cent par annum, and depreciating machinery and mill plant to the extent of £llO 10s. id., there is a profit on trade account of £8 14s. 41d. This is applied to reduce the balance loss; which now stands at £155 3s. 41.

ALLEGED WHOLESALE ROBE7.RIES AV WARRINGTON.— Ann Withingshaw, of Barrington, near Little Leigh, wife of a carrier and small farmer, was-charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Webster ard Captain Litton, with stealing from the shop of Mr. J Burgess, Bridge Foot, on Wednesday afternoon, one box of tea weighing 201bs ,value £2; with stealing from the shop of Mr. William Fairclough, corn dealer, Bridga Foot, one sack of Inuian meal, value ss. 41, on the same day; and also with stee"eg from the shop of Sergeant Brayshaw, milliner, Bridge-street, on Wedneeday, May 17, one chip hat, value £1 Is. On Wednesday afternoon the prisoner went into Mr. Burgess's shop and asked for halt a pound of tobecce and a quantity of candles, putting half a crown on the counter to pay for the same. Some other persons came into the shop and Mr. Burgess's assistant, Robert Smith, served them with the goods they required. The prisoner in the meantime made her way out of the shop carrying with her a box of tea which she placed in her cart, which she left in charge of her son whilst she went into the shop. She then took the cart to the Norton Arms. Mr. Burgess's assistant at once closed the shop and followed the prisoner to the Norton Arms Hotel yard. He then in- informed P.C. Pace, who queetioned the !Queen about the tea, when she replied that she thought the youog min in the AO told her to leave the tea at the Cat and Lion public-house. The constable then took the prisoner and the cart down to the police- station, and her son was sent home to inform his father that his mother was locked up. Mr. Wm. Fairhurst reported to the police that during the afternoon he had had a bag of meal, weighing 521b5., stolen from his shop, and he recol- lected that the prisoner had been to make some enquiries, and that her movements were very suspicioue.The police found the sack of Meal lo her cart,—:::;;ircv;.or co with P.S. Blair, of the Cheshire County Police, went to the prisoner's residence the same evening. They found a large store of goods of the value • of about £2O, which were produced in court, and among which were about 30 yards of Scotch plaid, a sealskin jackei, five new hats and one bc,nuet ; one roll of grey tweed, about 40 yards; about a dozen yards of winsey ; an electro-plated pint pot, supposed to be one of three missing from the Lion Hotel ; one hat, which had been stolen from Sergeant Brayshaw's shop; about Bilbs. of beef, valued at ss. 6d., which had been left at Mr. Bamford's shop; and a number of other articles.—Mr. Hunt asked for prisoner to be remanded until Monday for inquiries to be made.—The application was granted. IRISH CHURCH Messrows.—On Sunday, special sermons were preached in the Parish Church, St. Helens, on behal of these missions, by the Rev. Canon Shea, rector of Kilanin, County Galway. There were gool congregations and liberal collections.—On Monday evening, a public meet. ing in aid of the Missions was held in the Parish Church schoolroom. Councillor C. J. Bishop occupied the chair, and he was supported by a number of the local clergy.—The Chairman expressed his pleasure at seeing so many persons present, and said that the spread of the truths of the Bible in Ireland was at present a matter of the highest importance even from an economical point of view, from the fact that the Protestant population of Leland was a law-abiding population, and the spread of the truths of the Bible would go a very great deal further in preventing crime than any number of Crime Prevention Acts. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. H. J. Cheeseman, M.A., next addressed the meeting, and said that the Irish Church Missions were the best remedial agent which could be found for the many social evils existing in the sister country. Irish discontent and lawlessness had been ascribed to many causes. It had been ascribed to the reckless speeches of wild agitators, and to political causes, but he believed there was something deeper in the national life to ac6unt _for the havoc and ruin which had been brought about. Some said it was because the Irish were hot-headed, and set it down to their temper and dis- position, but the true cause after all was to be found in the religion of the vast majority of the people of that country. (Hear, bear.) He might say at the very outset that he did not come there to play the part of a bigot, and he did not deny that many Roman Catholics were noble upright men and, women, but he could not resist the conclusion without being false to his deepest convictions, that the direct tendency of Romanism was disastrous to the moral well- , )aeing of their sister country—lreland. (Hear, hear.) Where Protestantism prevailed in that country they were com- paratively free from outrage and crime, and he was pleased to say that their converts were staunch and true, and would not budge an inch from their loyal principles. He believed he could say that there was not one of their converts who had had anything to do with the Land League. (Applause.)—The Rev. Canon Shea, in addressing the meeting, referred to the efforts which were being 'made to depreciate the efforts of the Irish Church Missions, and asked his hearers not to credit all they might hear with regard to them. He then said they had been at work in many districts in the west of Connemara where they had brought out many from the Church of Rome and formed them into various little congre- gations, and in those places there had been no disturbances doctrines ef as regarded the land. They condemned tl the Church of Rome, and he referred to the RtlaearnmdaeoncmtCb.eerthooflica Archbishop of Tuam, who, he added, whassano id recommended temperance soNty. THE AMERICANS AND PLATE GLASS

Sir,—England has now got a riyal in glass making, a rival that will not be easily beaten, and that rival is the American people. Yes, the United States is exerting herself to beat the world in plate glass. I have been in corres- pondence with our cousins across tbe Atlantic just two years, therefore I should know what their intentions are. I have often heard people say this cap never be; America beat • England. But I, James Seddon, can positively Say that before two years are over the Americans will be making glass that England cannot make. You may think these are strong words. Cannot Ido too. But, nevertheless, it is true. If England cannot compete with France in colour, it speaks for itself that England can be beaten. It is also well known in America that the Belgians are sending to that country the best finished glass in the world. You will perhaps want to know how this can be. It is easily ex- plained. The Belgian machines for polishing are better than ours; therefore it is not the fault of the men. Their polishing machines work with a rotary motion, polishing both ways, giving the glass a better polish. England, no doubt, has done a great deal in altering and enlarging her machines, but these do not bring us any better a polish. The im- provement has been made to finish quicker, not better; not less work, but more work, which is an improvement after all. lam not allowed to mention names if I would have my writing published, therefore I hope the public will excuse me if what I say wants verifying, and I also hope that if my letters meet anyone who can contradict them with truth, he will do so at ence, but mind keep to the truth. The question to be asked is : "What will be the result when the americans can furnish all the States of America with glass ?" The reeelt will be this, England will have to look east among the Zulus and the Pharoahs. Egypt and Zulu- land will no doubt be two great countries some day ; and that day will tome sooner than we expect- if they send Cetewayo back again to be their king. He has seen England; the result will be good for that country there can be no doubt. I am instructed to tell anyone that if be can bring any im- provement out to these new works dollars will not be the question They will satisfy him or them who does this. littt I Must warn the public of this, that there are certain

• tbhditions. Ile or ti:.3" trust be steady. Only a few years will intervene between now and tba time when I say Eng- land must look east. But I .nust also point out to you that Franca stands between you and the east, another great rival not so easy to beat. There is also Germany, a great glass manufacturing country. But I can't see that she will be alai; ~(.liroent to F.:.';!an(l.—l am, &c., J. S. -243 Milk-street, St. Helens.

THE LICENSED VICTUALLERS' LATE DINNER. Sir,—l read with pleasure the letter which appeared in your last week's paper, signed "A. Warringtonian," protest- ing against the conduct of the Mayor in wearing his chain of office at the Licensed Victuallers' dinner. There is no doubt his Worship has committed a grave error by so doing, and has thus materially injured his previous reputation for I, strict impartiality. 1 trust, however, that no future Mayor will pay "such a compliment "in the future. I observed, Mr. Editor, that Alderman Davies was also present, andl took occasion to say one or too remarkable thins, especially as coming from the ii 3 of a magistrate, and ne a .ieember of the Borough Licensing Committee, too. In the first place he stated that the duties of the magistrates as far as the Licensed Victuallers of Warrington were concerned were light. He must express his approval of the excellent ne-anner in which the Licensed Victuallers of Warrington conducted their business. They were deserving of the empliment, and he was glad to cenvey it. Do you mean this, Alderman Davies, •or must we consider ,it an after-dinner speech? If you are in earnest, then you are unfit for your position as a magistrate. Your eyes must be closed and your ears stopped as you li,:ten to the cases brought before the Bench. What about last Monday's pro- ceedings at the l'olice-courf ? A number of young girls, whose ages ranged from 13 to 16, were brought before you, Alderman Davies, for drunkenness. Who served these girls with drink? Why, a publican. All right, Mr. Publican, go on; you are deserving of complineent; you conduct you business in a respectable manner, so says Alderman Davies. What abominable- nonsense. The whole morning last Monday was occupied in hearing drunken cases, and yet the men who are equally guilty with the prisoners before the magistrates for making them drunk are callcd "respectable." and their victims sent to prison. lam surprised at Alder- man Davies. I bad a higher opinion of him than thinking him capable of uttering such remarks. I would urge him to pay greater attention to the causes which produce so much misery and crime, and would earnestly hope that the time is near at hand when he will. learn by experience and observation that, but for drink, this fair country of ours would so change for the better that we should scarcely irnow it am, dac. ANOTHER WARRINGTONIAN.

law and its highest officers had been bearded, and the liberty which the constitution allows to every loyal citizen abused. Day after day articles appeared in the Freeman's Journal which could have no other effect that to destroy the moral influence of the convictions under the Crime Act. The severity of the sentence is proportionate to Mr. Gray's high position, and a tribute to the great influence of his journal, which has been made the instrument of incalculable mischief. The Freeman's Jour;ma believes there is no parallel for the unexampled character of the judgment. Mr. Gray was refused that which is granted to every man accused of an offence, viz., time to prepare his defence. If the statement in his journal were proved false, he would_ have made Proper reparation. The sentence was an exceptional one.

In compliance 'with a suggestion from Mr. Justice LawaOrl, who is presiding at the Special Commission now being held in Dublin, the Solicitor-General for Ireland on Wednesday brought formally before his Lordship a lettcr which recently appeared in the Freeman's Journal, signed by William O'Brien, and which contained statements of a scandalous nature with regard to the jury who convicted on Saturday a young man named Hynes for a cruel murder in county Clare. Those allegations, and an article based upon them, were held by the Crown to interfere with the free exercise I of the duties of jurors and the Solicitor-General moved that an attachment might issue against Mr. E. Dwyer Gray, , M.P., High Sheriff of Dublin, and proprietor of the Free- man's Journal. The learned gentleman read several of the articles, which imputed to the Crown authorities dis- honourable conduct in "packing " juries and rejecting honest and respectable Catholic jurymen. Those articles were described as a proof of "scandalous audacity on the part of Mr. Gray. In regard to the letter concerning the jury's conduct the Crown representatives did not attach any credence to its allegations, but they were prepared for a strict examination, if necessary, into its truth or falsehood. Mr. Gray denied that the articles, one of which he wrote, were intended to bring conretnpt on the Court or his Lord- ship. As to the letter, he wrote the arpended article "knowing the letter was bona fide and that Mr. O'Brien was not capable of saying anything but the truth." He asked for an adjournment in order that an investigation might be made. Mr. Justice Lawson refused the application, and said that in his opinion the articles constituted, in each and every case, a grave contempt of court. He believed the statements in the letter to be totally devoid of truth, and that Mr. Gray in acting as he did was intending to so influence the minds of Catholic jurors as to prevent the faithful discharge of the duties imposed upon them. His Lordship said that the articles were intended to destroy, in the public mind, the moral effect of the convictions obtained in agrarian offences, and to interfere with the trial of priso- ners yet to be tried. div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.
Tetters to the ditor.

THE NEW DANGER. Sir,—While Widaes is being threatened with a dire plague from pigs and Riggeries, Runcorn also is face to face with a danger of a dismal nature. On the testimony of the medical officer, in whose hands the health of the town is placed, we are on the eve of an epidemic of gastric fever. The dangerous nuisance on the Sprinch bas at last come be- fore the Improvement Commissioners, and surely some steps' will be taken towards abating it, Mr. Hazlehurst, an expert, has declared the stench as one that can be prevented, horrible as it is. I was astounded to read that Mr. Shaw had not yet detected the offensive odour. I wonder where his nese is. While I write the sickening fames arc hang- ing round like one of the pligues of Egypt, from which there is no escape. It may be that Mr. Shaw is so used to the varied vapours of the works of Widnes that this " horrible " and " organic " stink is rather pleasant than ethe rwise.—Hoping that something will be done to remove this frightful source of sickness and unpleasantness, I am, yours, cfze , ARCADIAN. Runcorn, August 12th, 1882.
