ARMY. Sir,—Will you kindly allow us, as the honorary secretaries of the above movement, to draw the attention of your readers to the advertisement which appears in your columns to-day? It is there announced that it has been arranged for Mr. T. E. Murphy to visit St. Helens in October nPxt, and to per- sonally conduct, a Gospel Temperance 'Mission for a fort- night, viz., October 15th to 29th. It is earnestly hoped and confidently exp2cted that the marvellous success which has aceompanied Mr. Murphy's visits to other towns will be repeated in the meetings which will be held here, and that the results will be seen in a decided lessening of drunken- ness and a corresponding extension of the principles and practice of sobriety.—We are, yours respectfully, W. CHAPLIN. • R. J. WARD, . J. H. BOYDELL.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882

DISTRICT NEWS. ASHTON. ST. THOMAS'S CHURCH.—The usual monthly collections in aid of the wardens' expenses were made in St. Thomas's Church, on Sunday morning and evening last, and nearly £8 was realised. The vicar, the Rev. H. Siddall, was the. preacher. FAILING TO APPEAR TO i SUMMONS.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before A. C. Smethurst and J. Eckersley, Esqs., Edward Jones, a collier, of Ashton, was brought up in custody on a charge of being drunk and disorderly at Ashton, on the 25th June last. The prisoner had been summoned to appear for that offence but had failed to do so, and a warrant for his apprehension was issued.—He was now ordered to pay the costs. CHARGE OF STEALING AGAINST LODGERS.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before A. E. Smethurst and J. Eckersley, Esqs., John Garratty and Peter Moran, colliers, of Ashton were brought up on a charge of stealing a vest, a handkerchief, and a door key, the property of Thomas Sharp.—The evidence showed that the two prisoners had been lodging at Sharp's house, in Cripping's- buildings, Ashton and left on the previous Monday. After they had gone the articles named were missed, and a few days later information was given to the police and the prisoners were apprehended. Garratty bad the handkerchief in his possession at the time of his arrest, but the other pro- perty was not recovered. Both pleaded not guilty. Garraty was fined 2s 6d and costs, and Moran was discharged. FRODSHAM. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHOIR TRIP.—The members of the choir belonging to the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodsham, had a pleasing trip to Chester on Saturday, and the grand Cathedral, ancient walls, and river side had their several votaties. The weather was exceedingly hot, and some of the party had a very enjoyable row up the river and found the river breeze to be cool and refreshing. Tea was partaken of in the city, and-all returned well pleased with their out. Mn. STEWARD'S CATTLE SALE.—This fortnightly sale of fat and store cattle was held at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frod- sham, on Tuesday, when there was a good attendance of buyers present. Fat calves realised from Cs. to 755. each. Fat cows £lB 15s. Gd. to £23 17s. 6d., four from one feeder averaging £2O lls. each. Fat sheep averaged 365. to 70s. each. There was a brisk demand for lambs, which realised from 275. to 445. each. Store pigs fetched 455. each. TRINITY WESLEYAN SERMONS.—Two sermons were preached in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, morn- ing and evening, by W. S. Allen, Esq., M.P., of Cheadle. A special children's se:vice, conducted by Charles E. Taylor, Esq., of Wavertree, was held in the afternoon. The hymns had been selected for the occasion, and the singing of the choir and children was very good. Mr. Samuel Smith pre- sided at the organ during the morning service, and Mr. W. H. Pickering, organist, accompanied during the after- noon and evening services. Mr. Sant was the conductor. The collections realised about £2l. TRINITY SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' EXCURSION.—The teachers in the Trinity Wesleyan Sunday school decided some time since to have a day's outing together, and a trip to Llangollen, which had been arranged by the Rev. John Lockwood for the annual treat to the Halton Parish Church choir, offered a favourable opportunity to visit the celebrated and "sweetest of vales." The party assembled to the number of 50 at the Frodsham station, on Monday morning, and started for the Principality at eight o'clock. Llangollen was reached at half-past ten, and pleasure-seeking was declared the order of the day. The scenery and antiquarian objects of interest were much admired, and the lovers of the picturesque, sentimental, or romantic had ample scope for their obqervations. The weather was highly propitious, and a delightful day was spent. An early tea was done full justice to, and the party commenced the return journey at six o'clock, the time toeing pleasantly occupied in singing and various amusing games, which relieved the monotony of railway travelling. Frodsham was called at half-past eight, the general expression of opinion being in favour of another trip next year. GOLBORNE, ACCIDENT TO A GOLBORNE MAN AT HAYDOCK.—A layer named John Heyes, residing at Golberne, met with a serious itcident, owing to part of a scaffold giving way at the Wood Pit, Haydeck, on Thursday morning. Details of the sad occurrence are given under our Haydock heading. PROPOSED LIBERAL SOIREE.—The committee of the Golborne Liberal Club have decided to hold a " soirée" and demonstration on an extensive scale early in November next, and several members of Parliament will be asked to take part. Ditt7NEENNESS.—At the Occasional Court House, War- rington, on Monday, before Edward Greenall, Esq., John McLoughlin was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Queen-street, Golborne. on Sunday night. He was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. TEMPORARY LICENSE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, John Dewhurst, of the Horns Inn, applied for a temporary licence, and, there being no objection, the magistrates granted the application. . PITCH AND Toss.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, John Charles and John Heres, two young men, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss, at Gol- borne, on the sth inst. Heres pleaded guilty and Charles not guilty. About a qnarter-past four o'clock on the after- noon of the date named the two defendants were seen throwing up coins. Both of them were caught, whereupon Charles put his hand into his pocket and said he had had ho money in his band. The defendant Charles said he had bad his hand in his pocket five minutes when the con- stable came. He was out on strike, and had no money to play with. In reply to the B .nch, he said he was willing to pay the costs. The Bench made an order for the defen- dants to pay the costs, amounting to Gs 61 each. SUNDAY DRINKING AT GOLBORNE: A SUSPICIOUS-LOOK- ING BUNDLE.—Before J. Pearson and T. J. Gillespie, Esqs., at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, James Foster, the holder of an " off " licence at Golborne, was summoned for having his house open for the sale of beer during prohibited hours on Sunday the Gth inst., and Sarah Carrigan was summoned for aiding and abetting. Mrs. Foster appeared instead of her husband.—Carrigan pleaded guilty.—A police-constable stated that he along with P.C. Smith was on duty near to the defendant Foster's house on Sunday morning, the 6th inst. About 20 minutes past ten o'clock' the defendant Carrigan entered the house and re- turned with a bundle beneath her apron, which she took into her house. About five minutes to eleven she did the same thing again. About half-past eleven she again went into the beerhouse, and as she was coming out he and P.C. Smith ran after and stopped her. They asked her what she had got in the bundle and she pulled out a tin can full of ale and which had been wrapped in a handkerchief. He produced the can in court. As they were returning to the house the defendant Foster's wife said, "It's opening time, is it not 2" but witness said "No, it was not opening time when you came the first time or the second time, and it is only half-past eleven now." When they told Foster, who was lying on the sofa, he said, "What's up? What's up ?"—P.C. Smith said the evidence of the last witness was quite correct. Mrs. Foster said what the constables had stated was quite correct, but Carrigan, she added, did not come in for beer the first and second time.—The Chairman: She got beer evidently? Mrs. Foster: Yes, she did, and very sorry I am.—The defendant Carrigan: One half gal- lop—Foster was fined 40a. and costs, the total amounting to n 135., and Carrigan was fined ss. and costs.

11[A.LTON. HALTON PARISH CHURCH : SIXTH ANNUAL PARISH TRIP.—On Monday last, 122 persons took advantage of this trip to Llangollen, which place has been twice selected for the annual trip. Of this number, 44 were friends from Fred- sham. All the various places in and around were visited both by young and old, and everybody—largely owing to the grand state of the weather—seemed to bs thoroughly satisfied with their day's outing.

HAYDOCK. ANOTHER SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT: A BRICKI:AYER SERIOUSLY INJURED.—About seven o'clock on Thursday morning a sad accident occured near to the mouth of the Wood Pit, between Eartestown and Haydock, and resulted in serious injnries being sustained by John Heyes. a brick- layer, 35 years of age, residing at Gelborne. Heyes was engaged by the firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and at the Wood Pit a new compressed air engine-house is being erected. At the time stated, be, along with a fellow workman named William Mather, of Haydock, were engaged following their occupation, and were working on a scaffold erected about 12 or 15 feet from the ground. Without any warning one of the cross-pieces of the scaffold gava way, and several of the planks fell to the ground, carrying Heyes with them. Mather fortunately stepped back at the moment the accident occurred and thus saved himself from an ugly fall, if not serious injuries. Heyes alighted on his back on a number of bricks and was rendered unconscious. A number of the men about the place quickly carried him into a neighbour- ing cabin, and Dr. T. E. Hayward, the colliery doctor, was immediately sent for. On his arrival it was found that the unfortunate man had received very serious injuries, his back being very much bruised. He was ultimately conveyed home in a trap belonging to the firm.

ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. The Rev. Edward Morris, who has been pastor of the Sale Congregational Church since 1842, has intimated his in- tention of resigning his charge at the close of the present year. The anniversary sermons in connection with the Ebenezer Chapel, Nantwich, were preached on Sunday by the Rev S. Sellars, of Yarmouth. The collections amounted to over £ll. The other afternoon Colonel France-Hayburst gave a treat to the children attending the Middlewich Parish Church Sunday schools, at Bostoek Hall, where they were liberally regaled. The committee appointed by the Nantwich Guardians to inquire into the desirableness or otherwise of having trien- nial elections of Guardians has decided to recommend the Board to let .natters remain as at present. An outdoor meeting in connection with the Nantwich Total Abstinence Society was held at Nantwich on Monday. Mr. J. T. Parratt presided. There was a large gathering, land the speeches were listened to with interest. The return shooting match between the shooting clubs of -the Nantwich Volunteers and the detachment from Wilmslow took place at Batherton on Saturday last, and resulted in the ' Nantwich team beating their opponents by three points. On Saturday, a large and enthusiastic demonstration was I held at Crewe, in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army. The proceedings commenced by the formation of a proces- sion at the Underwood-lane Mission-room. There were several hundreds in the procession, which attracted much attention on the lib. of march; and when the meeting began there were some 2,000 people present. Mr. Tomkinson, of Willington Hall, presided.

THE PROPOSED IMPROVEMENT BILL FOR CHESTER.—A poll of the citizens of Chester has been demanded on behalf of the promoters of the Boundaries Bill, which was so emphatically rejected at the large town's meeting held on Friday last. The poll will probably take place sometime about the third week in next month. The highest number ,of votes which any one person is entitled to give is six, and it is said that it is on those who are qualified to give four, five, or six votes that the promoters of the bill look to for success. But there is a strong opposition, and at present it seems a safe prediction to say that the decisioa of Friday last will be confirmed. THE HARVEST.—The fine weather of last week enabled the farmers of Cheshire and of the Welsh borders to get in the:remaining crops of bay in good condition. On Tuesday the long spell of good weather was broken, but there was then only here and there a small patch of grass uncut or ungathered. The agriculturists generally report that the hay crop is above an average in quality, and that it has been well gathered. Towards the end of last week many farmers began to cut their oats, and the fine weather caused the reaping machine to be in general requisition. On Monday there were a deal of showers, and Tuesday was showery, which checked operations; but Wednesday and Thursday were again favourable for field work. A dood harvest is generally looked forward to, for although there has lately been a deal of wet weather, the sky has been lately more propitious. ROWING.— A great number of Chester young gentlemen, fond of skimming the waters of the Dee, paid a visit to Farn- don last Saturday evening, in their handsome and gracefnl , canoes. This is a favourite " out " for the aquatically in- clined gentlemen of the walled city. From Chester to the border village of Farndon is about eight miles by road, but by the devious Dee it is about seventeen, and this is a favourite trip. The stream is an excellent one for the rower, and is a most enjoyable one in a scenic point of view, as it passes through Eaton Park, and winds amid the favourite glades and groves of the Duke of Westminster. Farndon is usual the resting place of the Chester oarsmen, but on Saturday a few of them ventured further up the Dee, and went as far as Bangor Iscoid, seventeen_ miles further up the Dee. On Sunday evening or Monday morn- ing they had a pleasant trip "homeward bound" down the river. QUOITS: LANCASHIRE V. CHESHIRE.—The return match between these county teams took place on Saturday on the Phoenix Ground, Liverpool, there being a large company present during the afternoon. Year by year these matches are looked forward to with keen interest, and the appear- ance on the scene of some sbining light, in the form of a rising young player, is always hailed with the greatest pleasure. The list of competitors selected for this match was, however, much the same as took part in the first en- gagement at Birkenhead on the 22nd ult., when Lancashire followed up her success by defeating Cheshire by 23 points. To wipe out this the Cheshire team made a gallant effort, and at the close of the twentieth game therappeared very formidable, their score standing at 400 against Lancashire 412. Great excitement then prevailed, and the Lancashire team made a spurt to retain the honours they had won, and in this they succeeded, for at the close of the match it was found they were 30 points in advance of their opponents. Some excellent play was shown on both sides. A NOVEL POINT UNDER THE LICENSING LAWS.—An application was made to the Crewe magistrates, on Friday, for a copy of a beer licence in respect teithe Forester's Arms Inn, the original having been, it was alleged, wilfully with- held by Ann Holland, the out-going tenant. Henry Mason arid Henry Hardstaff, the applicants, stated Mrs. Holland had given her landlords, Messrs. Gartside, brewers, a bill of sale upon her furniture, and the bailiffs being placed in posses- sion on Friday last she was ejected. When asked for the licence she refused to give it up, and the business had been stopped in consequence. It was argued on behalf of Mrs. Holland that she had incurred considerable expense by entering into a lease of tenancy with the landlords, and until that !else expired she had the right to retain the licence. At the magistrates' suggestion the applicants agreed to pay Mrs. Holland a substantial sum for the licence, which was then handed over, and the necessary authority 1%781 granted. HARVEST PROSPECTS IN CHESHIRE.—The Agrieultui;al Gazette, in its report of the present appearance of the crops throughout the country, publishes accounas from this county. Mr. J. Aston, Brassey Green, Tarporley, reports : —Wheat, mmtly very good, a few wet fields light and patchy; barley a full average crop, except on undrained land; oats exceed- ingly heavy on all free soils; beans the same as oats: very few grown in this district; potatoes, good crop, rotting badly; root crop very promising, growing very fast; hay., best for ten years, and is now being stacked in fine condi- tion. Date of harvest, now.—Mr. T. Balmer, of Tattenhall, reports :—Wheat: Good, and well-beaded on dry lands, but on cold clay, light. Barley: Will he fair average crop; not a barley neighbourhood. Oats: Leoking very fair, and should yield well. Beans: Likely to boa proitabie crop; quite average. Potatoes : Looking vigorous; no blight vet upon them. Root crop: Very promising; full average. Hay: Over average, not well harvested. Date of harvest; July: August, and September.
THE NEWTON, HA.YDOCK, AND GOLBORNE BUILDING SOCIETY.
THE ADJOURNED ANNUAL MEETING OF THE

MEMBERS. The adjourned annual meeting of the shareholders of the Newton, Haydock, and Golborne Permanent Benefit Build- ing Society Was held in the Town Hall. Newton, on Thurs- day evening. There was a very large attendance of mem- bers, the Court-room being crowded. At the last meeting, held on the 15th June last, a resolution was passed that a sub-committee be appointed to report to another meeting as to the best steps that could be taken in the present emergency, and that the passing of the accounts be adjourned to such other meeting which was to be fixed by the managers and sub-committee. The sub-committee appointed consisted of Messrs. Robert Farron, Richard Bradshaw, Vi'm. Richai dean, Henry Cunliffe Thomas Barton, John Simpson, and Henry Ashcroft; and the present meeting was called to consider their report. Amongst those present were Mr. Jno. Mercer, J.P., of Alston Hall, near Preston ; Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., Mr. B. B. Glover, Mr. Davies, solicitor, Warrington; and Mr. John Adams, secretary of the society. Mr. Gillespie was elected to preside. Mr. ROBERT FARRON, as chairman of the Investigation Committee was then called upon to read the report of the committee, which contained the following _

We have come to this conclusion, to recommend that you as members should ex oress your views, and that a change should be made, as far as the Secretary is concerned. We have re- ceived communications from members expressing theiropinion that a person ought to be elected to such position, and that it would be advisable for such person to devote the whole or the greater portion of his time to the affairs of the society, such as collecting, and pay over to the bank all cash, and look after the properties and the general interest of the undertaking; this object we fully recommend as advisable, and make the sug- gestion to the managers that steps be taken to obtain such a person, for we believe it will cost the society no more under such alteration than the cost at the present time, and be far more effective and satisfactory. We a'sa advise that the system on which the books are now formed be remodelled, and put on a better and mora accurate method, and so enable the management to have greater control, and be enabled to see the workings in a more business-like manner. (Applause.) We also think that the management should take into con- sideration the benefits that would result in placing the society under the rules and action of the Building Societies' Act, as many other similar sccities have done; it placing the accounts under a more stringent supervision with other advantages, one of which is security to be given by the officers. We have duly considered time question and mode of making advance, the result of our deliberations being that we think due care has not been taken in having such a margin on the allotments as to make a provision for any difficulty or loss which may arise with such advances. We are also of opinion that it is not judicioas to make further advances on the same property without reva/uation. The exorbitant allowance made to some of the managers for the inspection of the property and other duties should be reduced. The Managers knowing the condition of the society, have, in several ewes, systematically reduced their holdings to one share of £10; and we find that Mr. James Lip:rot has been sitting for two years, without a qualification, from May, 1880, to May, 1882, and Mr. John Ascroft, from October 18th to the day of annual meeting, when he was rejected as a manager. And find further Mr. John Adams, the secretary. has not held a qualifi- cation, as required by Rule, as an Officer of the Society. With rega-d to the withdrawals of investing shares.and the tun upon the society last year, we find that a sum of J 3875 33 had been paid to 23 members, without any record in the minute book, or notice given, as per Rule 43. Arn•ngst the said list we find the last name to be the Chairman of the Management, who: on the 12th Apflf, withdrew £9O. It is only fair to say that for some reason a similar sum was paid in again on the 12th June, 1882. The present condition of the society might, in our opinion, have been prevetited had the management clted a special meeting instead of deferring it untit the end of the Financial Year, and thus paying away the large amount of money reported in the Balance eheet, and in several cases, to persons in intimate relationship with the officers. (Applause,) We should not be doing or r duty without drawing your atten- tion to the fact of a recent chairman having withdrawn the whole of his investments, as well far several members of his family. Yet. a few years ago. a testimonial for his watchful care over the inte-est of the society, was presented to him We now reap the reward! as many of the lots of property will testify. The importa tqu st ion of members withdrawing ras had our seriou attention, and we regret that the acti n of the management in plac ns a forfel'ir e of 241 p r cent. oms each share on t' eir'own responsibi ity, was a very u• usual step to take, and has tended to increase the am ,unt of distrust and if rer isted in, wit probably beak up the soc:ety. The deter- mined retention of the r, soluti ,n empawerieg the smme, pro- posed by the chairman and second d by one of the managers, who had no qu-lification to sit, if nst illegal, is at all events a most moues ionable p ccesdi g, and w'll not we feel, meet with the support or the shsreho ders, bit will render ab mrtive our enaeavours to pace the sacas'y on a better basis. (Apple. se.) What we have to propose in the shap s of an imp ovement the ie an log and condi' ion of then dertaking is fi s ad- vise al; who am e not coo pelled, by necessity, to • etain their holdings for at least anot her yearly report, and then judge if the pm ets-nt ventila' fan cm: affairs d .m• snot bring a sat sfaom cry result. An impression has get afl rat that we are desirous tie bring about a winding up of the society, and that our actions are detri- man'al to its good. We beg most distinctly to deny such insinuation, but direct you to tha fact that on our appoiotment we held very near as large a shake, as investors, as the whole of the board of inanagemens, so that if thsy are acting for the good, we also hive no other object In view. In conclusion we would again impress noon yaus minds that mutual confidence Is the main essential for the suecesfut carrying on of our undei taking. The errors or mistakes of past, years will, we think, be guarded agaam•st by the present and future managers. Mr. DAISES (solicitor) then addressed the meeting at some length, stating that,whatever the report might contain as to default of management, or anything of that kind, he was glad to find that there was not the slightest insinuation of fraud or peculation of any kind against any one. As far as he understood the report, part of their remedy was that if any person withdrew his money they should absolutely for- feit 5 per cent., and of any interest that might be due, that was to say, if anyone had given notice of withdrawal of, say £lOO be would forfeit any interest to which he was entitled, and he would only receive £95 on receipt in payment of his full demands upon the society. They must either carryon the society or wind it up, and he recommended thatif they decided to wind it up let them *lo it in A cliff' business like way, and not take any rash action. Mr, PARRON recommended the shareholders not to wi.ll draw their money unless they were compelled by necess'ey. A SHAREHOLDER said he thought it would be advisable to adjourn that meeting, so that the managers would have an opportunity to consider what reply to make to the report, and also that the members themselves should have as opportunity of fully considering it. He moved a resolution accordingly. ANOTHER SHAREHOLDER seconded the _proposition. . .

Mr. DAVIES (solicitor) said he hoped tliey'would have a little discussion upon the report now that they had gathered together. They could afterwards adjourn the meeting. ANOTHER SPEAKER said that if they went in for winding up the society, it meant about 40 per cent. going into the lawyer's pockets. (Laughter and applause). He theught it would be the most suicidal plan they could adopt. (Hear, hear).

Mr. 111sCRAE expressed the opinion that be would rather see the society quietly wound up. (Groans). Notwith- standing the statement of the last speaker, he believed there was some means by which they could wind-up the society without any loss to the members, and it would be to the Mutual advantage Of both borrowers and shareholders. Mr. GLOVER, as one of the managers of the society, said he regretted that they had not had the report sooner in their possession. It would have been much more in accordance with his own feelings if he could have laeen prepared with a full reply. Mr. Farron and the sub-committee would have them to understand that the manaeers intended to take the 20 per cent retention money entirely and that they would never see it afterwards. He believed Mr. Farron used the words that it would not be seen again. But they did not intend that, • they were simply bound to put the rule in force in order to protect the interests of the society. For himself, he did not regret that they had done so—his only regret was that it was not done twelve months sooner. (Applause.) The report of the sub-committee would receive the most careful consideration at the hands of the managers, and also the various suggestions therein con- tained. He noticed there was a paragraph in the rep3rt which referred to himself, and that was to the effect that he withdrew the sum of £9O, and that his name was also one of the last. That was perfectly correct. It was.also correct that be had repaid the £9O, and therefore the society was no worse off so far as he was concerned. As to the position of the various properties, their agents report; were that they were all fairly well let and paying a fair rate of interest. (Hear,.bear.) The bulk of the property was plying 5 per I cent. upon the new valuation. He thought they ought to give the present managers their due, for very few of them were on the Boald when the property was bought—it was a legacy from their predecssors for which they were not responsibls. (Applause.) Mr. JOIIN MERCER, J.P., said that looking at the report he'did not think that they need be in any despondent way, and with a return of prosperity in trade he had no doubt the value of the property would greatly increase in value (Hear, hear.) Mr. LIPTROT said that with respect to the statement in the report that he was acting RS manager without qualifica- tion, he had to say that ever since he became connected with it, either in his own behalf or in the names of his children he had always had more than a £lO share. Mr. FARRON said Mr. Liptret knew that according to the rules a manager must hold one subscribed share. It did not say that his daughter and son should join him in supporting his candidature. If he himself did not hold a share he was not qualified, by rule, as a 'manager of the society. He asserted that the managers themselves did not know their position. A VOICE: I deny it. Mr. FARRON : The managers themselves to this day don't know the income on the property.
Mr. ADAUS: They do: . A VOICE: They don't. Mr. FermoN said they did not—at least a few days ago it had not been prepared. Mr. Glover rose to speak, but

Mr. DAVIES interposed and said that as solicitor to the society he hoped they would not turn a grave business meeting like that into a discussion of party matters. What they wanted was to resuscitate the society, and it would be better if personal feeling and temper were left out of tha business. He hoped they would not allow the meetin gto degenerate into assertions on one side and denials on the other side.

Mr. GLOVER said that as far as he and the managers were concerned they had done all they possibly could to assist the sub-committee in the examination of the accounts. Mr. ADAMS (the secretary) said he had been connected with various public bodies in that town for the last 25 years. He had also been connected with different committees in in that time, and had always been treated respectfully from the very first. But from the first that sub-committee had treated him almost as a criminal. He seemed to have been
condemned and executed before they had ever looked at the i matter at all.

A SPEAKER : I was on the committee, and asked for a statement two years ago and the secretary refused to get it out then. I believe there is something behind it: (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said he could -not say how rnhch he regretted the statements and recriminations that had taken place that night. They were the very -last things that would assist them in getting the society in a satisfactory condition.

Mr. GLOVER suggested, not with any desire to shirk an investigation or discussion that they should pass a resolution that the report be received and referred to the managers for their due consideration. He moved an amendment to the motion for adjournment to that effect. Mr. DAVIES (solicitor) expressed the opinion that the shareholders were entitled to have a subsequent meeting and have everything discussed openly. He thought a resolu- tion that the report be received, and reported to the mana- gers, and that their reply be received and considered at a meeting to be held as may be decided upon would meet the case.

Further discussion as to the day of adjournment, ckc., afterwards ensued, and the meeting was ultimately adjourned until that day fortnight at seven o'clock in the evening. The meeting, which at times got somewhat heated and lasted for several hours, then concluded.

PRESCOT UNION. RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. On Thursday a meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present—Messrs. Swift (in the chair), Newsome, Hall, Syder, and W. Long- ton, together with Mr. S H. Hartley (clerk), Dr. Hall (medical officer), and Mr. Twist.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

OUTRAGE ON AN IRISH FARM LABOURER.-011 Monday, at the Leigh Police Court, James Hodgkinson, John Whittle and James Whittle, three young men. were charged on remand with assaulting an Irish farm labourer, named Malley, on the afternoon of Sunday week.—Superintendent Jackson having stated the case, it was decided to abandon the intention to proceed against the prisoners for Lighway robbery.—Mr. Ferguson appeared for Hodgkinson, the other prisoners, who are brothers, being defended by Mr. Buck- ley.—Malley said on the day in question, when near Carr's railway bridge, he met the prisoners, and the Whittles asked for money. He replied that be had none, and then they led him about 100 yards into a field. John Whittle pulled his coat off, anel,said if he did not turn out his pockets he would kick him to death. Prisoner then ran at him and knocked him down, James Whittle holding him down, whilst his brother took 4d. from his pocket. They also searched him, and on Hodgkinson coming up he said prosecutor 'must turn more money up."—ln answer to Mr. Buckley, who appeared for the Whittles, prosecutor.said prisoners first asked him to treat them.—A boy named Timothy Ogden corroborated.— Mr. Ferguson, on behalf of Hodgkinson, contended that there was no proof of his taking part in the assault.—After the Bench had retired, Mr. Booth said the magistrates had carefully considered the evidence, and they believed a very grave charge had been proved. The Whittles must be im- prisoned for two months, and Hodgkinson for one month, With hard labour.
LYMM At the Sale Petty Sessions, on Monday, temporary authority was granted to Wm. Kay to sell at the Spread Ilagle, Lymm.

div.head: RAINH ILL.
div.p: RAINH ILL.

RIDING ON THE RAILWAY WITHOUT A TICKE'T AT RAIN- HILL.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a young man named Joseph Wcfod was charged with having ridden in a railway carriage between Liverpool and Rainhill, on the 23rd inst.—Mr. Ferrent appeared on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company to prosecute, and Mr. Mackenzie defended. It appeared that the defen- dant had for some time been suspected by the station officials at Rainhill of riding between Liverpool and that station without a ticket. He was often seen to leave Rain- hill station on the ‘aturday and Sunday afternoons, taking a single ticket, and afterwards seen at Raihill without any ticket having been reolived from him. A watch was set for him, and on the day in question he was seen to get out of the train and walk towards an unfrequented part of the plat- form, and before the porter could lay hands upon him he had disappeared. The stationmaster sent the ticket collector to his house the next day to ask latina for his ticket, but he replied that he had no ticket, as he had only been seeing a friend away. Some time after that, however, he went to the stationmaster, and offered to pay him the fare.—A fine of 30a. and costs was imposed. WAVERTREE.

STEALING A DUCK AT WAVERTREE.—A man, named John Potter, was charged, at the Prescot Sessions, on Tues- day, with having stolen a duck, the property of Henry Welsby, at Wavertree, on the 14th instant.—Wm. Searle, who said he lived at 12, Kellet-road, Wavertree, said he had seen the prisoner leaning over a wall at Wellington-road, Wavertree, feeding some ducks which were on the other side. After a short time prisoner got over the wall and caught one of the ducks, and was proceeding to tie it up in a pocket hankerchief when witness, having called to his assistance another man, took him in charge and handed him over to the custody of a policeman.—Prisoner having been previously convicted for a similar offence, was sent to gaol for one month's hard labour. WIGAN.

THE WIGAN COAL AND IRON COMPANY' LIMITED.— The report of the directors of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, Limited, for the half-year ended 30th June last, was issued to the shareholders on Tuesday, signeA by the chairman of the company, the Earl of Crawford and all- carres. In it the directors sly :—"The net results of the company's operations in coal and iron is a profit of £18,900 Bs. This sum, with £2,071 2s. 7d. carried forward from last halt year, makes £20,971 lOs 7d. available for dividend. Your directors recommend a dividend after the rate of 2i per cent. per annum, which will absorb £20,359." THE THEFT OF LORD CRAWFORD'S BODY.—The Crown authorities in Scotland have decided that Charles .outer, the man charged with stealing the body of the late Earl of Crawford, shall be tried at the Aberdeen Circuit of the sth September, before Lords Craighill and Adams. On Saturday the "productions " in the case, which include the oak coffin in which the body of the earl was placed, the shroud, and other articles, were brought into Aberdeen from Dun Echt. WINSFORD.

The chief events of this week have b3en the Wesleyan Sunday school treat, which called forth their teachers and scholars to Clive, their usual rendezvous, for a walk, tea, and sports; and that of the Weaver Church school to Weaver Hall for the same purpose. The young people mustered strongly on both occasions, and if there was any lack of enjoyment, it was not for want of effort on their part. This much for the religious side. The reverse presents a scene which it was thought Wins. ford had seen the last of—through the labour of the Salva- tion Army and other agencies—but that is a mistake. On Saturday last, before Captain Turner and the Mayor of Over (Jos. Slater, Esq.), there were three of the Winsford salt boilers charged with being drunk and assaulting the police in the discharge of their duty. Their names were Samuel Hulse, Frederick Pardoe, and Charles Bebbington. They were also the cause of others assaulting the police, which led to John Whalley and Edward Hassell being likewise brought before the magistrate!. The cases being proved, they were remanded to the Eddisbury Sessions for the 28th instant, since lenient sentences are not a sufficient deterrent for such disgraceful condatt.—They had to find bail in £lO each and £lO surety for each likewise,

div.head: CLERK'S SALARY.
div.p: THE CLERK'S SALARY.
A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the payment of 150 per annum to Mr. Hartley for his services as clerk to the Authority.

THE AUTHORITY AND MR. Mr. HARTLEY read the following letter, dated Bth July, whiph he had received from Mr. Leslie, surveyor's office, Knowsley, viz. :—" Mr. Hall has handed me your letter of yesterday, in which you call attention to some works pine on in Knowsley, of which no plan has been sent to the Prescot Sanitary Authority. I can assure you there is no disposition, here to disregard the bye-laws of the Authority or to slight in any way those who administer them. It is not necessary to allude to the childish babbling of one of the members of the Authority as reported in the local papers, beyond saying that were all the members equally silly the Authority would indeed be only deserving of contempt. The omission of sending a copy of the plan was due to an oversight which shall be at once made good." —Mr. HARTLEY said he had written back simply ackno*ledging- the receipt of this letter. He had also received a letter from Mr. Hale regretting having failed to send a plan, and asking that he might be furnished with a copy of the bye-laws, so that in 'future he might know the requirements of the Board. In reply to this letter, he (Mr. Hartley) had enclosed till bye-laws as requested, also stat- ing that his letter of the 7th inst. had been replied to by Mr. Leslie on the following day in language which he felt sure Mr. Hale could not approve of. Mr. Hale's answer simply acknowledged the receipt of the bye-laws.— Mr. HALL, referring to Mr. Leslie's letter, said it was the most impertinent and unwise letter he had ever heard read.—Mr. NEwsomE thought it was the most insulting letter ever placed berm%) a committee. Mr. Hale he added, wrote like a gentleman.—Mr. HALL said Mr. Hale would never think of insulting the Authority. It was a monstrous shame that such a letter should-have been written, and their best plan would be to send it to Lord Derby, from whom they would get some reply, he had no doubt.—Mr. NEWSOME thought the letter redounded more to tile discredit of Mr. Leslie than to anybody else.—lt was agreed that a copy of Mr. Leslie's letter should be sent to Lord Derby as suggested by Mr. Hall.

div.head: WHISTOW WATER. COLLECTOR.
div.p: WHISTOW WATER. COLLECTOR.

Mr. HARTLEY acid he had a letter from the Local Govern- ment Board respecting the salary of the water collector for Whiston, which they thought ought to be paid out of the general fund of the Union, but which the Sanitary Authority thought ought to be specially paid by Whiston township. If they would allow him he would prepare an answer to the letter.—This suggestion was agreed to.

MEDICAL OFFICERS REPORT. Dr. HALL reported that the district was in a remarkably healthy state at the present time, there not being a single ease of anything of an infectious nature that he was aware of. Two samples of water had been submitted to Dr. C. Brown, from Hale, neither of which were of good quality. A sample of water sent to him by Mr. Twist, about a month ago, with no label on it, he had analysed and found to be of faulty quality. A virulent case of diphtheria had occurred at Hale. The place had been thoroughly disinfected ; the premises were clean and in good order. At the Post Office, Hale, there was a well in close proximity to a large open and wet midden ashpit. The mouth also wanted puddling, as the washing often fond its way back to the well. He mentioned two years ago that he had never found any water in Hale fit for drinking, and it was partly in conscquenca of that that the Hale sewerage had been undertaken in the hopes that ,by better drainage the well water might improve. He was sorry to say that so far this did not appear to be the case, and it was a matter which would require their serious consideration.—ln answer to Mr. Hall, Dr. HALL said the only remedy he could suggest for the bad water at Hale was to get a supply from somewhere else.—lt was agreed after a little discussion that the Surveyor should prepare an esti- mate of the cost of carrying a drain to the nearest point of the water supply of the Widnes Local Board, and should re- port thereon at the next meeting. This concluded the business of the Authority.

SUICIDE OF A GENTLEMAN WELL KNOWN IN ENRLESTOWN. A peculiarly painful case of suicide took place on Sunday evening, the deceased being a gentleman well known in Earlestown and neighbourhood, 114 r. Thomas William Willett, C.E. The deceased gentleman had for some years acted as private secretary to William Hargreaves, Esq., J.P. (of the firm of Messrs. Hick,-Hargreaves, and Co., proprie- tors of the Soho Ironworks, Bolton, and had for nearly ten years officiated as the secretary of the extensive concern of the Bolton Iron and Steel Company, in which Mr. liar- greaves has also a great interest. Mr. Willett was originally a resident in London, but prior to his business connection with Bolton he was the managing director of the Neath Gunpowder manufactory. 113 was alst, one of the founders of the Cotton Seed Products Menu facturing Co., at Earlestown. This business consisted in the extraction of the oil in the waste cotton seeds, which as seeds are believed to be worthless stuff. He likewise formulated and patented some plan for the extraction of the oil, but the whole business at Earles- town proved a failure, and the undertaking was given up sotne years ago. Though he never was what might be termed a " resident " in this district, yet his business trans- actions aud almost daily presence in Earlestown brought him into contact with a large number of persons, and he became, as stated above, very well known. In addition to his connection with the Cotton Seeds Company alluded to, the deceased bad the oversight of a paper mill adjoining these works, and which belonged to the firm of Messrs. Hick, Hargreaves, and Co. The latter took the premises from their previous owners, Messrs. Rose and Gibson, and a limited company was formed, in which it was understood the deceased had a large number of shares. Both the oil and paper works came into possession of the company, but after being run some time some differences between the partners, it is stated, resulted in the works being closed some eight or ten years ago. Since that time the premises, which are situated on the bank of the canal, near to the vitriol works, have been standing idle, though the deceased has paid periodical visits to Earlestown in order to pay the "watchman "_ left in charge. The deceased resided at Burnden Bank, Great Lever, near Bolton, for several years, and became a widower nearly three years ago—his wife dying in Sep- tember, 1879. He has four daughters who have been ' recently staying with their grandfather, R. Valentine Leach, Esq.,,Devizes Castle, Wiltshire, and during their absence from home the only occupants of his residence at Burnden Bank have been Mr. Willett and two domestic female ser- vants. He had been unwell for a shot period, suffering from some nervous ailment, and had experienced a difficulty in sleeping; but had been able to attend to business up to the latter part of last week. He went to London on Sunday, the 6th inst., and returned on Wednesday, the 9th. On the evening of last Friday, the servants noticed something apparently serious was amiss with the deceased gentleman, and Mr. Burgess, assistant to Dr. F. B. Mallett, promptly attended Mr. Willett. Mr. Burgess found him suffering from some affection of the brain, and he desired the servants 'to keep a strict watch over him, and to remove all danger- ous implements from his reach. At that time no one had the slightest knowledge that he kept any firearms. One of the men employed at the Soho Ironworks was sent by Mr. Hargreaves, and he remained to look after Mr. Willett , throughout Saturday night. Dr. Mallett's assistant was at the house for some time on Sunday, and about half-past five ' o'clock in the evening he left Mr. Willet in bed—which was in the front room overlooking Manchester-road—and proceeded into the kitchen to give certain directions to the servants. Just at this moment a sharp crack was heard, and Mr. Burgess hastened upstairs, but prior to reaching the bedroom there was ne suspicion that any wbapon had been fired. However, on the bedroom being reached, a shocking sight presented itself—Mr.Willett lying dead upon the floor, with only his underclothing upon him, and a six-chambered revolver near his right foot. He had, instantly upon being left to himself, jumped out of , bed, taken the revolver out of a locked drawer in a cabinet I on one side of the room, and pointing the weapon between his right eye and the upper part of his nose, had discharged I it. The bullet had penetrated the brain and completely I shattered it, though there was a fracture at the back of the head caused by the shot, the bullet did not make its exit. A large pool of blood was upon the floor. The whole six chambers of the firearm bad been loaded. Dr. Scowcroft, who was in the immediate neighbourhood at the time, was called in, and he made an examination of the unfortunate g'entlernan's injuries. Mr. Willett, who was about 56 years of age, was understood to be a gentleman of independent means; and it is said he was on the point of being married again, the lady being a resident in London. The banns were read out for the third time on Sunday, the 6th inst., at Great Lever Church. An inquest on the body was held on Wednesday, when the following verdict was returned :—"That the deceased, at No. 1, Burnden Bank, Great Lever, committed suicide by shooting himself in the head with a pittol, whilst labouring under temporary insanity."

div.p: MARRIAGE A r RUNCORN. ' A marriage, in which more than ordinaly interest was I 'manifeited, was solemnised at Runcorn Parish Church on Tuesday morning. The bridegroom was Mr. Edwin Imison, pawnbroker, Church-street, Runcorn, son of the late Mr. C. C. Imisen (who during his life occupied several public positions, and was held in high esteem), and the bride was Miss Mary Elizabeth Savage, eldest daughter of Mr. Joseph Savage, farmer, of High-street, Runcorn. Rain fell in tor- rents whilst the ceremony was performed, but there was 'nevertheless a large assemblage of friends and well wishers in the pretty church, and Church-street was gay with bunt- ing. Soon after half-past nine, the hour fixed for the mar- riage, the bridal party entered the church, and the service, which was full choral, commenced by the surplfced choir singing the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden." Mr. Fred Savage (the brother of the bride) officiated as best man, and the bride was given away by her father. She was attired in a beautiful dress of white cashmere, trimmed with brocaded satin, and wore a long white veil, and a wreath of orange blossoms. The bridesmaids were the following young ladies: Miss Imison (who wore a flowered satin dress), Miss A. T. Imison, and Miss Eva Savage (the two latter wearing dresses of nuns cloth with cardinal trimmings. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. J. J. Bryant, MA., who was assisted by the Rev.W. R. Worthington, of Bromborough Pool. At the conclusion of the service as the party was leaving the church, Mr. J. Johnson played the Wedding March or! the organ. The guests present at breakfast included : Mr. and Mrs. Hale- wood, Miss Savage (Woodsi.le) Mr. and Mrs. Coles (Wood- side), Mr. and Mrs. Gorst (Runcorn), Mr. and Mrs. Imison (Bold), Miss Worrall and Miss M. Worrall (Birkenhead', Mr. J. Worrall (Birkenhead), Mr. A. Jordon (Runcorn), Mr. H. Bamford (Huddersfield), Mrs. Handley (Runcorn), Mr. Arthur Savage, Mr. W. H. Savhge, Miss E. Savage, and Miss E. Collier. In the course of the day the newly-married pair departed for the West of Scotland, where they will spend their honeymoon. The following is a list of the presents:— Gold bracelet, pair of silver bracelets, crown Derby and silver cruet, glove and handkerchief box, lady's work basket, jewel case, card basket, fancy fern stand, two crumb trays and brushes, cushion, cosy, glass sugar basin and cream jug, pair glass ornaments, rarian ornaments, pair fancy flower stands, fancy mustard pot, crown Derby, silver biscuit box, lady's bag. pair footstools, pair china ornaments, breakfast stand, teilet set, Parian ornament, pair of brackets, travelling bag, set of carvers, case of cutlery, six volumes English poets, book "Heaven our home," jag, tea caddy, a shawl, several antimacassars, teapot, cheese stand, dinner service, tea service, quilt, set of Honiton lace cuffs and collar, Honiton lace hankerchiefs, vases, opposum rug, ottoman, iron stool and bar, butter dish, lady's bag, footstools, china ornaments, frosted flower stand, beaded gipsy table, set of painted trays, silver ladles, table napkins.

THE SAD ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. GOLDING'S WORKS,. WIDNES. On Monday an accident of a sad nature occurred at the chemical works of Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Co., to a young man named John O'Brien. It appears that about eight o'clock on that day he went upon a wooden platform above the fly wheel of the engine, which works the Har- greave's process, in order to help his foreman to fix the strap on the wheel. The engine was started slowly, and imme- diately afterwards O'Brien was discovered entangled in the .strap, and held against the upright of the engine. His head was horribly crushed, and but a glimmering of life remained, his lips, when he was picked up, moving as if in prayer. He died in a few minutes. How he got in his unfortunate position can only,be conjectured, but the fly wheel, it was stated at the inquest, was totally unprotected. The deceased had only been in England a short time, and in the employment at Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Co., but three weeks. The county coroner (Mr. C. E. Driffield) held an inquiry into the circumstances on Wednesday, at Simms Cross Hotel. Mr. H. S. Richmond, her Majesty's inspector of factories, Liverpool, was present. and Mr. Peter Ireland, the foreman over the fitting department, watched the pro- ceedings on behalf of the firm. James Gharghan, of 42, Cromwell-street, said he was foreman of the Hargreave's process at the works, and the deceased and a boy named Nicholas Gillon were his assis- tants. It was the work of deceased to put salt into the elevator. About nine o'clock on Monday morning the strap connected with the engine was slack, and would not stop on the wheel. After tightening it he said to deceased and Gillon, "Now, lads, let's have this strap on." Deceased jumped upon a stage, which is about three feet higher than the wheel, and threw the strap over the wheel. The engine was standing at the time. He told deceased to be sure and. put it well over, so that it would not slip again, at the same time getting a knife out of his pocket to cut a piece of rope which he obteined. With this rope they put the strap on the wheel to keep it from slipping; and he (witness) got under the wheel to tie the rope. Whilst he was doing so, the deceased held the strap in its place. As soon as he had tied the rope he looked round to see where Gillon and the deceased were. Deceased was standing on the stage, which is used for putting salt into the fires when the ovens are being heated, and Gillon was against the steam valve. He asked deceased if he was "all riebt," and he replied "Yes." He then told Gillen to start the engine. The strap fell off the fly-wheel, and looking round he saw the deceased fast to the strap by one of his legs, and he was held against the upright. He got deceased in his arms and shouted for help to liberate him from the strap. A man named Ryan pent to his assistance, and he (witness) was unable to hold him longer as he was so affected by the accident. He had, of course, previously stopped the engine. A'man named Cawley was sent for the doctor, but it was seen that the head of the de- ceased was cut open and that he was dead. For a short time at first there was life in him, for his lips were moving as if he were in the act of praying. The strap was put on ten times a day sometimes, and the smallest lad could put it on.—The Coroner: I hope he doesn't, though. Patrick O'Brien, of 4, Princes-street, labourer in connec- tion with the salt cake process, said the deceased was his nephew and lived with him. He was 18 years of age. He had only just come "across the water" from Ireland< and had been in these works three weeks, and a month in Liver- pool. He was at the works shortly after the accident. The deceased's head was badly crushed—all in pieces.—By the Coroner: He could not tell where the mistake was, and not being present he could not say if there was anything wrong 'with the strap. He did not know if anybody was in fault. —By Mr. Richmond: The engine drives the Hargreaves' patent. He used re. help to put the strap on.—Mr. Rich- mond: Who did you help to put it on—boys or men? Boys ' and men, as it happened.—Answering the Coroner, witness said Gharghan was on one turn and he was on the other.— Mr. Richmond: Is the fly-wheel open to the stage? Yes.— Has it got no protection at all? No.—Mr. Ireland here interposed, and said the engine was a vertical one. The witness Gharghan was then re-called, and cross- examined by the Coroner. He said ha was unable to tell how the accident occurred as he could not see the stage at the time. He did not think he went round the wheel more than once. He knew he (deceased) came under the wheel. He must have slipped, and became entangled in the strap. Answering Mr. Richmond, he said the strap was on the shaft, and the deceased's leg between the strat and the shaft. Nicholas Gillon, 32, Eleanor-street, said he minded the engine, and gave evidence in substance similar to that of the foreman Gharghan. He stated he could not see whether the deceased was carried round the wheel or not.—Cross- examined by Mr. Richmond, he said he was 17 years of age, and had sole charge of the engine. He could not say at what speed the engine was going at the time of the accident. When the wheel began to move the strap came off. He did not know the horse-power of the engine. The bottom of the wheel is about 24 feet from the floor, and the wheel is about 54 feet in diameter.—Mr. Richmond: Did you put more steam on on this occasion than commonly? No. We just put as much on as will start the engine.—How do you start it? By a little wheel.—The Coroner: So that you can put the steam on quite gently—as slowly as you like? Yes. Mr. Ireland asked if he could give any'explanation of the occurrence. He stated that so far as he could learn the deceased got on the stage to put the belt on, and as soon as he had done that it was his duty to come away from it. It appeared that he had put his foot over on the strap or against the wheel—he could not say which and no one appeared to knew. The deceased could not have travelled a fourth of the distance round the shaft because as soon as the belt came round it would relieve his foot, and he would come down on the man's shoulder who was standing under- neath.—The Coroner: Where has the mistake been? I cannot understand.—Why has it happened when it should not have happened? He should have come away altogether. He had no business there.—Ah, that is not his fault. He is a lad. Why did Gharghan leave the lad in the wrong place? Gharghan and the other witness did not tell us as you have done, but said everything had been done properly. —Witness said if he had been putting the strap on he should have put it on, and then told the deceased to go away. The other witnesses were far more accustomed to it than he (witness) was. Manch= had, been at the work about twelve months.— Mr. Richmond: Is there any rail or anything in front of the wheel? Well, you see it is not a place where anybody goes or ought to go.---What is the stage there for? To fire some furnace.---The fly-wheel then is properly open to the stage? Yes.—But you, as foreman know that fly wheels are obliged to be fenced? Yea ; arid if it were fixed near where men are at work we should have fenced it. We have fenced all such places. I went round with the inspector some few weeks ago. He pointed out what he wished to be done, and so far as I know it has been done. This fly wheel was not pointed out.—Mr. Richmond: No, but the Act of Parliament directs that all fly wheels shall be fenced, and you have a copy of the Act hung up.—The Coroner (smil- ing to Mr. Richmond): They will show those that are fenced no doubt readily, but I am afraid you will have to find the others for .yourself. It is human nature as well as chemical nature.—Witness said it was not considered neces- sary to fence the wheel, as the boy had no right to be there. —The Coroner: But the boy is sent by a man, and allowed to stay there. There has been some mistake somewhere.— Witness: If there had been a rail deceased would have been in a worse fix.—Mr. Richmond: It seems to me he must have gone down on the shaft. If it had been fenced there he could not have gene down. The Coroner, addressing the jury, remarked upon the great help which the presence and inquiries of the Factory Inepector had been to the jury. It was for the jury to say whether the death of the deceased had been the result ofj

accident, or whether blame was attached to any person. Had the foreman called the deceased away from the wheel, it was probable the accident would not have occurred; and now that attention had been called to the unpretected state of the fly wheel it would, perhaps, be fenced. At all events, the Inspector would have an opportunity of taking action in the matter. Mr. Hirst (a juryman) said there seemed to have been a great deal of mismanagement somewhere. It was a peculiar thing to send a young fellow who had only just come from Ireland, and been in the works a few -weeks, on a stage so close to a fly wheel, and thereby to lose his life in an in- stant. The Coroner : I don't see that there is anything you can call distinctly censureable. Mr. Hirst thought it was very censureable for the fore- man to send such a young fellow ignorant of the werk. The principal witness, too gave his evidence very evasively. The Coroner said the witness gave everything except the measurements of the wheel. Mr. Hirst stated that the fault of the accident lay with the foreman of the work. The Coroner: Yes; but do you mean to hang the fore- man? Mr. Hirst: Not in the least, sir; but he is deserving of censure. The Coroner suggested that a verdict of accidental death should be returned. It was for the jury to say whether any blame was attached to the foreman or not. The jury returned the •verdict suggested by the Coroner, and appended no remarks. ,The Coroner I think we shall be quite safe in leaving this matter in the hands of Mr. Richmond, who will no doubt look into it.
Mr. Richmond: Yes. Tho inquiry then concluded.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES CHEUICAL WORKS. –
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES CHEUICAL WORKS. -

The County Coroner, Mr. Driffield, held an inquest at the Wellington Inn, Widnes, on Wednesday, to inquire int() the circumstances attending the death of John Holden, a brakes- man, who was employed by Messrs. Gaskeli, Deacon and Co. About noon on Monday the deceased was engaged in shunting a wagon of lime, which was attached to an engine, and in doing so be stood on a buffer. In some inexplicable way he appeared to slip, and fell on to the metals. The wheel of the wagon went over his bead, which was severed from his body, and badly crushed. His arm was also terri- bly mutilated. Dr. McDonnell was sent for, but the unfor- tunate mm was, of course, then quite dead. The first witness called was

Ann Holden, of 37, Wellington-street, who stated the deceased was her husband, and 30 years of age. He hid been employed as a brakesman at the works of Messrs. Gaskell for about five years, and was accustomed to. the duties he had to perform, having been previously in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany. She knew of no fault on the part of anyone which could account for the accident. The deceased was wearing boots. • . _

John Beech, 10, New-street, West Bank, employed as a discharger at Messrs. Gaskell's works, deposed that on Mon- day morning he was discharging a wagon load of lime near the scene of the accident, which happened on tte cross- over road. An engine, pushing a wagon of limestone, was moving slowly, and on the left hand buffer of the wagon was sitting the deceased. Before the engine stopped the deceased jumped off the buffer, and in doing so overbalanced himself and fell backwards across the rails. The wheels of the wagon passed over him. Witness called out to the engine driver to stop, and went for help. The cross-over road was level. He did not know why the deceased wished to get off at that particular spat unless it was to move the points in order to turn the wagons into another siding. The engine was moving very slowly; not faster than he could waik, and he did not see it jolt Early that morning he saw the deceased, who seemed all right. In reply to Mr. Fowler (the foreman), witness said be believed the deceased was a very steady man. Richard Lee tha engine-driver, said he lived at 61, Oak- land-street, Widnes. When the accident happened they were going with a load of limestone from one part of the works to another, and they had only a few yards further to go when it occurred. The deceased rode on the buffer of the wagon for about 25 yards, but he could not tell whether 1 he was sitting or standing. He (witness) had to work according to the signals given him by the deceased, but no signal was given him on this occasion. He saw the front wheel of the wagon give a jump, and he instantly reversed the engine, alighted, and lifted the deceased from the metals on which he lay. The wheel had gone over his bead, which was crushed in a frightful manner, and lay on the 1 metals. He was quite dead. By the Coroner: There was nothing to show how he came to slip or fall. The only explanation he could give of the accident was that deceased must have slipped in getting off the wagon. It was against the orders of the works to ride on buffers in any way. After the accident the buffer was examined, and found to bear marks of the deceased's cor- duroy trousers, thus showing that he must have been in a sitting posture. He had cautioned the deceased abDut sitting on the buffer. - In reply to a juryman, witness said the deceased was quite sober. He had been working since six o'clock-on the morning of the accident. Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, who represented the firm, also stated deceased was a steady man. The Coroner then summed up, and the jury returned a , verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: TA_RPORLEY AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. PROPOSAL TO HOLD THE NEXT SHOW AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE TA_RPORLEY AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. PROPOSAL TO HOLD THE NEXT SHOW AT RUNCORN.

An adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Commissioners was to have been held on Wednesdayafternoon,to receive a depu- tation from the Tarporley Agricultural Society who propose to hold their next show at Runcorn. Only three members of the Board—Dr. Steele (chairman), Mr. Lake, and Mr. Wil- liams—put in an appearance at the appointed time, and quarter of an hour afterwards Mr. Handley presented him- self. Another member was still required to form a quorum, but after Mr. Barker reported that he had seen two members, one of whom could not and the other would not attend, the chairman said the members present would be glad to heat what the deputation had to say. The deputation consisted of Messrs. Keay, chairman of thesociety, Tarvin ; Steward, Chester; Cooke, Clayley Hall; Cheers, Barrow; Howcroft, Tarvin ; and J. Hall, Kingsley. Mr. KEAY said a short time ago the Tarporley Agricul- tural Society, met at Chester, and it was agreed to apply to the Commissioners to me if they would receiye n deputation in reference to the holding of the annual show of the society at Runcorn. After the courteous reply they had received from the chairman they were present that day to hear what the Commissioners could do for them in the way of assisting them with money and helping the proposal forward in every" Way. Perhaps Mr. Steward would be able to explain matters more fully. Mr. STEWARD said the society, in casting their eyes about for a site for holding the next show, thought Runcorn, lying as it did, just on the borders of the society's district, would be a very suitable place. They had held their annual show for the past few years at Crewe, Chester, and Tattenhall, and they thought this part of their district had been entirely neglected, and that they ought to hold a show in Runcorn. There had been a show held at Chester very recently, but there had been one at Runcorn for a number of years, and if the people of Runcorn would only hold out a friendly hand he was sure the Tarporley Agricultural Society would be glad to come there. The only requirements of the society were a field, and a local committee to collect subscriptions ; and he felt sure, from what he saw there when he endeav- oured to get the Cheshire Agricultural Society's show held at Runcorn, that at least £2OO could be easily obtained in the district. Runcorn seemed to him to be a very quiet place, and he thought it required waking rm. .(Laughter.) He was sure an agricultural show wou,id be the means of bring- ing hundreds—he might say thousands—of people into the town, and an enormous number of people could not go into tbe town without spending money and benefiting someone, and he thought hotel proprietors especially ought to support the proposition, inasmuch as people attending the show arrived the night before, and occupied their rooms. What he desired was that the chairman, at the next Board meeting, should ,ask the Commissioners to take the matter in hand. The CHAIRMAN : We shall not hold a Board meeting until next month.

Mr. STEWARD: We ought to hold the show at the end of September or beginning of October. The CHAIRMAN : Of course, the Commissioners can do nothing as a body, but they might help individually. Mr. COOKE remarked that they did not require a great deal of help. All the society asked for was a local fund towards fitting up the show yard. At Tattenhall last year they raised £lOO, and the society thought in a place like Runcorn something like that amount might easily be raised. There was no doubt it would be a capital show, and might be the means of doing much good in the neighbourhood. Mr. KEAY observed that the society had thought about Runcorn for some time as it was an excellent centre for a show.

The CHAIRMAN was very sorry the deputation had been received by so small a number of Commissioners. He ad- journed the meeting in order that there might be a full attendance of members to discuss the matter, but he was sorry he could riot give the deputation very much encourage- ment to hold their show in Runcorn. Last year or the year before, when they talked of having the Cheshire Society's show at Runcorn, they sent out about 200 post cards to people in the neighbourhood. but only about two persons attended. He should be very glad to subscribe to the fund in order to assist the society to carry out their object. Mr. HANDLEY said there was so much disappointment last year but one in the Cheshire Society's show not being held •in the town that there was great difficulty in getting a meet- ing last year. He felt sure if the Torporley Agricultural Society's show were held in Runcorn it would take well, for they had not had an agricultural show in the town for 18 or 19 years.
_ After a few further observations, Dr. STEELE promised to call a public meeting to consider the matter, and the deputAtion, after expressing their obliga- tion to Dr. Steele, withdrew.

Opinions differ as to the probable duration of the autumn session, but, taking into account all considerations as to the attitude of parties on the question of Parliamentary proce- dure, it is not expected that the autumn sitting will extend beyond four or five weeks.

div.head: EXAMINE sktuRDA y, AUGUST 19, 1882:
div.p: THE EXAMINE sktuRDA y, AUGUST 19, 1882:
ACTION AGAINST THE RUNCORN PROPERTY COMPANY.

In this action, which was heard on Thursday, at the Palatine Chancery Court, Liverpool, before Vice-Chancellor Bristowe, specific performance was sought of an agreement to lease certain land and buildings at Appleton-in-Widnes, and the facts were of a somewhat extraordinary character. IBy an agreement entered into on the 11th of February, 1879, the company agreed to lease the land in question to Charles Sayer, for 999 years, at 3d. per yard; and the same land Sayer shortly afterwards contracted to sub-lease to Edward Brotherton, at an improved rent of 4d. per yard. On a portion of the land Brotherton, in the spring of 1879, commenced the erection of six houses; and on these the company, on the 25th of April, agreed to lend Brotherton £350, the money to be advanced by weekly instalments as the buildings progressed. As security for the loan, the company took from Brotborton an equitable mortgage, pre- pared by the company's solicitor (Mr. Linaker), Brotherton and Sayer also joining in promissory notes for the several advances. The Joan was completed in July, 1879; and subsequently IBrotherton applied for and was granted by the company a further loan of £165 on other buildings which he partly erected on the land. The last-mentioned loan was obtained independently of Sayer, who did not join in the securities. At this time Mr. Beasley acted as Brotherton's solicitor, and he advanced from time to time considerable sums of money to Brotherton on security of the property. Notice of Beasley's charge was given to and acknowledged by the company, who thereupon refused to advance, and, in fact, never advanced any more money to Brotherton without the written authority of Beasley. In the month of February, 1880, an action was brought by the company against Brotherton and Sayer to recover the £350 and interest, and although judgment was obtained no step was ever taken to enforce it by execution against the property or otherwise. The £165, although then due, was not sued for. Subse- quently proceedings in bankruptcy were commenced by the company against Sayer, not only in respect of the £350 advance, but also in respect of the loan of £165, notwithstanding that Sayer had been no party to the raising of the last-menaioned sum. In the course of these proceedings it seems to have been proposed to Saver that he should grant the company a mortgage of Brotherton's properties to secure their Claims, and accord- ingly on the 24th of January, 1881, a mortgage prepared by the company's solicitor was executed by Sayer, an authority being at the same time obtained from Sayer to proceed to an immediate sale. The same day the company instructed their solicitor to sell the property, and an auction sale on the Bth of February following was forthwith adver- tised. On these transactions coming to the knowledge of Brotherton and Beasley, the present action was brought on the Bth February, 1881. The writ having been served upon the company's solicitor, the auction sale was not proceeded with; but notwithstanding that an injunction was claimed to restrain the defendants from parting with the property, the company sold it privately immediately afterwards to a Mr. Robert Wright, of Runcorn, to whom it was conveyed on the 25th February, 1881, for £725, it haying cost upwards of £1,400. A month later the company bought back the pro- perty for £730, a surrender being executed by Wright to the company's trustees on the 23rd March, 1881. The plaintiffs contended that the alleged sale and re-sale were a sham and fraudulent, and, therefore, sought to havethem set aside. The defendant company, on the other band, whilst admitting that the two transactions were substantially one, contended that they Were bona file, and it was sworn on their behalf, in answer to interrogatories, that the two purchases were carried out and the purchase-moneys paid in the usual way, and that Wright, although he obtained a profit of only £5 on selling back the property, paid the usual solicitor's costs. These statements, however, were not consistent with entries contained in the company's books and the solicitor's diary, from which it appeared that so far as Wright's purchase- money was concerned, that was paid to the company with money obtained by means of a cheque drawn for the pur- pose 1-oy the company on their own account in favour of one of their directors, the money being directly afterwards taken back, less the solicitor's costs, and replaced to the company's credit. The company's solicitor acted throughout for all parties. The plaintiffs in the action were Brotherton and Mr. Henry Bolland (in whom Beasley's interest had become vested), the defendants being Sayer and his trustee, Mr. T. H. Sheen ; the Property Company and their trustees, Messrs. John Simpson and John R. Ross. The substantial parties were, however, Mr. Bolland and, the company. The counsel for the plaintiffs were Mr. Rotch and Mr. W. R. Kennedy, of the Common Law Bar (instructed by Messrs. Morris and Howard Jones, of Liverpool, and Mr. T. Beasley, of Widnes), the company being represented by Mr. Snow and Mr. Walton, of the Common Law Bar (instructed by Messrs. Wright and Co., of Liverpool) ; Mr. Browne, representing Sayer and Sheen (instructed by Mr. J. C. Parkinson, of Liverpool). Mr.Rooke Pennington, solicitor, Bolton, also attended to watch the Case on behalf of Mr. Ross.

On the case coming on on Thursday morning, before the learned Vice-Chancellor, Mr. Rotch announced that terms had been arranged between the parties, subject to His Honour's approval, which would render it unnecessary for His Honour to be further troubled with the matter. These terms included the granting by the company of three leases of the land at 3d. per yard ground rent, and the usual pro- visious for redemption and the payment of costs of the action by the defendant company. His Honour assenting, an order was taken accordingly.
