.A RUN TO. THE SOUIR COAST. As soon as the summer sun breaks forth andthe foliage of the trees affords a shelter from its rays, as soon as the fields are verdant with the germinations of the newly sown seed and the roads are cleared of their months' mud, many persons weary of their winter quarters, become possessed of an ardent desire• to be "on the wing:" Troops of tramps then forsake familiar haunts in town and go "on circuit" through once lonely lanes, and the arrival of the first contingent of visitors gii,esto water-,1 ing places signs of life long unknown. .With the advance of summer piles of luggage obstruct the platforms of the railway stations, the trains become more crowded, and other means of locomotion are provided to accommodate the ever increasing number of persons who now make for pleasure and health resorts. The stream of excursionists reaches its height in the month of August, but why so many flock to the sea-side at this particular period has doubtless puzzled hotel and boarding-house keepers, as I once heard one of the latter say he did not know what there was in "this blessed month " that caused such num- bers of Lancashire people to le iv e home then. But the in- flux of visitors to watering places during August should be no puzzle after all. It is the month in which the weather is most settled,. the month in which occurs probably the best kept Bank Holiday, the month in which the " murders " on the moors commence, and the month in which the House of Commons takes its holiday. With the return of the time popularly regarded as the begin- ning of autumn, I began to think a change of air desirable, and cast about for a—to me—new path, and after some deliberation I decided this year to have a run to the south coast. By a "run " to the south coast Ido not mean to infer that I undertook one of those coaching, journeys so delightfully described by Dickens, or that I pro- pelled myself thither on a six-feet spider-like machine from Coventry, but that I proceeded to my destination drawn by an improved type of that wonderful invention of George Stephenson—the locomotive. Booking with an excursion advertised by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, and Great Northern Railway Companies, I left the War- rington Central Station a few days ago for Brighton, the popular resort of Londoners. The train was to time and was [soon speeding through the well-stocked gardens which supply Manchester with fruits and vegetables on its way to Stockport, where a brief stoppage Was made. On the train resuming its course we caught a glimpse of the. picturesque hills and dales of Derbyshire, which excited the admiration of my two German companions, who were pro- ceeding to Fatherland via Hull. At Godley Junction I quitted the train, and before the arrival of the Manchester express formed the acquaintance of a gentleman whotn I noticed on the platform at Warrington, and with whom I journeyed some distance. Soon after leaving Godley we reached far-famed Sheffield, one portion of which was enveloped' in smoke as dense as that of St. Helens and Widnes. From Sheffield we proceeded to Ret- ford in Nottinghamshire, where we joined the Great Northern main line, which runs through a fine agricultural district to the metropolis. At length the cold, grey clouds, through which the sun had hitherto sent fitful gleams, dispersed, and were replaced by fleecy ones and an azure sky from which the sun shone in all its summer splendour, giving an additional charm to the interesting scenery. Since leaving Lancashire verdant plots of potatoes and slate-coloured cabbages had alternated with fields of rapidly-ripening cereals, stretches of luxuriant russet hay grass, and newly-mown meadows of emerald brightness; but now the hay fields became less frequent, and the tracts of corn, growing more extensive and of a more' golden hue, sparkled in the Ban light as the grain bent beneath the gentle breeze. The hills had long ago been left behind, and we steamed terough an undulating plain along the border of the fens. After quitting Newark, the place which has the honour of being Mr. Gladstone's first constituency, we found ourselves at Grantham, re- nowned for the manufacture of labour-saving agricultural implements, and were soon again on our way for Peter- 'borough, a city frequently mentioned in the early history of our country. The clean red bricks and tiles of the houses in the towns and villages skirting the railway, afforded a pleasant contrast to the dirty exterior of the dwellings in manufacturing towns, and the country had an air of repose and solitude quite refreshing to those who spend the greater portion of their lives amid the bustle and excitement of northern towns. On went the train, but at length it pulled up at Peter- borough, where my companions alighted, and I was left to make the rest of the journey to London alone. After travelling in the confined area of a railway carriage for four and a half hours, it was a relief to he able to alight for five minutes and stretch one's legs on the platform, calmly watching the rush for refreshments and the bustle attendant on the arrival of an express train. At last the time as up, the bell rang, porters exercised their lungs in itrviting dilatory passengers to retake their seats, there was a general. hanging of carriage doors, the guards whistled, the driver responded, and we were off once more. For the next hour and a half the train ran past quiet homesteads, conspicuous by their lime washed walls; by villages hidden in the trees, whose presence was only revealed by the tell-tale church tower or steeple which rose against the sky; across fussy streams, hurrying to mingle with mightier waters, reflecting the vegetation upon their banks, and here and there a lover of the gentle art practising in shady nooks. The train dashed along at an accelerated speed, scaring flocks of crows that took to their wings only to alight at the same spot 1 when the affrighting thing had passed; station followed station in quick succession; and presently we approached , pleasano - situated villa residences, then rows of , neat looking houses, and the recurring name of a city firm of house furnishers, whose advertisement was seen as often as Lewis's in Liverpool, told us we were draw- ing nigh the at once wealthiest and 'pooreat city in the world ; and in a few minutes we found ourselves at the King's Cross terminus. I immediately made for the city, and in the coutse of half-an-hour was in the midst of "the I eager, anxious throng, which- moves with busy haste along" Fleet-street, where I took up my abode for a brief period, during which I visited some of bite sights of London. After spending a day in the metropolis I proceeded to the Victoria Station of the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway, and resumed my journey soutk. The route lay through a well wooded, picturesque tract of country, resonant with the whir Of mowing machines at work in the ripened fields of corn which adorned the hills of chalk, and looked at their best in the morning sun. Hurrying down deep cuttings and , through long tunnels, in one of which I was reminded Lefroy perpetrated what was known as the Brighton tragedy, the train ultimately came to a stand at Brighton, probably the most populous watering place on the south coast. At the beginning of the eighteenth century, says Macaulay's history, "Brighton was described as a place which had once been thriving, which had possessed many small fishing harks, and which had, when at the height of prosperity, contained about two thousand inhabitants, but which was ' fast sinking into decay. The sea was gradually gaining on the buildings,which at length almost entirely disappeared. Ninety years ago the rains of an old fort were to be seen iyina among the pebbles and seaweed on the beach, and ancient men could still point out the traces of foundations on a spot where a street of more than a hendred huts had been sWallowed up by the waves: 'So desolate was the

div.head: DANGEROUS NUISANCE AT RUNCORN,
div.p: THE DANGEROUS NUISANCE AT RUNCORN,

For a number of weeks past the inhabitants of Runcorn have suffered from a most sickening nuisance, of which general complaint has been made, and understand that a memorial, signed by about 20 inhabitants, was on Thursday presented to the Board of Commissioners. It was afterwards considered at the meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee. At the outset the memorial complained of the nuisauce, which was alleged to proceed from a certain works on the Sprinch, and observed that since their erection the fountain stream, which is believed to pass under the works, had become so polluted as to ba unfit for drinking or culinary purposes, thereby inflicting considerable hardship on the surrounding neighbourhood. The smell from the works, the memorial went on to say, WitS so intolerable that the houses in the streets surrounding the works were fast becoming depopulated, as the occupants were seeking a more salubrious atmosphere. The rnt.morialis,s prayed the Commissioners to exercise the powers vested in them by the 114th section of the Public Health Act, 1875, for the speedy abatement of the nuisance. The Commissioners,we are informed, bad a long discussion on the matter, and eventually decided to place the memorial before the proprietors of the works, as the expression of an influential section of the in- habitmts, in the hope that they will abate the nuisance without the Commissioners having reeJurse to their powers possessed under the Public Health Act.

div.head: SUPPOSED MURDER OF A RUNCORN
div.p: SUPPOSED MURDER OF A RUNCORN
MAN,

During the present week there has been considerable sensation in Runcorn consequent upon a rumour that a young man named Thomas Cliffe, belonging to Runcorn, had been murdered at South Shields. The Facts that have transpired show that Cliffe, who was a fireman on board the S.S. Haworth Castle, of Sunderland, had a quarrel with an Arab named Hesson, who is now in custody, on Monday ni4ht. ‘Vhile they were drinking together in a public-house the Arab called the deceased a foul name, upon which he said he would not allow that, and struck prisoner with his fist, and he, the prisoner, returned the blow. Another man named John Barber who belonged to the same vessel, parted them, and put Cliffe outside and requested Hesson to go on board. The Same night, between eleven and twelve o'clock, Barber heard the Arab come en board the Haworth Castle, and also heard him mutter something about a knife, and that he would "kill the trimmer." Afterwards Cliff's body nas found in the middle dock by an inspector of the river police with a slice of saveloy in his hand. It is averred by some that deceased, who was seen walking unsteadily in the direction of the dock, might have fallen over and thus come by his death. The two men were on bad terms all through the voyage. On Wednesday morning the prisoner was again brought before the magistrates. The result of the inquest was stated. There was no evidence offered against Hessen, and he was formally discharged. The young man, Cliffe, is well known in Runcorn. He was for some time an infantry soldier, but had not served in any action. His parents are very respectable people, and the sad end of their son is much to be regretted.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

A meeting of the Library Committee was held at the Public Offices, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Dr. McDouv.:all (chairtntn), Messrs. Handley, Friar, I Riley, Hazlehurst, Brookes (secretary), and Jones (librarian). The Secretary was instructed to forward the thanks of the committeito Superintendent Williamson for his kindness in marshalling the procession on the day of opening the library. Accounts amounting to £36 183. 7d. were passed for payment. It was resolved that the hours at which the library be open should be as follows :—Tuesday, 7 D.M I 9 30 p.m.; Saturday, 2 p.m. to 4 p.m ,and 6 p.m. to 9-30 p.m. In consequence of the press of borrowers on those two nights, and the resulting inconvenience, it was decided to ask the Commissioners to allow the committee the use of the Board room every Thursday night. Twenty volumes selected by the librarian from the library of Camden IWesleyan Sunday School, were ordered to be purchased for the sum of 6d. each. The librarian presented the following report :—Number of books issued during July, when the library was open six times, 837, classed as follows :—Theo- logy, 25; political economy, tc., 9; history, travels, biography, 13; science and art, 44; poetry and the drama, 14: prose fiction, 534; miscellaneous, 48. There had been pres,nted during the month, Topography of England (16 vols.), by Mr. J. R. Frith ; National Register for 1810. by Mrs. Rogers; pamphlets, Sze., written and presented by the Rev. Wm. Preston, M.A.; Plutarch's Lives, by Mr. Wm. Handley; Epistles of Grotious, Mr. H. Sefton; Spectator, (8 vols.) Mr. A. CampLell ; Memorials of Liverpool, Sir James A. Picton ; the Catalogue (2 vols.) of the Liverpool Free Library, by the committee.—The thanks of the com- mittee were tendered to the donors. A discussion arose as to the decision of the Commissioners with regard to the public offices, and it was ultimately decided, on the motion of Mr. Hazlehurst, seconded by Mr. Riley, that the follow- irg letter 'should be forwarded to the chairman of the Board ;

div.head: LATEST NEWS. THE WAR IN Eaff-
div.p: LATEST NEWS. THE WAR IN Eaff-
TROOPS RE-EMBARKING: THE GUARDS GOING TO
ABOUKIR.s

wawa mrrespondent telegraph big from Alexan- dra at 9-15 a.m. yesterday says :—" A force composeu ea the Guards, the Household Cavalry, the 60th and 46th Regiments and a company of Engineers, arrived here from Ramleh this morning, and embarked in the harbour. Their destination is officially given out to be Aboukir. The fleet is prepared to leave." At 11-15 a.m, the same correspondent says :—" Almost the whole of the British force here is now embarking in the transports, only three regiments remaining as garrison. I leave this afternoon with the troops for the front, and hope soon to send news of our doings. The Egyptian Monarch and two other transports have arrived." An Exchange telegram from Alexandria at 11.30 a.m, is as follows:—" The troops are now embarking, and the fleet and transports sailing with sealed orders."

div.head: ARRANGING FOR THE BATTLE.
div.p: ARRANGING FOR THE BATTLE.

A Reuter's telegram from Alexandria at 11.30 a.m. yester- day is as follows:—" Various military movements are in progress to-day. The Guards division and the 60th Rifles marched in from Ramleh early this morning, and are now embarking. The troops of the second division are taking their places, and march out ta Ramleh to-day. The Man- chester Regiment lands to-day, and will take over the police duty in the town, relieving the Berkshire Regiment, which joins Geoeral Sir Evelyn Wood's brigade at Ramleh. The Berkshire and South Staffordshire Regiments will occupy the barracks. The Gordon and Cameron Highlanders are also going to Ramleh to form the nucleus of Sir Archibald Alison's Highland Brigade, and will encamp near the sea- shore, in the position vacated by the 46th Regiment."

div.head: THREATENING ATTITUDE OF THE SULTAN.
div.p: THREATENING ATTITUDE OF THE SULTAN.

A Constantinople telegram says :—"The Sultan, relying on Russian support, is disposed to send a force to Egypt, independent of England, in direct defiance of the warnings he is said to have received from Lord Dufferin that no such steps will be permitted. It is denied that certain Turkish officers..bave returned home on leave from-their regiments, which for the past week have been lying in Suda Bay."

EXPECTED INVASION OF TURKISH TERRITORY. A Times telegram says :—There is a belief at Erzerdum that Russia is about to occupy the whole of Asia Minor up to the Bosphorus, and seeing the undefended state of that part of the Ottoman Empire, it is thought that the troops of the Czar could easily do this without much bloodshed. Such an occupation, say the Turks at Erzeroum, would be the complete downfall of the Turkish Empire, as a continuation of its existence in Europe, in view of the insignificance of its Turkish popula- tion there, would be impossible. Whatever ideas, however, the Russian Government may entertain, they are a complete mystery even to the best informed part of the Russian Press.

The Daily Telegraph Paris correspondent says,—" It has for some time past been no secret that Russia has been con- centrating a formidable army in the Caucasus, with a view, it is believed, to another invasion of Turkish territory. The Cologne Gazette declares that Russia has in the Caucasus a grand total of 78,000 men. A Paris journal expresses the opinion that Russia is preparing for another war with Turkey by way'of compensation for England's occupation of Egypt. Commenting on this statement, the Soir says this evening :—Russia's attitude must be carefully watched, for perhaps from that quarter the final difficulties will come. We have already drawn attention to the concentration of troops in the southern provinces. The Vienna Allenteine Zeitung publishes a telegram from St. Petersburg of a report current at Erzeroum according to which Russia purposes to occupy Anatolia. It has been announced lately from different quarters that Russia was concentrating treops in the Caucasus.
The Duke and Duchess of Albany visit Glasgow early in Septmber. _

bn Thursday night Mr. Trevelyan arrived in Londonderry by special train, on a visit to Sir Edward Reid. The gunboat Bullfinch, at Chatham, is to be used for experiments with a new torpedo, said to be superior to all others.

A Special train, conveying Her Majesty's Ministers, arrived at Portsmouth at 11 30 yesterdey morning, and the party embarked for Osborne immediately. Colonel Gordon, who succeeds Major-General Clarke as Commandant of the School of Military Engineering, Chat- ham, took over the commandyesterday morning. At the Westminster Police-court, yesterday, Alfred Mille, plasterer, of Knightsbridge, was remanded on a charge of stabbing his wife. The injured woman deposed that the prisoner Cagle home the worse for drink and asked her for money. She did not comply and he then took up the knife and, threatening to settle her, stabbed her in the arm and hands severely. The charges against a number of gentlemen for being present at a cock fighting exkibition near Althrey Hall, Flintshire, will be heard to-day. Great interest is taken in the proceedings,-and. it is stated that cock fighting has been very 'extensively carried on in the district for a long time past. In obedience to the request from Mr. Parnell, Mr. Mooney, president of the Land League in America, telegraphed on Thursday to that gentleman, stating that the Central Land League Association of Philadelphia has passed a resolution discountenancing any such scheme to send either men or money to Arabi. Mrs. and Miss Gladstone, accompanied by Mr. Herbert Gladstone, left London for Spithead yesterday morning for a cruise in Lord Wolverton's yacht. The Prime Minister will join them this afternoon, and the cruise will extend to ten days, when Mr. Gladstone will return to town for a few days prior to visiting Flawarden. Late on Thursday night James Buir...ock, a well-known farmer in Pendle Forest, succumb2d to injuries received on Monday night. He was returning home about ten o'clock on Monday night with his horse and trap, and when in a dark portion of the road he came into collision with a fence and was thrown out. He died from concussion of the brain. The road was asphalted at this point. THE TRIMUON GRANGE COLLIERY EXPLOSION.

The report of Mr. Snagge to the Home Office on the Trinadon Grange colliery explosion, in February last, when sixty-nine persons were killed, was issued yesterday. Mr. Snagge says there is no room for doubt thai, the explosion was caused by the diffusion of a sudden outburst of gas, foi•ced towards the working face by a heavy fall of roof, and further that the Davy lamp affords no security against the occurrence of similar disasters. THE FEVER EPIDEMIC AT ACCRINGTON.

Another fatal case of scarlet fever occurred at Accrington yesterday morning, making seven during the. week and 22 since the beginning of the month. There have been three deaths in one house, and in several instances two of a family have succumbed to the epidemic. No new cases had been reported yesterday morning up to eleven o'clock, but two fresh outbreaks were reported on Thursday. THE GOVERNMENT AND THE IRISH NATIONAL

div.head: PARTY.
div.p: PARTY.

The several speeches delivered by members of the Irish National party in Dublin since the sentence on Mr. Gray• for contempt of curt have occupied the attention of the Castle authorities, and it is understood that law officers of the Crown have been requested to express an opinion upon them, with the vidw to a decision being arrived at as to whether action should be taken thereon. A CONVALESCENT HOSPITAL FOR BOLTON.

Twelve years ago, Mr. Stephen Blair, bleacher, Bolton, left £30,000 for the erection and endowment of a hospital for the town. The Charity Commissioners have just issued a notice, directing that a sum, not exceeding £20,000, be appropriated by the trustees, to the erection hnd furnishing of a convalescent hospital at Turton, and that the income derivable from the investment of the remainder of the bequest, be applied to the maintenance of the hospital.

div.head: BURGLARY AT A MINISTER'S HOUSE.
div.p: BURGLARY AT A MINISTER'S HOUSE.

The Hanley magistrates yesterday morning committed George Frost, of Bedford, for trial on a charge of breaking into the house of the Rev. Mr. Herne, Congregational minister, and stealing a number of silver spoons, plate alai other articles, a week ago, whilst the prosecutor and his family were at the seaside. The prisoner is said to be a notorious housebreaker and has been for some time past wanted by the police authorities for breaking into a house at Stoke-on-Trent. LARGE HAUL OF POACHED SALMON.

John M'Grath, fisherman, liandbridge, Chester, was sum- moned at Chester Police Court yesterday morning for salmon fishing during the close tims on Suuday. A water bailiff employed by the Dee Board Conservators saw M`Grath come from the river with a bag. M'Grabh ran away, leaving a bag containing no less than 13 poached salmon. This being the prisoner's second offence he was fined £5 and costs, or one month's hard labour.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAY.

Their Lordships assembled at half-past two, by which hour several ladies occupied seats in the House. The Lord Chancellor awl the other Royal Commissioners in their scarlet robes having taken their seats in front of the throne, the Commons were summoned. On the arrival of the Speaker, the Royal assent was given to the "Appropriation Bill" and several other measures. The Commons then returned, and their Lordships adjourned until Tuesday, October 24th.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAi. The Speaker entered the House at 2-20 p.m., but there not being the necessary quorum present, he did not take the chair until twenty minutes to three, when the Deputy Usher of the Black Rod entered, and summoned the House to the House of Peers to hear the Royal assent given to several bills. The 113eaker, in compliance with the summonses, then proceeded to the House of Peers, followed by Mr. Childers, the Marquis of Harrington, Sir W. Harcourt, and other members present. At three o'clock th 3 Speaker returned to the House, and announced that Her Majesty had signified her assent to the" Appropriation Bill" and several other bills. Mr. Biggar then put a question to Mr. Childers relative to Lieut. Ferrer, of the Grenadier Guards, which the right hon. gentleman s.tid he could not answer; the notice given not being sufficient for him to make inquiry. The House then adjourned till Tuesday, October 24th.

COWLEY'S MIDDLE SCHOOL.—These Schools will be OPENED for tuition on MONDAY the 9th OCTOBER N. E. J. SIMPSON. M.A., Trinity College, Cambridge, Head- master of Hinckley Grammar School, has been appointed Head Master of the boy's school, and Miss Kate Jurgenson, L.L.A., Andrews, late assistant mistress at Norwich High School, Head Mistress of the girls' rchool. Tuition fees : boys, £8 per annum: girls, £7 per annum; entrance fee, £l. To enable the governors to determine the number of assistant masters and mistresses required, intending pupils are requested t ) apply for admission to the schools without delay. Applications for ad- mission must be made on forms to be obtained from me, the undersigned. Pupils applying for admisstm before the 7th September next, will not be charged the entrance fee of £l. No boy or girl uncir 8 years adnaittel. The examinaticn for admission will be held at the schools on Thursday, the sth day day of October next, the following being the standard. Read- ing simple narrative, writing text hand, sums in the first rules of arithmetic with the multiplication table. THOMAS BREWIS, Clerk to the Governors. Town Hall, St. Helens, 10th August, 1882.
